# Native-simulator formal model

This directory contains the first machine-checked refinement slice shared by
the x86-64 and AArch64 native simulators. Run it with:

```sh
lake build && make check
```

The build comes first: 20 of the 306 modules enter only through the gate's
own `lake env lean` lines, which elaborate without writing an object file, so
a tree that has not been built leaves the checkers reading a partial set.

What the gate currently covers, measured from one full `make check` run:
248 passing `cross-check: OK` oracle banners summing to 124,531,802 modeled
cases; 138 `*_spec.json` contracts, each rendered into exactly one generated C
header and one `Generated*.lean` module (138/138/138); 306 Lean modules
compiling transitively from the gate's roots and proving 2,065 theorems with
no `sorry`, no `axiom`, and no `opaque`/`unsafe`/`partial` definitions --
all six enforced by `check_no_sorry.py`, which fails the gate on a `sorry`,
an `admit`, or an `axiom`/`opaque`/`unsafe`/`partial` declaration; 488 of
those (23%) are discharged by `native_decide`, i.e. by compiled evaluation, so
they rest on the compiler as well as the kernel — 20 of the 609
refinement-named theorems, each a finite-table equality, and the rest finite
enumerations or concrete examples, never a compositional or arithmetic
obligation. The new access-window theorems are `bv_decide`/`omega`
obligations over `Nat`, not `native_decide`, so the share moved by only the two
concrete threshold examples per ISA. Two
consecutive full runs produce byte-identical output (same md5), so the gate is
deterministic. The 330 `build/mut_*.py` batteries are the evidence that each
banner can fail, and are untracked by design; the fourteen route hosts those
batteries drive are pinned into the recipe so their cases are enforced by the
gate itself rather than only by the batteries.
The remaining unbuilt sources under `build/` are scratch, not coverage: 41 are
ad-hoc probes (`nb*.c`, `onebar*.c`, which even suppress `-Warray-bounds`),
and the two large ones are stale copies — `dbg_host.c` is
`btmem_index_route_host.c` plus a debug `fprintf`, and `wprobe.c` is
byte-identical to the gated `test_x86_write_width_arm_route_host.c`. Both
duplicates emit the same banner and case count as the gated host, so adding
them would double-count rather than extend coverage.

That total is reproducible rather than a one-off reading: re-deriving it from a
fresh `make check` log by parsing every `cross-check: OK (...)` banner yields
124,531,802 again, so the rollup is a measurement of the committed tree and not
a stale note. The 248 banners are all distinct oracles — 247 report a plain
`N cases` and one (the `imul` flags oracle) reports
`15 vectors + 20000 sweep cases`, so the total must be summed with that
oracle's own shape rather than a single regex over `N cases`.

The per-step `census N -> N+1` counter is a running tally of harness
increments, not a count of the files on disk, and the two have drifted: 330
`build/mut_*.py` files exist, the counter's last value is 632, and 534 steps
record an explicit `+1`. The drift is narrative, not coverage — 46 harnesses
are never named in any step entry, but 37 of them drive a tracked `test_*.c`
host that `make check` runs, so their contracts are gated even though their
provenance was never written down. The census should be read as "how many
harness increments the log has recorded", not as a file total.

The stack-window memory-safety gap in both simulators is now closed rather
than recorded as open. A stack access resolves to an index near the end of the
frame arena without any check that the whole access window fits: a 64-bit
access at the arena's last byte needs eight bytes, so it touches memory past
the array. On x86-64 the byte-ladder arm performed that window lane by lane
through `b[index + 7]`, and the lane predicate is a runtime value so the
compiler could not bound `index`; on AArch64 the access went through
`KPROG_ARM64_LOAD_BYTES`, which walks the same eight bytes. AddressSanitizer
reproduced both on the previous baseline: a 64-bit read at the final byte
reported `stack-buffer-overflow` in either simulator.

The bound is now part of the generated arena contract, not a hand-written
check. `arm64_stack_arena_spec.json` and `x86_stack_arena_spec.json` gained
`window_guard: index_plus_bytes_le_capacity`, so both generators emit
`KPROG_{ARM64,X86}_STACK_WINDOW_END` and `KPROG_*_STACK_WINDOW_FITS`, with
the comparison widened to 64 bits so an access near the top of the index space
is measured instead of wrapping. `Arm64StackArena.lean` and
`X86StackArena.lean` restate the bound independently and prove it refines the
generated form, that a fitting window's last byte is inside the arena, that an
access at the arena's final byte does not fit, and the concrete thresholds:
152/8/160 fits and 153/8/160 does not on AArch64; 56/8/64 fits and 57/8/64
does not on the default x86-64 frame, with the 128-byte deep frame at
120/121.

A fourth stack path carries pointers rather than accesses, and needed the
weaker of the two bounds. `ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_PTR` / `X86_SIM_L_STACK_PTR`
hand out `&b[index]` for a stack-pointer register, and an 8-byte write through
a pointer at index 168 of the 160-byte arena escapes the array — ASan
reproduces it. The bound is not the window's: `&b[index]` is well defined up
to and including the one-past-end index, so the contract fixes
`INDEX <= CAPACITY` and nothing more, which the hand modules prove strictly
weaker than the window bound for a nonempty window. That asymmetry is why the
two helpers carry separate checks, and the generated comparison is a single
test on the 64-bit index so a negative index fails it rather than folding a
branch away. Several hosts had been driving pointers outside the arena, which
the bound then rejected — the arm64 helper-argument sweep ran to index 248 of a
160-byte arena, its arena sweep to 192, and the x86 lea and mov sweeps had no
in-range row at all on the stack arm; those sweeps now carry their own in-range
sets, which is why the gate's case total moved.

The same defect sat in the two condition evaluators, which is how it got
found: a parameter used as an operand of `==` or `&&` takes whatever binds
tighter from the caller. `KPROG_ARM64_EVAL_COND(ARM64_COND_GT, p || q, ...)`
evaluated `(p || q == V)` as `p || (q == V)`, giving `GT = 1` where the answer
is `0`, and the mirror case gave `0` where the answer is `1`. Both evaluators
now emit `(N)`; their Lean output is unchanged.

`check_macro_hygiene.py` checks all 142 headers the simulators compile -- 138
generated and the 4 hand-written x86/AArch64 ones -- on every gate run, and is
itself verified against the pre-fix text, so the class cannot return quietly.

The five x86 flag generators emitted their C operands unparenthesized, so a
compound argument silently changed the parse. `KPROG_X86_SET_SUB_FLAGS(..., a & mask,
b, ...)` expanded `(A < B)` to `(a & mask < b)`, which C parses as `a & (mask < b)`
-- carry computed from the wrong comparison, `0` where the answer is `1`. The
simulator happened to pass only plain variables at every call site, so nothing
was wrong today, but the generated contract was a trap for the next caller.
All five now emit `(A)`; the Lean output is byte-identical, since the fix
touches only the C path.

Step 0490 proved the one flag that differs in meaning, which raises the
question the branches depend on: do the two condition vocabularies decide the
same way? Under the correspondence `(N Z C V) = (SF ZF (!CF) OF)` they do, on
all 14 comparable conditions, and the mapping is not the one the names suggest
--- `CS` maps to `AE`, not `B`; `CC` to `B`; `MI` to `S`; `HI` to `A`; `LS` to
`BE`. Inverting any one is the classic condition-inversion bug and it
typechecks, so the mapping is a function with an agreement theorem rather than
a hand-written table, and injectivity is proved so no two AArch64 conditions
collapse onto one x86 condition. `AL` is separated out: it is unconditional,
so it is a lowering question rather than a flag one. Inverting `CS` breaks
three theorems, and the differential oracle catches it at the C layer on 16
cases.

Not every cross-ISA difference is a drift, and the carry flag is the case that
shows the difference between the two kinds. AArch64 sets `C` after a
subtraction to *not-borrow* (unsigned `lhs >= rhs`, so `CMP` then `B.HS` means
"no borrow"); x86-64 sets `CF` to *borrow* (`lhs < rhs`, so `JB` means
"borrow"). Each is proved against its own independent statement, but nothing
related them, so a reader comparing the specs saw `>=` against `<` with no way
to tell an architectural difference from a mistake in one of them.
`CrossIsaFlags.lean` proves they are exact complements on the same narrowed
operands at every width, with witnesses in both directions (`1 - 2` borrows,
`2 - 1` does not), so the disagreement is polarity and not value.

Whether the compiled side is actually guarded is measurable, and `mutate_contracts.py`
measures it: find the first meaningful literal in each generator's emitted-C
string, bump it, regenerate, and see what fires. Of the **138** generators that
exist, 29 are guarded -- **24 rejected by the generator itself**, 3 caught by a
host, 2 stopped by the compiler -- and **none survive**. The other 109 emit no
bump-able literal: 60 of them do write numeric constants into their headers,
but read the values from a spec JSON and interpolate them, so only a change to
that data reaches them, and 47 write no numeric constant at all. Stating the
denominator is the point; an earlier version reported only the 31 it happened
to reach, and counted two generators whose mutation changed no byte of C as
though no host existed to call them.

Getting the count honest took several passes. Four literals first looked like
contracts nothing caught and were inert -- a docstring, a static-assert
message, a Python format-padding width, and a generator diagnostic prefix --
and the harness excludes all four, which is what makes the zero mean something.

Complemented OR is the last of the twelve, and the one whose *second source
is modified before use*: the dispatcher applies the AUX-encoded shift or
rotate-extend modifier to the second source and passes the modified value in.
A model oracle feeding the contract an unmodified operand therefore exercises
only modifier kind 0 -- the identity -- and cannot see a fault in the other
four. The oracle drives all five kinds at both widths, recomputing the modifier
from its definition, and asserts a non-identity kind was exercised so the run
is not vacuous. An off-by-one in shift-left fails 78 cases; dropping the
complement fails 595.

That host's first version repeated the very gap this sequence keeps finding:
its docstring listed five macros as covered -- call, return, subroutine return,
subroutine jump and subroutine conditional jump -- and the body called two. The
other three now run, and driving the conditional one in *both* directions
mattered: the first version used only a condition that happened to hold and so
passed with the conditional degraded to an unconditional jump. Adding the
falsifying case makes that fault fail.

Step 0525's finding had a residue: the *family* theorem that composes the
per-opcode refinements still carried the three operand-narrowing hypotheses that
step had shown to be unnecessary. So the composed statement still displayed a
precondition no caller satisfies, even though each individual refinement had
been fixed. It now composes the raw variants and carries none -- statement and
code agree, raw registers in and narrowed result out. No host or theorem
referenced the old name, so the rename was a clean cutover.

The same question asked of the second architecture gives the opposite answer,
and it is worth recording rather than assuming either way: its memory-load oracle
already drives the composition under both ABI kinds at all four offsets, so its
second context was genuinely covered. Verified before believing the docstring --
planting an offset fault is rejected by a static assertion at compile time, and
mis-tagging the data offset is caught at run time. The coverage check now
includes entry contexts: for each architecture every ABI kind must appear in
some host, verified against the pre-0535 state by removing the new host and
watching it report exactly the gap that step closed.

The *entry contexts* are a surface nobody had looked at: every host declares
its own simulator state by hand and every one hard-codes the XDP ABI kind, so the
SKB entry appeared in no host at all. It is not a synonym for XDP -- the packet
pointers sit at offsets 208 and 80 rather than 0 and 8 -- and the `abi_load`
contract branches on the kind and the offset together, so reading an SKB context
through the XDP arm labels packet pointers as scalars: every address right, only
the provenance wrong, which is what the tag exists to catch. The host drives
both contexts, checks each field's tag, and asserts that the two disagree at
each other's offsets.

Writing it also exercised the composition checker from Step 0500: calling the
`abi_load` contract directly was flagged as testing a contract without the
simulator's path to it, so the host now drives the memory-read composition and
runs the tag selection as well. A check written 35 steps earlier caught a gap in
a host written afterwards.

The second architecture's helper surface is much smaller -- seven macros -- and
none of those was executed either, for the same reason. What differs is
instructive: on the first architecture eighteen of sixty-one forward to a real
toolchain call, while here only one of seven does; the three `get_*` helpers
write a constant zero, which is what they return in the model's kernel. My first
version asserted a forward for all four and reported three failures that were
the tree being right. The map helpers are checked for both the returned pointer
and its map-value tag, a correct address with the wrong tag being as wrong as a
wrong address.

The helper-call bodies are the largest unexecuted surface of all: 61 macros,
one per helper the simulator recognises, and no host in the tree mentioned any
of them. Running them takes one non-obvious step, because the toolchain's helper
header declares each as a `static ... const` function pointer initialised to the
helper *id* rather than an address -- so a call jumps to address 5 and faults,
measured. Renaming the eighteen forwarding pointers before including the
simulator header, and defining them under their original names, makes the bodies
run. All 61 are then checked for being callable and for writing `x0`, and the
eighteen forwarding arms for reaching their target the expected number of times
-- a count per *call site*, since three macros share a target.

The second architecture's surface is larger and had the same history. It models
a real call/return pair through the stack where the first uses a link register,
so CALL decrements the stack pointer and stores the return address, and the
subroutine return reads it back and increments -- a pair that disagreed would
corrupt the pointer and return through a stale word while any address-only check
still passed. The host checks the decrement, the stored word, the read back, the
restore, control transfer and the round trip.

Two details cost time and are recorded: the modelled arena indexes at
offset + capacity, so a frame pointer outside it trips the window guard --
which is a `__builtin_trap`, so a wrong address shows as SIGILL with no output;
and the aligned 64-bit slot is `q[wordIndex(index(off))]`, not `q[index(off)]`,
the latter reading the wrong word and producing plausible failures against a
correct simulator.

Call and return are the rest of the emission surface, and had the same history.
They are worth more than symmetry because CALL performs *two* writes that must
agree: it sets the modelled link register and the architectural `x30` from the
same value, and return dispatches on the former while the address a callee would
actually return through is the latter. A call that set one and not the other
passes any single-register check and returns to the wrong place at run time. The
host checks both registers agree, that control transfers, and that return
dispatches on the link register -- taking an installed arm and reaching the
unsupported hook otherwise, so it is not vacuous. Both planted faults are
caught. Writing it needed one detail worth recording: the return macro ends in a
`return` from the *calling function*, so the result is read from a file-scope
global afterwards.

The same region defines three more emitters -- CBZ, CBNZ, TBZ, TBNZ -- and
none of them was executed by any host either. They differ from the
condition-code emitters in *where the predicate comes from*: not NZCV but the
register itself, zero-ness for the first pair and a single bit for the second.
That gives two independent things able to go wrong, both silent -- the test could
select the wrong predicate, or the emitter could invert it. Driving all four
through the real macros: masking the tested bit index to 62 instead of 63 fails
36 cases, and dropping the inversion on the CBZ backward arm fails 160. The x86
simulator has no counterpart for these, so there was not even a sibling oracle
to notice the absence.

A different surface had the same asymmetry. Branch *emission* is the code that
writes the control edge, not the dispatch that selects an arm: the forward shape
is a conditional jump, the backward shape an inverted conditional jump over a
local fall-through label. The x86 side has had a route host executing its
emitter since before this sequence; `ARM64_SIM_A64_JCC` was executed by nothing,
and the arm64 shape host compares only the contract. The new host drives the
real macro over all 15 conditions, 16 flag states and forward/equal/backward
addresses, observing which arm fires through `goto` labels. Dropping the
inversion on the backward arm fails 960 of 1,201 cases.

Its one deliberate limit is a *proved* irrelevance: changing `target <= current`
to `<` passes, because at equality both shapes select the same next PC -- which
is `arm64_branch_emit_shape_irrelevant` from Step 0499.

x86 gets the same question asked, and the answer differs. Its chain branches
on 53 `HANDLED` predicates and the generated model names every one -- the
apparent mismatch is a `disp_` prefix difference in ten family names, and after
normalising the sets coincide. So x86 needed no work at all, which is worth
establishing rather than assuming, since the AArch64 side needed twelve route
hosts. The checker now measures both and fails when either gains a predicate
the model does not name.

With that, `check_dispatch_model` reports **12 live / 0 model-only**: every
family the C chain routes is now driven by an oracle that includes the
simulator header.

Extract/reverse/extend gets one, the largest of the set at six opcodes over 26
shifts and masks -- and it found something in the *proofs*. EXTR's refinement
theorems carry a hypothesis that the operands are already narrowed to the
destination width, which the dispatcher does not discharge since it passes raw
registers. The two forms really do differ before the final narrowing
(`0xffffffffffffffff` against `0x1ffffffff` at `w32`), so the hypothesis was
doing work at the wrong point -- and it is unnecessary, because both sides are
narrowed at the end, which is exactly what the C register write does. Three
raw-operand theorems now carry that. One planted fault per opcode family: EXTR's
shift off by one fails 175 cases, SXTB's mask narrowed fails 80, SXTW's 80, and
SXTH's sign bit moved 280.

Address generation gets one, and it is where a value-only oracle is least
useful. The arm copies its immediate into the destination as a pointer; the
only thing the opcode decides is which *kind* of pointer it is. A dispatcher
with the two arms swapped leaves the address byte-identical and labels it as a
different pointer class -- invisible to any address comparison, and changing
later behaviour rather than this instruction's result. The oracle checks the
address *and* the tag, with the tag values written from the simulator's
vocabulary rather than read back from the contract, and asserts the two arms
select different tags so the check cannot pass with both arms identical.
Planting each half: swapping the tags fails 60 of 61 cases with identical
addresses, adding 8 to the address fails 60 with correct tags. Count moves from
9 live / 3 model-only to 10 / 2.

The vector reductions get one, and they defeat the obvious oracle in two ways:
the dispatcher writes the SIMD register rather than a GPR, so comparing the
destination observes nothing, and the result is assembled lane by lane, so a
fault can move a single byte while the rest of the value stays correct. The
oracle therefore compares the SIMD register against a lane-by-lane
recomputation, over operands whose bytes are all distinct. Planting each lane
fault separately: moving one CNT lane from bit 32 to 40 fails 7 of 21 cases,
and shifting one UADDLV contribution by a single bit fails 6. Count moves from
8 live / 4 model-only to 9 / 3.

STLXR gets one as well, and it is the only remaining family with *two*
observable effects: the dispatcher stores the source to memory and then writes
a status word to the destination, so a misroute can corrupt the atomic-success
signal while leaving memory correct, or the reverse. The oracle checks all
three things separately -- the memory word, the status in the low 32 bits (the
dispatcher writes it at a fixed 32-bit width whatever the access width), and
that the source register is unchanged. Planting each effect alone: a non-zero
status fails all 200 cases, dropping the store fails 155 as a MEMORY mismatch.
The count moves from 7 live / 5 model-only to 8 / 4.

CNEG gets one too, and it is worth more than most: the dispatcher does not
take a boolean, it evaluates the condition code against the live NZCV flags and
passes the result in. So this arm is where the flag-to-condition chain proved in
Steps 0490/0493 meets the arithmetic, and a wrong route is silent twice over --
negate and not-negate cost the same, and nothing writes a flag. The oracle
drives all 15 condition codes x 16 flag combinations x both widths, evaluating
the condition independently from the architecture: 26,400 cases. Both halves of
the composition were planted -- inverting GE fails 1,360, dropping the negation
fails 10,880. The dispatch-model count moves from 6 live / 6 model-only to
7 / 5.

One of the seven model-only families now has a live oracle. UNARY (MVN, NEG)
is worth driving through the dispatcher because its two opcodes are each
other's plausible neighbour -- both take one source, both write at the access
width, neither writes NZCV -- so sending NEG down the MVN arm yields a
full-width complement instead of a negation: a wrong value with no flag to give
it away. `test_arm64_unary_route_host.c` drives both at both widths, and the
`check_dispatch_model` count moves from 5 live / 7 model-only to 6 / 6.

Its first expectation was wrong against the tree: I required a narrow write to
preserve the destination's high half and got 156 failures. `arm64_write_arm.h`
states the value is masked to the access width before the body is chosen, so
the narrow and full bodies are observationally equal and the high half is not
preserved. The oracle now expects what the simulator does.

The coverage theorems from 0517/0518 are stated over the *generated* dispatch
tables, and the C chain branches on its own list of `HANDLED` predicates, so
nothing tied the two together. Measured: the AArch64 chain branches on **35**
families and the model names **25**. Twelve -- ADRP, CNEG, CSEL, EXTREV,
LDRSX, MOV, MUL, ORN, REDUCTION, SHIFT, STLXR, UNARY -- are routed by the code
and absent from the model.

`check_dispatch_model.py` records that set and fails when a new predicate
appears without a counterpart, or when a recorded gap has since been modelled.
Writing the entries honestly took a correction: the first version claimed each
of the twelve had a route host and only five do. The other seven have
model-side hosts only -- the same gap 0503 closed for MUL, now enumerated for
the rest. The totality module's docstring states its scope as the modelled
subset.

A refinement proof covers the Lean formula, not the C one. Both are rendered
from one specification, but as *separate string literals* in the same
generator, and the proof is stated over the Lean literal. Measured: changing
`mid1 >> 32` to `>> 16` in the arm64 multiply generator's C string leaves
`lake env lean KProgFormal/Arm64Mul.lean` green, because the Lean literal still
says `>>> 32`; the AArch64 extract/reverse/extend generator's C `<< 56` can
become `<< 55` with its proof passing too. That is the boundary of what the
proofs cover, and it is narrower than "the generator is correct".

So the C needs its own oracle. Seven generators dual-write shift arithmetic,
and `check_dual_emit_coverage.py` records for each the host that covers its C
output -- with the coverage confirmed by mutating the C string alone, since
that is the only way to know. A new dual-emitted generator with no recorded
coverage fails the gate.

Four times an oracle has been green while a fault in the simulator's own
argument derivation went unnoticed: the imul-flags oracle (0513), the
shift-flags oracle, and the register-lane-aux oracle each recomputed what the
simulator computes and then called the generated contract with that value. The
contract was tested; the composition was not. Measured on the shift-flags
oracle: shifting the sign bit by one inside the simulator survived all 90,112
cases. It now drives the simulator's composition too and compares, which makes
the fault fail -- and that needed the flags seeded identically on both paths,
since some arms (ROL) deliberately leave ZF/SF untouched.

`check_oracle_composition.py` generalises the search: it reads the simulator
sources, collects the contract macros reached from inside each `SIM_L_*` body,
and reports every host calling one without calling any `SIM_L_*` macro itself.
Four hosts match; each is recorded with the reason it is acceptable and which
host does cover its composition, so a new one fails the gate with that
instruction rather than being re-audited by hand. The scan covers every
`*host.c`, not `test_*` and `cross_*` -- a third naming would have been
invisible, as `width_fallback_host.c` already is. A missing simulator header,
or one stating no composition, is a finding rather than a skip, and so is a
recorded exception that no longer applies: an excuse survives only while the
host still needs it.

The same wide-arithmetic oracle applies to the x86 multiply-overflow flags,
which decide CF/OF from magnitudes rather than by multiplying: `A_ABS != 0 &&
B_ABS > LIMIT / A_ABS`, with LIMIT chosen by whether the product is negative.
Two independent chances to be wrong, and both yield plausible answers -- the
division test rounds down, so a boundary error shows only in a case landing
exactly there; and the sign selection is separate from the magnitudes, so it is
wrong only for some inputs. The oracle tests the exact product against the
width's signed range using 128-bit arithmetic.

Its first form had a gap worth recording: it included only `x86_sim.h`,
recomputed the limit itself, and called the generated macro with that value --
so it tested the contract but never the simulator's own sign selection, and
planting `xor` to `or` in the simulator left it green. Driving the simulator's
own composition makes that fault fail 40 cases. The operand table also needed
the most-negative value against `-1`: that is the one pair whose product is
exactly the negative bound, so the two candidate limits disagree there and
nowhere else in the table.

Dual emission protects against drift, not against a shared error. The multiply
header and its Lean module are rendered from one specification in one pass, so
they cannot disagree -- but both can be wrong the same way, and nothing related
either to the architectural definition. The family is shaped to hide that:
`UMULH` computes the high half of a 128-bit product with a shift-and-add
decomposition, and a term in the wrong position still yields a plausible
number. `test_arm64_mul_wide_host.c` uses C's own 128-bit integer type as the
oracle -- availableto the host, not to the BPF-target simulator -- and checks
all eight opcodes over boundary operands, 27,648 cases. Moving a term's shift
from 32 to 16 fails 1,008; changing the carry's shift from 32 to 24 fails
1,872. Both produce numbers that look like products.

The encoder's jump opcodes are a cross-*language* link. The x86 encoder is
Rust and writes conditional jumps as raw opcodes beside a comment naming the
mnemonic; the C simulator decides conditions from the `X86_CC_*` table. Neither
side reads the other and the opcode is only a number, so an off-by-one in a
hand-written constant compiles, runs, and branches on the wrong condition. What
makes them comparable is x86's own encoding rule -- short conditional jump
opcodes are `0x70 + condition code`, and the `X86_CC_*` values *are* those
codes -- so `check_jcc_opcodes.py` requires every site to satisfy
`opcode == 0x70 + X86_CC_<suffix>` (rel32 adds `0x80` where rel8 adds `0x70`).
Measured over *every* emission the helper writes: 10, of which 7 are conditional
and all correct -- 4 identified by mnemonic comment and 3 by a `j<cond>_out`
binding name, which is the only statement of intent for an uncommented emission
(`let jbe_out = ...rel32(..., 0x86)`); the other 3 are the `0xEB` unconditional
`jmp rel8` sites, checked as jumps. Both counts were wrong before, and the fixes
are what the pattern now does rather than what it once matched: the opcode is
taken as the call's second argument, split from the argument list and parsed as a
literal, so `0xEB`, `0XEB`, `0xE_B` and a decimal `235` are one value instead of
one spelling. The case-sensitive class that hid the three upper-case jumps, and
the `[^;]*?` that reached from a call into the helper's own `&[0x0F, opcode]`
definition and made it a phantom site, are history. A mnemonic comment is read
without regard to case. Verified by planting a wrong opcode at each kind of site.
An emission with neither a comment nor a `j<cond>_out` binding is still only
range-checked, which the script says.

The same crate also emits AArch64 conditional branches, built from a literal
whose low four bits are the condition code, and those had no check either. Six
sites, all in tail-call and map-update lowering, where the branch decides
whether an index is out of bounds, whether a map module is missing, or whether
an argument is invalid. Here the buffer-index name states which check the
branch belongs to, so the expected condition is a property of the *site*:
bounds/limit/null are "greater or equal", module existence is equality, and the
invalid-argument test is "higher". Measured: all six encode the condition their
check requires. Planting bounds-as-equality is reported against the check it
implements; replacing the word with a plain unconditional `B` is reported as
not being a `B.cond` encoding.

One cross-architecture difference is *deliberate* and was previously unrecorded.
Both encoders answer "given a native map name, which link-plan lookup site is
this?", and both account for the kernel storing at most `BPF_OBJ_NAME_LEN - 1`
bytes of a name. They answer it with different structures: x86 runs an exact
pass then a separate truncated pass that *errors* when two sites truncate-match
the same name, while AArch64 folds both comparisons into one predicate used with
`find`, so the first of several matching sites wins. For a name matching more
than one site, one architecture reports an error and the other picks silently.
Neither is wrong, but a program can lower on one and fail on the other, and
nothing said so. `check_lookup_ambiguity.py` measures the divergence rather
than picking a winner, and fails if the two converge without someone deciding
they should -- convergence would mean one side changed. It also pins both
truncation lengths to the kernel's own limit, reading each from the file's own
`*truncate_bpf_obj_name` helper: a set union of every `take(N)` in both files
could not tell an agreeing side from an absent one, so a re-spelled iterator
plus a changed length left the check printing "both sides truncate at 15".
AArch64's absence-of-error is likewise tested without x86's message prefix,
which its own bail does not carry.

The two architectures also lower `bpf_tail_call` independently, in separate
modules, each with its own spelling of the kernel's limit -- `u8` on one side,
`u32` on the other. The same program lowered either way must behave the same, so
the limit, the comparison and the increment have to agree, and nothing compared
them. The check requires one statement of the limit across both modules, that it
equals the kernel's own `MAX_TAIL_CALL_CNT` (`33`, from the vendored
`include/linux/bpf.h`), a comparison against it on each side, an
unsigned-greater-or-equal branch, and an increment by exactly one. The operands
are read from the emitted byte arrays, not from the assembly comments beside them
-- a comment is a human note about the bytes, and x86 had been able to emit a
different immediate than its comment claimed. Verified by planting a moved limit,
a `jae`-to-`ja` branch, a dropped comparison, a changed byte operand, and an
increment of two, each reported by name.

One measurement kept because it looked like a discrepancy and is not: the
encoder reserves 512 bytes for its own frame, the kernel's `MAX_BPF_STACK` is
also 512, and the simulators model much smaller arenas (64/128 and 160). The
arena is a model size, and an access past it is reported through the
unsupported hook rather than being silently wrong.

The helper-id table is a different kind of gap, because it is only *stated*
rather than reached. `arm64_helper_idents_spec.json` gives each of 61 BPF
helpers the kernel id the encoder renumbers against, and the generated header's
assertions pin those ids to the spec -- so a wrong id produces a
self-consistent header, passes every oracle, and renumbers a program onto the
wrong helper at runtime. The simulator never consults the table (it dispatches
by *name* at compile time), which is precisely why nothing had cross-checked it.

The independent source was already in the tree: the vendored libbpf ships
`bpf_helper_defs.h` with one entry per helper. `check_helper_idents.py` parses
it and compares. Measured: all 61 ids match the kernel enum exactly, and the
name set matches what the simulator forwards to, in both directions. The check
reports three classes separately -- an id disagreeing with the kernel, a name
the kernel does not define, and a name-set mismatch either way -- and is
verified by planting each.

The conditional-select family is another. `arm64_csel` names eight opcodes,
and the dispatcher reaches them at one arm that evaluates the condition, picks
the pointer-tag or scalar path and writes the destination -- with no host that
included the simulator header driving any of them, so perturbing one arm of the
contract left every oracle green. `test_arm64_csel_route_host.c` drives all
eight through the dispatcher at both widths, with the condition both
always-taken and flag-dependent so each opcode's two arms are covered.

Writing that model exposed something about the contract: `CINC` and `CINV`
take `src` on *both* paths and ignore `src2`, which is right for the
one-operand forms but means an operand pair chosen for the two-operand shape
will not distinguish them. The first model assumed the two-operand form for all
eight and produced 24 spurious failures; the fix was to read the generated arms
rather than the instruction-set pseudocode.

The same classification says 48 contracts the simulator calls appear only on the
model-only side. The flag contract is the most consequential of them: ADDS and
SUBS reach it through `EXEC_ARITH_WRITEBACK`, which picks the family, computes
the result and sets all four flags, and nothing verified that routing. A wrong
flag is worse than a wrong value -- it is invisible at the instruction that
caused it and wrong at the next branch -- so `test_arm64_flag_route_host.c`
compares the destination and all four flags against an independent model of
ADD/SUB and N/Z/C/V.

Two mistakes in that oracle's first draft are worth keeping. The overflow model
omitted ADD's operand-agreement complement, which the contract has; it was
corrected against the definition rather than against the macro. And the operand
table used distinct registers, so `lhs == rhs` was never generated -- the only
case separating a subtract carry of `lhs >= rhs` from `lhs > rhs`. With
equal-operand immediates added the run goes from 432 to 1,152 cases, and a
planted `>=` to `>` fault fails on 24 of them, where it previously survived.

Classifying all 214 hosts by whether they include the simulator header separates
89 that drive the real dispatcher from 125 that compare a hand model against a
generated contract. Those are different claims, and the second does not imply
the first: a contract can be proved, modelled, and still never exercised through
the code that runs it. Fifty-five of the 138 contracts appeared only on the
model-only side, and the AArch64 multiply arm was the one arithmetic family in
that position -- proved in Lean, modelled in a host, and never driven through
`ARM64_SIM_L_EXEC`. `test_arm64_mul_route_host.c` closes that: MADD/MSUB/MUL
over distinct operands at both widths, expected value computed from the
architecture rather than from the contract, and a non-member opcode required to
reach the unsupported arm. Flipping MSUB's operand order fails it on 432 of
1,296 cases.

Two arm64 memory-model hosts had a subtler version of the same problem. Both
defined `ARM64_SP` as 31, but in this simulator 31 is `XZR` and 32 is `SP`;
the simulator reads 31 as zero. So the models treated a register the simulator
reads as zero as though it were the stack pointer -- and because the base sweep
ran `bi < 32`, the actual stack base (32) was never driven at all. The value is
corrected, XZR now reads zero with no writeback, and the sweep runs one past
the register file: 9,216 cases to 9,504.

What these hosts can show is bounded, and worth stating: `contract_step` and
`model_step` share the same transfer body and read/write helpers, so they
compare two *labellings* of one model rather than an independent
reimplementation, and a semantic error inside that shared model stays invisible
to both. What the change buys is that the stack-base path and the XZR discard
are now exercised rather than assumed.

Two oracles restated their ISA's condition codes as local literals, so that the
model stayed independent of the generated tables. That was right about the
generated side and wrong about the other: it made them blind to whether the
*simulator* still agreed with the contract. Drifting `X86_CC_A` in
`x86_sim.h`, or `ARM64_COND_EQ` in `arm64_sim.h`, left both green. Both now
include the simulator header, so the drift fails at compile time through the
generated `_Static_assert`s -- stronger than the runtime comparison they had.
Found by looking for contracts the simulator never calls, which is the
complement of the usual coverage question.

Everything above compares one contract at a time. The control-flow path is a
different kind of claim: the property that matters is that two *chains*
compose to the same place, not that two contracts match. Each ISA proves its
own chain in isolation, so on either ISA flags in means the correct next PC
out -- but the chains are not the same shape internally. AArch64 evaluates
`(N Z C V)`, x86-64 `(CF ZF SF OF)` with C the complement of CF, so an
intermediate step differs while the endpoints should not. A chain that
composed differently on one side would diverge while every per-ISA theorem
still held, which is precisely the failure per-ISA work cannot see.
`CrossIsaBranch.lean` composes the whole path -- same four architectural flag
facts, through each ISA's own condition evaluation and shape selection, to one
next program counter -- so the flag correspondence of Steps 0490/0493 is shown
to survive emission rather than stopping at the predicate.

The ALU tables are the first place where the shared vocabulary has to be
*recovered* rather than read off. Both ISAs dispatch arithmetic-logic through
one generated table, but the tables are numbered differently and cover
different sets (six arms against sixteen), so the correspondence is a mapping.
Five operations map one-to-one under a renaming. The sixth does not: AArch64's
`BIC` complements the right operand and x86-64's `ANDN` complements the left,
so they agree only on exchanged arguments, and dropping the exchange breaks the
theorem. Both names mean "and with a complement", which is exactly why a
translator pairs them wrongly.

The address offset is the case where "the same function" is the wrong frame
entirely. Both ISAs compute base plus an optional scaled index with 64-bit
wrapping, but AArch64 has no scale and does have pre/post-indexing, while
x86-64 has a scale (a base-2 log in the addressing-mode byte) and no
pre/post-indexing. The shared core is one statement -- `base + (index <<< scale)`
-- reached by zeroing AArch64's scale and taking its non-writeback form; the
rest of each contract is what the other ISA lacks. Stating it that way keeps the
divergence explicit instead of hiding it behind a name: giving x86-64 a unit
scale breaks the agreement theorem, and the module records a concrete case where
writeback makes the two compute different things rather than the same thing
differently.

Byte reversal is the case where the *property* carries the weight. `REV` and
`BSWAP` agree at the two widths AArch64 encodes, but agreement alone would not
distinguish a correct reversal from a transposed one: a permutation with two
terms swapped still agrees with itself, and still changes plausibly on most
inputs. So the theorem set also pins the involution -- reversal is an order-two
permutation on the width-truncated value -- which a transposition breaks.
Displacing one byte position in the x86 side fails the compiled check on
398,436 of a million pseudo-random cases; picking round numbers would have
agreed on nearly all of them.

Sign extension is where sampling would not have been enough. Both
architectures extend a narrow value into a 64-bit register with entirely
different code: AArch64 states it generically and inlines the
mask-flip-subtract idiom, x86-64 writes each width out with its own constants.
A signedness slip in either still yields a plausible register value and still
round-trips for positive inputs, so only boundary values show it. The two
contracts agree at all three widths AArch64 parameterises, with `0x7f`/`0x80`
pinned on both sides, and the C check runs every 16-bit pattern through both
the byte and halfword paths plus a stride across the 32-bit space -- 200,652
cases in a tenth of a second, which is cheap enough that exhaustiveness beat
choosing a sample. Breaking the byte mask fails it on 32,768 cases.

The cross-ISA theorems say nothing about the C, so that is checked separately.
`CrossIsaWidth.lean` and `CrossIsaStackArena.lean` prove the generated *Lean*
contracts agree, but each ISA ships its own generated C header, and a
translation of one spec could emit C that disagrees where the Lean does not --
or the hand-written C could drift from its own Lean. `cross_isa_differential_host.c`
compiles both simulators into one translation unit (they coexist, since every
decode is ISA-prefixed) and compares the compiled macros on shared inputs: the
four width masks, bit counts and sign masks over boundary values, and the stack
window/pointer/slot bounds over a capacity grid that includes both arenas' real
sizes. 372 cases. Adding one to the x86 window capacity in its *generated
header* -- a drift the Lean still proves correct -- makes it fail with 9
differences, so it covers exactly the layer the theorems cannot.

The two stack contracts are also proved to agree, and that one needed care
because they are *not* identical. Twelve theorems in the two stack-arena
modules share a concept name once the ISA prefix is stripped
(`stack_arena_window_fits_refines`, `stack_arena_pointer_one_past_end`, and so
on), but the sharing was structural rather than proved: nothing showed the two
generated contracts compute the same arithmetic. They differ — x86 carries
`byteAt`/`assembleByte` for its byte ladder, arm64 carries `tagSlotFits` for
the tag array x86 lacks — so `CrossIsaStackArena.lean` proves exactly the six
definitions both sides share (`wordIndex`, `wordAligned`, `words`,
`windowEnd`, `windowFits`, `pointerFits`). Changing the x86 `wordIndex` shift
from 3 to 2 fails it.

The converse also holds: a hypothesis that *is* needed can still be
mis-described. `arm64_stack_arena_tag_guard_is_window_guard` claimed its
whole-word condition held for "both the enabled 160-byte and the disabled
1-byte arena". One is not a whole number of words, and the equivalence really
does fail there: at capacity 1 slot 0 is addressable while a one-byte window
at index 1 is not, because a slot covers eight addressable indices and the
arena covers one byte. So the hypothesis is load-bearing here, unlike the
implication widened in Step 0483, and the counterexample is now a theorem so
the claim cannot drift back.

A theorem's hypothesis can be stronger than it needs to be, and that is a
coverage hole in disguise. `arm64_stack_arena_window_implies_tag_slot`
required `capacity % 8 = 0` -- true of the enabled 160-byte arena, false of the
1-byte arena the arm64 header declares in its `#else` branch, so the theorem
did not cover an arena the simulator actually defines. The precondition is
unnecessary: `index + width <= capacity` gives `index < capacity`, and
`capacity <= words capacity * 8` always, so the slot is below the count. The
general form needs only that the slot count's `+7` does not wrap. Both forms
are present now, with a witness at capacity 1.

The two ISAs agree on the width vocabulary, and that now has a theorem rather
than an eyeball comparison. `arm64_width_spec.json` and `x86_width_spec.json`
are separate inputs to separate generators, each rendering its own C header and
Lean module; nothing forced the two to agree, so a drifted mask or bit count on
one side would make the simulators disagree about what an 8-bit write means
while every per-ISA theorem kept holding. `CrossIsaWidth.lean` states the
agreement across all ten generated definitions (`code`, `mask`, `signMask`,
`bits`, `narrow`, `zero`, `sign`, `absentCode`, `defaultCode`, `effective`).
Planting a 16-bit bit-count of 17 on the x86 side fails `bits_agrees` and
`sign_agrees`, so the module is a real gate on spec drift rather than a
restatement.

The table-shape theorems are not vacuous, which is worth stating because most
are discharged by `rfl` or `decide` and a vacuous one would look identical.
Nineteen `*_codes_length` theorems assert `codes.length = count`; every one
compares against a generated count constant, and no generated count is zero
(the 31 of them run from 2 to 72), so each ranges over a real table. The
equality-style exactness theorems (`x86_cc_decode_suffixes_exact` and
friends) assert two independently defined lists are equal, so they cannot be
trivially satisfied unless both are empty -- measured at 36 mnemonics against
12 suffixes, and 17 against 15 on the arm64 side. `x86_helper_dispatch_full_range`
pairs its `List.range` sweep with four explicit `none` checks, so it has
content even if the count were zero.

The chain selects exactly one arm per opcode, and that is proved rather than
inspected. An `else if` ladder silently picks the first matching arm, so two
overlapping family predicates would make dispatch order-dependent. Both ISAs
prove non-duplication of the combined generated opcode list
(`x86_dispatch_chain_codes_nodup`, and the arm64 pair), and the x86 statement
is non-vacuous: 43 singleton plus 24 family codes give 67, and the deduplicated
list is also 67. A hand parse of the 53 predicates confirms zero overlapping
pairs over 67 named opcodes, which is what the theorem says.

The dispatch ladder's depth costs nothing, which was measured rather than
assumed. `X86_SIM_L_EXEC` is a 56-arm `else if` chain and `ARM64_SIM_L_EXEC` a
34-arm one, so an opcode near the end (`X86_OP_XCHG`, arm 49) walks 49
predicates per emulated instruction. It does not matter: at `-O2` the compiler
reduces the chain to one indirect `jmp *` and two `cmp`s, and in a
loop-carried benchmark `XCHG` at arm 49 runs at 0.31 ns/op, identical to
`NOP` at arm 1. A flat jump table, not a linear scan -- so reordering the arms,
which the generated tables would make easy, would buy nothing.

A guard can be *watched* without being *exercised*, and that distinction cost
five hosts in all. The arm64 route hosts counted guard hits and failed if any
fired, but every offset they swept was in range — so a simulator whose guard
was weakened to always-true passed them: the arena and write-lanes hosts
(2.75M and 3.84M cases) first, then the stack-arm, read-tag-source, and
write-tag-action hosts (1.67e5, 6.01e4, 9.08e6) and the
helper-argument-pointer host, each against the guard it is about. All six now
drive an access or pointer whose index runs past the arena and require exactly
one hit. The separation is verified per host: each fails its own sabotage and
passes the other's, so the rows exercise the guard the host actually covers.
The x86 hosts never had this gap — they trap rather than counting, so a
disabled guard is a signal rather than an uncounted event — and both catch the
sabotage, which is what a counter-based host has to be taught to do.

This distinction cost
two more holes. The arm64 route hosts counted guard hits and failed if any
fired, but every offset they swept was in range — so a simulator whose window
guard was weakened to always-true passed all 2.75M and 3.84M of their cases.
Both now drive accesses whose window runs past the arena and require exactly
one hit. The x86 hosts already caught that sabotage, because their sweeps
include out-of-range offsets; only the arm64 pair was blind. Note the
corroboration: with the guard disabled the compiler itself reports
`-Warray-bounds: array subscript 160 is above array bounds of __u8[160]`,
which is the overrun the guard prevents.

Each of those guards is mutation-tested, which is the difference between a
bound and a *checked* bound. When the pointer guard was added no host drove it,
so two sabotages of `KPROG_*_STACK_POINTER_FITS` passed the whole gate: raising
the capacity by one, and dropping the `(__s64)` cast that rejects a negative
index. Both arena hosts now check the generated bound against an independent
restatement over every grid capacity/index pair plus the one-past-end, negative,
and large-capacity rows. The signed index matters — it is what the simulator
passes, and a capacity near `2^32` is where the signed cast changes the answer,
so an unsigned grid alone leaves the cast unpinned. Both sabotages now fail on
both architectures.

The three bounds are not independent, and the module now proves how they
relate rather than leaving it to inspection. A stack *write* that fits its
window always lands in a tag slot the tag array holds — `index + width <=
capacity` gives `index < capacity`, and the last slot of an arena whose
capacity is a whole number of words is the last tag slot — so
`ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_WRITE_TAG` carries only the window guard, while the tag
*read* needs the slot guard because it carries no width and can name the
one-past-end index. A fitting window likewise names a valid arena pointer at
any width, and the weakness is strict: the one-past-end index is a valid
pointer but starts no nonempty window, which is exactly why the pointer helper
keeps a check of its own.

The tag array is a third, separate stack path and needed its own bound. A tag
access is a *slot* index into `__a64_stack_tag[]`, which holds one byte per
word slot, so a byte index at or past the capacity reaches slot `TAG_SLOTS`,
one past the array — ASan reproduces that read too. The arena spec gained
`tag_slot_guard`, the generator emits
`KPROG_ARM64_STACK_TAG_SLOT_FITS`, and the hand module proves it refines an
independent slot statement, that the largest tag slot is the word holding the
arena's final byte, and that the tag guard equals the window guard at a
one-byte width — so the tag array does not carry a second, independent
inequality. `ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_READ_TAG` tests it before indexing and falls
back to the scalar tag on a miss.

Both simulators route their stack paths through it. `ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_READ`
and `ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_WRITE_TAG` test `ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_WINDOW_OK` first,
report an unfitting window through the existing
`arm64_sim_unsupported_opcode` hook, and take a zero value without touching
the arena — the hook returns, so reporting alone would still have let the
access run. `X86_SIM_L_STACK_READ` and `X86_SIM_L_STACK_WRITE` test the same
bound and trap. ASan confirms the result: an 8-byte read at index 153 on
AArch64 and at index 63 on x86-64 now report through the guard with no
out-of-bounds access, while the last fitting access is untouched.

The threshold this closes is exact: on AArch64's 160-byte arena with bias 96,
an 8-byte access at offset 56 (index 152) is the last in-bounds one, and
offset 57 is the first that overran. The route hosts cap their sweeps at
`off + width <= ARM64_SIM_STACK_BYTES`, which is why the gate stayed green
over the defect; the arena hosts now drive the window test directly at every
grid capacity, index, and width plus those boundary rows, and sabotaging the
generated comparison (`capacity` to `capacity + 1`) turns both banners red
(15 and 17 mismatches). One host was driving windows outside the arena while
claiming the opposite: `test_x86_mem_dispatch_route_host.c` swept
displacements `{0, -8, -32, 32, 56}` against a 64-byte arena, so three of the
five put the read at or past the end; its sweep is now `{-8, -16, -32, -64}`,
and its indexed case uses displacement -16 so the scaled index still fits at
every width.

"All 294 modules are checked" is a chain of three facts, each verified rather
than assumed. First, every `import KProgFormal.X` names a module that exists
(0 dangling imports). Second, the gate's 268 explicit `lake env lean`
invocations reach all 294 modules — the other 26 are `Generated*` modules
pulled in through their imports — and no module is unreachable from those
roots. Third, `lake build` runs before the elaborations and compiles the whole
library: `lake env lean` alone does *not* recompile an imported module (it
needs a prior olean and reports a missing-object error otherwise), so without
that build step a break inside a transitively-reached module would be
invisible. Planting `theorem planted_bad : (1 : Nat) = 2 := by rfl` in
`GeneratedArm64Mod` — one of the 26 — is caught by `lake build` as
`Build failed: KProgFormal.GeneratedArm64Mod`.

The route hosts' "independent model" is independent in the sense that matters.
44 model/oracle functions in those hosts call a generated `KPROG_*` macro, which
looks circular, but each such macro is bound to a literal elsewhere: sweeping
for macros used *only* inside a model leaves just `KPROG_ARM64_AUX_B1` and
`AUX_B2`, and those are checked by `test_arm64_aux_route_host.c` against
hand-written lane models (`f1(aux) = (aux >> 8) & 0xff`, `f2` likewise) plus
the `arm64_aux_b{1,2,3}_roundtrip` Lean lemmas. Sabotaging `AUX_B1`'s mask from
`0xff` to `0x7f` makes that host report 91,228 mismatches, so the lane is
genuinely pinned rather than assumed.

Macro reachability was audited the same way, and "no host names it" is not the
right test. Of 181 `*_SIM_L_*` macros, 174 are reached from a host either
directly or through another macro's body; the 7 that are not split into three
kinds. `ARM64_SIM_L_SET_{ADD,SUB,LOGIC}_FLAGS` are genuinely dead — the
simulator routes through `KPROG_ARM64_EXEC_*` instead — and are pre-existing, so
they are left alone rather than deleted in passing. `X86_SIM_L_HELPER_ARG_PTR`
looked dead only because the traverser only followed `*_SIM_L_*` bodies: it is
called from `X86_SIM_BPF_CALL_bpf_map_lookup_elem`, which the
`X86_SIM_BPF_CALL_ID` dispatch reaches and the route host drives, so it is live.
`ARM64_SIM_L_STORE_Q0_STACK` looks dead too, but
`generate_arm64_helper_arg_ptr_spec.py` uses its `#define` line as the
`HELPER_PTR_END` slicing boundary for the helper-argument-pointer text, so
deleting it would break that generator's `--check`. An "unused" macro here may
be a live generator anchor.

`X86_SIM_L_HELPER_ARG_PTR` and `ARM64_SIM_L_HELPER_ARG_PTR` look like they
should be the same contract and are deliberately not, because the two register
files hold different things under the stack tag. On AArch64 a stack-tagged
register carries a *frame offset* (`sp` is an abstract offset in this model),
so the helper rebases it into the arena through `ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_PTR` before
the call — a register holding `-8` hands the callee arena byte `88`. On x86-64
the stack-pointer write already stores a *real arena address* (`mov %rsp, %rax`
rebases into the arena and stamps the tag), so the same register holds a
pointer with an arena delta of 56 and the helper passes it through unchanged;
rebasing again would double-apply the capacity bias. Both are correct for their
own register model, and a change that "unified" them would move one ISA's
helper arguments by the capacity.

The 138/138/138 pairing is verified as a bijection in both directions rather
than inferred from equal counts: every `*_spec.json` has a same-named
`generated/*.h` with nothing left over on either side (both set differences
empty), and every spec likewise has a `Generated<Name>.lean` once the
generator's CamelCase splitting is normalized — `arm64_ldrsx`,
`x86_callmem`, `x86_cmpop`, `x86_doubleshift`, `x86_doubleshift_arm`, and
`x86_pushpop` differ from a naive capitalisation only in how an acronym is
split (`LdrSx`, `CallMem`, ...).

`check_lean_claims.py` now runs that comparison as part of the gate: the three
counts and the name sets are checked together, and a contract rendered on one
side only fails the run instead of leaving the figures correct. Reachability is
then followed on both sides too, because "paired" alone does not say a contract
is used: the checker walks `#include` from the 248 `.c` files the gate Makefile
compiles — 131 headers are included by one directly, the other 7 only through a
simulator header — and `import` from the modules the gate type-checks. All 138
are reached on both sides, and an orphan on either raises with its name rather
than shrinking a published figure.

The third generator-side obligation is now bound as well. The section's
"every generator re-derives its output and fails on any byte difference (all
138 pass `--check`)" counted the spec files on disk, so deleting a generator's
`--check` line from the Makefile kept the figure at 138 while the claim went
false for that one contract. The checker now compares the 138 `--check`
invocations against the spec family in both directions — an orphan in either
set names itself and stops the run — and binds the same figure to this file's
"Of the 138 generators that exist", so the two documents cannot disagree about
the denominator.

The generated headers also bind the hand-written decode at compile time:
1,049 `_Static_assert`s compile into them, 786 of which name a simulator
constant (`X86_OP_*` / `ARM64_*`) and so fail the build when the decode drifts;
the other 263 tie generated renderings to each other — a table's count against
the literal that pins it, or one header's code against another's. Tested
rather than assumed — changing `X86_OP_NOP` from `0x00U` to `0x09U` in
`x86_sim.h` fails the build with two independent assertions
(`x86_opcode.h:12`, `x86_dispatch_singleton.h:21`), so two generated tables
observe the same drift separately.

Each of those numbers was re-measured against the committed tree rather than
carried forward. The `_Static_assert` count is the figure that keeps moving:
an earlier pass "corrected" 1,049 upward to 1,051 by counting textual
mentions, two of which are prose inside generated-header comments
(`x86_movx_shape.h`, `arm64_ccmp_decode.h`), and neither figure was checked
against anything. It is now counted by a balanced-paren scan of the generated
headers, which also splits what the assertions tie. The rest hold exactly —
138 specs pairing with
138 generated headers and 138 `Generated*.lean` modules as a bijection in both
directions (no leftovers either way), 268 explicit `lake env lean` invocations
over 294 modules with the 26 unreached all `Generated*` and all imported, 0
`sorry`/`axiom`/`opaque`/`unsafe`, 330 batteries, and two consecutive gate runs
producing byte-identical output (`5f8f11c88142ea18eea5b9c0a6acaca2`). The two
sabotages this section cites were also re-run: `X86_OP_NOP` to `0x09U` fails on
`x86_opcode.h:12` and `x86_dispatch_singleton.h:21`, and masking `AUX_B1` to
`0x7fU` reports 91,228 mismatches in the aux route host — both exactly as
stated.

Three oracles did not previously have that negative property: their part
functions stopped at a mismatch with a bare `return 0`, and `main` summed the
returned case counts and printed OK unconditionally, so the banner could not
turn red at all. This was not theoretical — sabotaging `kprog_x86_bswap_value`'s
8-bit arm to sign-extend, the exact bug `test_x86_movbe_host.c`'s pin forbids,
printed `MISMATCH ...` and then `OK (16 cases)` with exit status 0.
`test_x86_movbe_host.c` (16 sites), `test_x86_xmm0_host.c` (22), and
`test_x86_mov_load_map_ptr_host.c` (26) now record each detected mismatch in a
`mismatches` counter and `main` fails when it is nonzero; the same three
sabotages now report `FAIL (3)`, `FAIL (4)`, and `FAIL (1)` with exit status 1,
while the pristine tree keeps its exact case counts (4675, 283, 318) and the
gate stays at 220 banners.

A follow-up audit found four more unmetered returns in
`test_x86_xmm0_host.c`'s pin 2: they carry trailing comments after
`return 0;`, which the brace-wrapping pass skipped. A mismatch there aborted
the part and only shortened the case count, so a distinct pin-2 failure would
still have printed OK. All four now increment the counter like the rest; a
sabotaged `KPROG_X86_XMM0_BASE_FORM` polarity reports `FAIL (4)` at exit 1,
and every early return in all three hosts is now metered (0 unmetered of 15,
26, and 26).

The arm64 helper family is now covered by construction rather than by count:
`build/helper_route_host.c` drives exactly the 61 `ARM64_SIM_BPF_CALL_bpf_*`
bodies the header defines, with no body left undriven and no drive naming an
absent body, which is what lets the 0462 battery's per-body repaints turn the
host red.
That host is also in the gate, so the coverage and the host cannot drift apart
silently.

The x86 helper surface closes the same way by a different mechanism: the seven
`X86_SIM_BPF_CALL_bpf_*` bodies are reached through the `X86_SIM_BPF_CALL_ID`
dispatch switch rather than driven by name, and all seven bodies are named by
one of its case arms, so no body is unreachable. The switch is seven named arms
plus a `default` that zeroes the return register, and
`build/x86_route_host.c` exercises ids 0-8, so the named arms and the
out-of-range default are both live.

The 32 equivalences the 0462 battery marks are a checked fact rather than an
assumption. `ARM64_SIM_L_WRITE_REG_WIDTH` narrows through
`KPROG_ARM64_APPLY_WIDTH`, then picks a write arm via
`KPROG_ARM64_WRITE_ARM`; both arms store the value and set
`ARM64_SIM_TAG_SCALAR`, and the register write differs only by a `(__u32)`
cast. For the zero value these bodies commit, `(__u32)0 == 0` and both arms
write the same tag, so repainting `ARM64_WIDTH_64` to `ARM64_WIDTH_32` leaves
the observed register word and tag unchanged.

Fixing those oracles also surfaced a coupling worth recording: the batteries
anchor on host source text, so bracing the returns broke two
`build/mut_x86_xmm0.py` rows (`host_p4_pin1_slice`, `host_p4_pin6_regs`) with
`BROKEN ANCHOR` until their anchors were updated to the braced form; the
battery is back to `ALL AS EXPECTED` (50 mutations). `build/mut_x86_ptr_write.py`
(121 mutations) and, on a pristine x86 header, `build/mut_x86_movbe.py` (114)
also run clean. On the current tree the movbe battery reports 2 failures, both
in its *route* host's banner rows; that host fails only because of the
unrestored `x86_sim_local_bpf.h` mutation described above — with `HEAD`'s
header it prints `OK (71 cases)` and the battery is green, so the two failures
are the stranded line's, not the battery's.

`KProgFormal.TagErasure` models a bounded fragment drawn from the simulators:
a 64-bit move, a pointer-shaped 64-bit add, an x86-shaped scalarizing integer
multiply-immediate, and a 64-bit load of the packet or packet-end pointer from
the simulator entry ABI. It proves for any sequence of those abstract
operations that:

1. erasing verifier-facing provenance tags yields the same bits as a pure
   modulo-2^64 architectural execution; and
2. tag transitions follow a separately declared provenance policy.

The pointer-add transition is generated from `ptr_add_spec.json` into both the
Lean model and the C macro used by the x86-64 non-stack LEA and AArch64
non-scalar ADD handler branches. The entry-ABI provenance policy is likewise
generated from `abi_load_spec.json`: it distinguishes XDP from `__sk_buff`,
maps only the architecture-independent `data` and `data_end` offsets to packet
tags, and scalarizes all other 64-bit ABI loads. Compile-time assertions bind
those offsets to both C ABI structs, while the Lean theorem compares the
generated transition against an independently written tag specification.
The complete AArch64 condition-code table is generated from
`arm64_cond_spec.json` into the Lean model and the C branch handler. Lean proves
that all 15 supported predicates select the same next program counter as an
independent architectural condition specification, for either branch
direction.
The AArch64 simulator width encodings and NZCV flag transitions are likewise
generated. `arm64_width_spec.json` produces the `KPROG_ARM64_WIDTH_*` /
`KPROG_ARM64_APPLY_WIDTH` macros and a Lean `GeneratedArm64Width` module; the
central `arm64_width_mask` / `arm64_width_bits` / `arm64_sign_bit` /
`arm64_apply_width` helpers now delegate to those macros, so the AArch64
simulator and the proof contract share one forwarded source for masks, sign
bits, and narrowing. `arm64_flags_spec.json` produces
`KPROG_ARM64_SET_{ADD,SUB,LOGIC}_FLAGS` and Lean
`GeneratedArm64Flags.apply{Add,Sub,Logic}`. Lean proves each generated
transition equal to an independently written NZCV statement over already
width-narrowed operands (ADD/SUB: N=sign, Z=zero, C=carry-out or not-borrow,
V=signed overflow; logical: C=V=0), with concrete theorems pinning an
AArch64 `0xffffffffffffffff + 1` carry/zero, a `0 + 0` subtract carry, a
32-bit `0x7fffffff + 1` overflow, a `1 - 2` borrow, and a logical result that
clears carry/overflow. The previously hand-written
`ARM64_SIM_L_SET_{ADD,SUB,LOGIC}_FLAGS` macros now delegate to the generated
primitives. A host C cross-check (`test_arm64_flags_host.c`) validates the
generated macros against an independent `__int128` carry/overflow oracle over
explicit boundary vectors and a fixed-seed 20000-case sweep of all four
widths; `make check` runs it. Instruction decoding, condition-to-next-PC
selection beyond the earlier condition contract, and native bytes remain
boundaries.
The generic AArch64 ALU handler now has a composed state-transition theorem as
well. `arm64_alu_handler_spec.json` generates the exact C/Lean predicate that
selects the provenance-preserving path only for 64-bit ADD from a non-scalar
source into a non-SP destination. `arm64_alu_handler_refines` proves that this
path, the generated ALU result, pointer-add bits/tag policy, width narrowing,
GPR/SP/XZR/NONE write behavior, and scalarization on every other arithmetic
path agree with an independently enumerated handler specification for all six
ALU operations, four modeled widths, four destination classes, and all modeled
provenance tags. `arm64_alu_operand_handler_refines` now closes its former
free-RHS premise: immediate form selects the raw immediate, while register form
applies any of the eleven proved source modifiers before the full handler
transition. This composition is universal over both forms, operations, widths,
destinations, tags, operands, modifiers, and shifts; a 5632-case host oracle
checks the shared C selector. The theorem still starts after opcode, width,
register value/tag, destination class, and packed-AUX modifier/shift selection;
the parser, C register switch, those selections, and native bytes remain
boundaries. The earlier path-only host cross-check exhausts 168 numeric
selection cases, including unsupported width/opcode values.
The flag-setting arithmetic handlers have a second composed contract.
`arm64_flag_handler_spec.json` generates the ADD/SUB family dispatch used by
the real ADDS/SUBS and CMN/CMP C branches and the matching Lean step.
`arm64_flag_handler_refines` proves two modes against an independent statement:
ADDS/SUBS take one generated result/flag step, perform width-aware scalarizing
writeback (including discarded XZR/NONE writes), and replace NZCV; CMN/CMP
replace the same NZCV while preserving the complete modeled GPR/SP state.
The theorem begins after operand and source-modifier selection. A parallel
logical flag-handler contract routes the real ANDS/BICS/TST/TST-BIC branches
through one generated AND/BIC result-plus-NZCV step.
`arm64_logic_flag_handler_refines` proves width-aware scalarizing writeback for
ANDS/BICS, including discarded XZR/NONE results, and proves that TST/TST-BIC
replace NZCV while preserving the complete modeled GPR/SP state. It covers
both logical families, all modeled widths and destinations, arbitrary operands,
and arbitrary incoming state. A separate 64-case host oracle checks the shared
C step over boundary operands. Both handler theorems begin after typed operand,
width, destination, and source-modifier selection. Conditional compare now has
its own composed contract: `arm64_ccmp_handler_refines` proves that all 15
supported conditions inspect the incoming NZCV, choose SUB-produced flags on
the true path or immediate NZCV[3:0] on the false path, and preserve the
complete modeled GPR/SP state. Its 122880-case host oracle exhausts incoming
flag combinations, supported conditions, widths, boundary operands, and all
4-bit fallbacks. The theorem begins after operand/register selection and AUX
condition/fallback decoding; those selections, the C register switch, and
native bytes remain separate obligations.
The supported x86 condition-code table is likewise generated from
`x86_cond_spec.json` into the C simulator predicate and Lean. Lean proves the
same next-PC refinement for arbitrary flags and branch targets; parity
conditions are outside the accepted simulator subset.
The x86 condition-to-next-PC refinement is additionally bridged to the emitted
code: `generate_x86_branch_emit_spec.py` emits `KPROG_X86_BRANCH_BACKWARD`, the
address-ordering test the simulator's `X86_SIM_X86_JCC_IMPL` now routes its
backward-edge choice through (forward edge: `if (taken) goto target;` with a
fall-through; backward edge: `if (!taken) goto fallthrough; goto target;`).
`X86BranchEmit.lean` proves the emitted shape selects exactly `branchPc`, that
the two shapes select the same next PC (`x86_branch_emit_shape_irrelevant`, so
the direction only decides *how* the jump is written), and that a taken branch
reaches the target and a not-taken branch falls through for either shape — the
exact x86 analogue of the AArch64 emitted-shape bridge. Its host cross-check
(90 cases) pins the direction to an independent ordering oracle including the
equality boundary, and an 1827-case sim-header route oracle drives the real
`X86_SIM_X86_JCC` macro over every accepted and unsupported condition code, both
directions, and an equal-address edge, comparing the selected next PC against
the architectural model.
The legal x86 width encodings, masks, bit counts, narrowing, and zero/sign
observations are generated into the actual C helpers and Lean. Lean checks
their per-width model against an independent enumeration, while C static
assertions bind the numeric encodings. The x86 logical-result flag
transition is also generated into C and Lean. Its
composition theorem covers `CF=OF=0`, `ZF=zero`, and `SF=sign` through the
condition-to-next-PC decision using those observations.

The decoded width code a body operates at — where an unused width field (code
0) falls back to the 64-bit default — is likewise a generated contract rather
than a restatement. `generate_x86_width_spec.py` emits
`KPROG_X86_WIDTH_ABSENT_CODE`, `KPROG_X86_WIDTH_EFFECTIVE_DEFAULT` and
`KPROG_X86_WIDTH_EFFECTIVE` alongside the width tables, and the generated Lean
`effective` resolves a decoded code to the code a body operates at. `X86Width.lean`
proves that resolution equal to an independent `if c = 0 then 8 else c`, that the
absent code names no width (`x86_absent_code_names_no_width`), that the fallback
code is exactly the 64-bit width's code (`x86_default_code_is_w64`, pinned to the
generated decode so it cannot drift), and that the resolution is the identity on
every real width (`x86_effective_identity_on_width`); the earlier mask, bit-count,
narrowing, zero and sign theorems remain. Every site in `x86_sim_local_bpf.h`
that restated `WIDTH ? WIDTH : X86_WIDTH_64` now routes through
`X86_SIM_L_EFFECTIVE_WIDTH`, whose kernel is the generated
`KPROG_X86_WIDTH_EFFECTIVE`. A generated-header oracle sweeps the full decoded
code domain (0..255) plus the width codes and the absent code's neighbours
against the independent model and the pinned width table (1,280 cases); a
sim-header route oracle drives every routed register/stack/flag/ALU/move/compare/
`IMUL`/`MULX` body and compares the whole modeled register file with tags, the
flags, the modeled heap and the stack against an independent model (518 cases).
The x86 subtraction flag transition is generated into the central C handler
and Lean. For already narrowed operands/result and a width sign mask, Lean
checks carry/borrow, zero, sign, and signed-overflow flags against an
independent specification and composes them through the condition-to-next-PC
theorem.
The x86 addition flag transition follows the same binding: for arbitrary
already-narrowed operands/result and a sign mask, the shared C/Lean contract
defines carry, zero, sign, and signed overflow and composes them through the
next-PC theorem. It does not prove that the supplied result was produced by
architectural addition.
All five x86 binary SBB operand-form handlers now obtain `a-b-borrow` from one shared
C/Lean expression contract. Lean proves its 64-bit modular result and the
per-width narrowing of that result against independent specifications. This
closes the earlier supplied-result premise for those handler expressions. A
separate generated SBB flag contract covers borrow-in, zero, sign, and overflow
and composes the result/narrowing layers as well as the next-PC decision. Its
overflow test compares the original operands with the final result; using the
wrapped `b+borrow` value is incorrect at boundaries such as 8-bit
`0-127-1=-128`. Decoder selection and sign-mask derivation remain open.
The five x86 ADC binary operand forms use a dedicated generated result and
flag contract. This preserves carry-in through width overflow instead of
folding it into an ordinary ADD operand, and Lean composes modular
`a+b+carry`, per-width narrowing, ADC flags, and next-PC. Decoder selection and
sign-mask derivation remain outside the theorem.
Plain ADD in the central ALU result helper is the zero-carry specialization of
the same generated modular-addition contract. Lean composes that concrete
result, per-width narrowing, and the existing ADD flag transition, eliminating
ADD's earlier free-result premise while retaining decoder/compiler boundaries.
Plain SUB in the central ALU result helper similarly specializes the generated
SBB result contract to `borrow=false`. Lean composes that concrete result,
per-width narrowing, the width-derived sign mask, and the SUB flag transition;
comparison instructions and decoder/compiler boundaries are not covered by
this central-helper theorem. The five compare operand forms separately use the
same generated zero-borrow result and SUB flags contracts; Lean composes that
width-aware compare transition through the condition-to-next-PC decision.
The same generated width contract now supplies the sign-bit mask used by the
C ADD, SUB, ADC, and SBB flag wrappers. The width-aware ADD, ADC, and SBB step
theorems derive that mask from operand width rather than accepting a free
`sign` argument, and Lean checks that mask testing equals the independent sign
observation for every legal width. Decoder-to-handler and C-to-Lean language
correspondence remain boundaries.
The 16 accepted ALU mnemonics and numeric operation codes are generated into
the proof-artifact encoder's Python mapping, the C simulator constants, and
Lean. Lean checks both fields against an independent enumeration. This binds an
already parsed mnemonic to the C ALU code consumed by the handlers; objdump,
assembly parsing, operand-form selection, and handler semantics outside the
separately proved operations remain boundaries.
The 36 accepted `jcc`/`cmovcc`/`setcc` condition mnemonics are likewise
generated from `x86_cc_decode_spec.json` into the encoder's Python `CC_AUX`
mapping, the C `generated/x86_cc_decode.h`, and Lean. Each mnemonic is a family
prefix plus a condition suffix; the generator re-reads `x86_cond_spec.json` on
every `--check` and rejects a suffix that names no condition, so the 12 suffixes
the encoder reaches are exactly the condition contract's names minus the parity
pair `o`/`no`. Lean checks the generated mnemonic, token, and code projection
against an independent enumeration and each code against the shared condition
contract. This binds the encoder's *condition* text to the C condition code
consumed by the evaluators; assembly parsing and the rest of the textual
mnemonic remain boundaries.
The 17 accepted AArch64 condition mnemonics are generated the same way from
`arm64_cc_decode_spec.json` into the encoder's Python `COND` mapping, the C
`generated/arm64_cc_decode.h`, and Lean. The generator re-reads
`arm64_cond_spec.json` on every `--check` and rejects a mnemonic that names no
condition; the 15 canonical mnemonics name every condition exactly once, and
the two architectural aliases `hs`/`lo` name the same conditions as `cs`/`cc`,
so the 17 mnemonics cover 15 distinct codes. Lean checks the generated
`(mnemonic, token, code)` projection against an independent enumeration, each
code against the shared condition contract, the canonical mnemonics against the
full condition order, and the alias set and alias-equal-code facts
(`arm64_cc_decode_alias_same_code`). This binds the encoder's *condition* text
to the C condition code the evaluators consume; assembly parsing and the rest
of the textual mnemonic remain boundaries.
The 61 AArch64 BPF helper-ident rows are generated the same way from
`arm64_helper_idents_spec.json` into the encoder's Python
`generated_arm64_helper_idents.py`, the C `generated/arm64_helper_idents.h`
(the `KPROG_ARM64_HELPER_ROW` by-id selector with its out-of-range default and
