The AArch64 packed-AUX layout contract binds the `KPROG_ARM64_AUX` packer and
its four `KPROG_ARM64_AUX_B0..B3` lane decoders plus the
`KPROG_ARM64_AUX_REG_NONE` sentinel — the 32-bit operand word the simulator's
ALU, shift, MOVK, memory, bitfield and CCMP handlers share, with lane 0 (ALU
opcode / memory index register / bitfield kind / shift kind) in bits 0-7, lane
1 (source modifier / bitfield LSB / CCMP NZCV) in bits 8-15, lane 2 (shift
amount / bitfield width / MOVK column) in bits 16-23, and the memory-flag byte
in bits 24-31. `Arm64Aux.lean` proves the four lane decoders recover exactly
the packed bytes, that the lanes do not interfere, and that the
`ARM64_REG_NONE` sentinel round-trips; the six simulator packers
(`ARM64_AUX`, `_ALU`, `_SHIFT`, `_MOVK`, `_MEM`, `_BITFIELD`, `_CCMP`) and seven
simulator decoders (`ARM64_SIM_L_MOD`, `_SHIFT`, `_MEM_INDEX`, `_MEM_FLAGS`,
`_BITFIELD_LSB`, `_BITFIELD_WIDTH`, `_CCMP_NZCV`) are thin aliases of that one
machine-checked layout, so the *lane assignment* the handlers share is no longer
in the trusted computing base. The sim-header route oracle drives the real
decoders and packers against an independent `(aux >> 8k) & 0xff` restatement and
the host cross-check drives the generated macros directly (1,115,374 and 586,829
cases).

The AArch64 stack-arena storage contract binds `KPROG_ARM64_STACK_WORD_INDEX`,
`KPROG_ARM64_STACK_WORD_ALIGNED`, `KPROG_ARM64_STACK_WORDS`, and
`KPROG_ARM64_STACK_TAG_SLOTS` — the arithmetic the simulator's stack helpers
use to reach the arena, a union of two overlapping views
(`__u8 b[ARM64_SIM_STACK_BYTES]` and
`__u64 q[KPROG_ARM64_STACK_WORDS(ARM64_SIM_STACK_BYTES)]`, 160 bytes and 20
qwords when the arena is enabled). `Arm64StackArena.lean` proves the generated
word-slot shift and alignment guard equal independent quotient/remainder
statements, proves the rounded-up word count covers the capacity without
wasting a whole slot, proves a word-aligned index times eight round-trips, and
proves the word arena's byte 0 is the value's low byte, so the 64-bit fast path
through `q[]` and the byte path through `b[]` reach the same storage. The
AArch64 stack-index contract binds `KPROG_ARM64_STACK_INDEX(OFF, BIAS)` and
`KPROG_ARM64_STACK_PTR_INDEX(OFF, BIAS)`, the map from an abstract frame offset
to a byte index in the biased arena: the offset is added to the bias
(`ARM64_SIM_STACK_BIAS`, 96) and truncated to the helpers' 32-bit index type, so
the frame base lands at index 0 and an offset of zero at byte `bias`.
`Arm64StackIndex.lean` proves the generated truncation equal to an independent
low-32-bits statement, proves the frame base lands at zero, proves the index is
affine in the offset, and proves that two offsets differing by a multiple of
`2^32` alias. The host cross-checks drive the *real* generated macros over
capacity/index/value grids and exhaustive sweeps (70,558 and 536 cases), and the
sim-header route oracle drives the real `ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_{INDEX,WRITE,
WRITE_TAG,READ,READ_TAG,PTR}` helpers against an independently maintained byte
and tag arena over the full frame window, every width and tag (2,754,329 cases).

The correspondence between C unsigned bit operations and Lean `BitVec`
operations remains a trusted language-semantics premise; these theorems do not
verify the C compiler or native instruction bytes.

This is still a deliberately bounded proof. It does not establish full
equivalence between the simulator and native instruction bytes, cover complete
instruction decoding/dispatch, helpers, or the full workload-derived instruction
subsets, or prove the paper's complete O1--O4 obligations. The proved branch
predicates and the AArch64 and x86 emitted-shape bridges are local control-flow
refinements (one conditional edge at a time); the whole-program control-flow
trace contract chains those edges over arbitrary-length paths, but the emitted
shapes are still not tied to concrete native instruction bytes.

### Step 0763 - the repaint applies and the host still passes

The battery that reported one failure repaints the LEA RODATA gate from a named
constant to zero, and the routed oracle does not notice: it compiles against the
mutated header and passes. Measured by applying the repaint by hand, compiling
the host with the harness's own include flags, and running it.

So the row is right to fail. The gate change is real and the detector is blind
to it, which means the harness's hundred and fifteen other passing rows say less
about that body than the totals suggest: a row whose stage cannot observe its
repaint reports a pass whichever way the repaint goes.

Every other mutation string in the battery still matches its file, so the
repaints are applying; what this one shows is a gap between the repaint and the
detector rather than a stale string. Census 631 -> 632.

### Step 0762 - measuring the battery count turned up a battery that
is not green

The section says three hundred and thirty mutation batteries re-derive the
failure of the contract each anchors, and nothing counted them. The figure is
the files under the build directory, so the tree states it, and it matches
today.

Measuring that surface turned up a battery that is not green. One harness row
repaints a line whose trailing whitespace has since changed by two spaces, so
the repaint matches nothing, nothing drifts, and the row that expects a catch
reports none. The harness reports one failure in a hundred and sixteen mutations
and prints a mismatch.

The row is a real defect in the battery rather than in the section, and it is
recorded here rather than fixed: the harness is an untracked build file, and
changing its mutation strings is a change to the instrument. Census 630 -> 631.

### Step 0761 - a claim is not a figure, and the line reported only
one of them

The success line reports a hundred and fifty-four claims, and a claim is not a
figure: one figure is often stated in two sentences, and one sentence often
states two. The line now reports both, so a reader can see that the run accounts
for a hundred and twenty-six distinct case figures rather than a hundred and
fifty-four claims.

The difference is not cosmetic. A checker that matched each claim would still
leave a figure unread if that figure appeared only in a form the claim patterns
miss, and the count of claims would not show it. The distinct figure is what the
section states; the claim is what the pattern found.

Every one of the hundred and twenty-six resolves, either to a banner or to the
grid arithmetic on a bare grid, which is the other thing the checker has always
accepted. Census 629 -> 630.

### Step 0760 - the sentence states the count and its reason, and both
are in the contract

The section says the reached condition suffixes are exactly the shared
contract's names minus the parity pair. That sentence states the count and the
reason for it together, and both come from the contract: fourteen names, two of
them the parity pair, twelve reached.

The pair is the whole point of the figure. A contract that grew a condition
would leave the sentence describing a set one short, and the sentence would
still read as a statement about the contract rather than about a past reading of
it.

This is the same join as the cell counts, on a set rather than a table, and it
is the cheapest kind: the two figures the sentence relates are both in one file.
Census 628 -> 629.

### Step 0759 - a present-tense claim had frozen a count from the step
that wrote it

The section says the route hosts the mutation batteries drive are pinned into
the gate recipe, and it said seven. The recipe now names fourteen of them, every
route host under the build directory, so the sentence had frozen the number from
the step that first pinned five of them.

It is a present-tense claim rather than a record of that step, which is why the
number mattered: a reader taking it as a description of the gate would think six
hosts were still unpinned. Both halves are now checked, the stated count against
the number the recipe names and that number against the hosts on disk.

The check also catches the failure the sentence is about. A route host present
but not named by the recipe is exactly the state the sentence denies, and one
added without a recipe line now reports itself. Census 627 -> 628.

### Step 0758 - the failing message names the checkout, not the
sentences

The row claims resolve to nothing on an unbuilt checkout, and the message blamed
the sentences. It now names the two things a built tree needs and reports
whichever is short: how many modules have object files, and how many files the
ignored build directory holds against how many of them are tracked.

On a clone the message reads as zero of three hundred and six modules built, and
four build files present and four tracked. That is the whole diagnosis, and it
is what a reader needs before deciding whether a sentence is wrong or the
checkout is.

The two figures are computed from the tree each time rather than written down,
so a tree that becomes complete stops reporting anything. Census 626 -> 627.

### Step 0757 - the gate could not run on a clone of the repository

A clone of this repository could not run the gate. Two separate causes, both
measured on a fresh checkout rather than reasoned about: twenty of the three
hundred and six Lean modules are elaborated only by the gate's own per-module
lines, and those lines do not write object files, so the axiom census reads a
partial tree; and most of the mutation harnesses live under an ignored build
directory, so the row claims resolve to nothing.

The first is the sharper of the two. The gate names all twenty modules, so it
does elaborate them on a tree that was built once, and the difference never
shows there. On a clone, `lake build` covers two hundred and eighty-six of the
three hundred and six, and the twenty that remain are exactly the ones the
per-module lines exist for.

The readme now says to build first, and the failing message says which two
things a built tree needs. A nondeterministic `bv_decide` timeout in one module,
which succeeds on retry, is noted but not changed: it is a property of the
solver rather than of the tree. Census 625 -> 626.

### Step 0756 - a short checkout makes every join find nothing, which
looks green

The row counts this checker reads come from mutation harnesses under the build
directory, and a fresh clone holds four of the three hundred and thirty on disk.
Every join then finds no harness, which reads exactly like a sentence that is
simply right, so a checkout holding a fraction of the tree would report the same
green line as the full one.

The population is now stated: a harness set far smaller than the tracked set is
reported, because the counts describe the tree on disk rather than whatever the
caller happened to have. It does not fail the gate, since the gate does not run
this checker at all, but a reader running it on a fresh clone learns why the
figures went unread.

This is the same lesson as the swallowed parse error, one step further out.
There the population was harnesses the extractor could not parse; here it is
harnesses the checkout does not have. In both cases a smaller population makes
the check quieter, never louder. Census 624 -> 625.

### Step 0755 - the success line named three of the things it had just
checked

The line the checker prints when it passes named three of the things it had just
verified: the case counts, the two gate totals, and the split across simulators.
It now names four, adding the figures the section states about itself, which is
where the axiom partition, the census sequence and the cell counts live.

The count of claim classes was left out on purpose. A number in the message
would be a claim about the checker that nothing recomputes, which is exactly
what the two docstrings corrected a step ago had become; naming the classes is
what a reader needs to know whether their sentence was covered.

Reading the message is how a reader decides that, so a message that undercounts
the checks is a check that looks narrower than it is. Census 623 -> 624.

### Step 0754 - two docstrings counted sentences the section no longer
holds

Five docstrings in the checker state how many sentences carry the pattern the
function reads, and three of those counts are still right. The other two had
drifted: one says eight sentences where the section now holds five, the other
seventeen where the pattern the function reads is stated in eleven.

Rather than correct them to today's numbers, both now say only that the
sentences exist, because the count is not what the function checks. A number
written into a docstring is a claim nobody recomputes, and the two that were
wrong had been wrong for many steps without anything noticing.

The three that remain are ones the function itself would break on if they moved:
the growing harness is required to be recorded at five sizes, and the section is
required to hold the nine banners it says stayed at. Those are checked, so they

### Step 0753 - the check's own description had drifted from the code

and that gap is deliberate.

Census 585 -> 586.

### Step 0716 - the count-valued probes follow the count

Two probes named a count: the message a generator raises, and the banner total a
full run prints. Both were correct when written and both would go stale the
moment either count moved, which is the same decay the readme probe had in the
previous step.

They now read the count from the file and move it, so the probe follows whatever
the count becomes. Moving the recorded constant by one and asking what the probe
would target gave the new value plus two, which is what the derivation means.

Three of the harness's probes now derive their perturbation, and the four that
name an opcode, a truncation length and an id are structural: those values are
properties of the encoding rather than of the current run, so naming them is
right. Census 585 -> 586.

### Step 0715 - both key fields, and a probe that could not go stale

The distinctness check read the opcode code alone. A row's name keys every table
that has one and a code keys the opcode tables, so both are checked now, over
every table in every specification. A duplicate is reported with the table and
the field, not just the value.

That widening had to distinguish a key from a decision output. One specification
holds thirty-two rows mapping four booleans to an arm name, and the arm repeats
because the table is a decision, not a key; reading it as a duplicate would have
been a false finding on a correct table.

The harness's readme probe named the current census figure, so it went stale the
moment the figure moved. It now reads the figure from the file and moves it.

Census 584 -> 585.

### Step 0714 - one property behind twelve routing claims

A sweep of the word exactly found twelve claims of the form selects exactly one,
and most rest on the same property: the numbers a table holds are pairwise
distinct, so dispatch on the numeric code resolves to one arm. A repeated code
makes the selection ambiguous and every such sentence false at once.

The property holds across all one hundred and thirty-eight specifications.
Duplicating one code in the BT table is reported by specification and by the
code, which is what the sentence about that chain asserts.

This is the widest-reaching invariant found so far: a single distinctness
property backs twelve sentences about routing, and it is checked over every
specification rather than the three the sentences happen to name. Census 584 ->
585.

### Step 0713 - the two checks outside the gate, and a probe that
disabled nothing

The harness covered the ten checks the gate runs and not the two it leaves out,
which are the two that need a log the gate is producing. Both are now probes:
the paper checker against a changed banner count in the section, and the readme
checker against a moved census figure. Twelve checks name their break.

The paper probe needed a claim written on one line. The first target was a
sentence that wraps across three, and a substitution on raw text does not see
it, which is the same wrapping trap that has caught several censuses this
session. A one-line claim about the banner count settled it.

The harness was verified by disabling a check, and the verification itself took
two attempts: the first substituted an exit line that one script does not use,
so nothing was disabled and the harness reported that check as passing. Both are
now recorded, because a probe that fails to disable anything looks exactly like
a check that fires. Census 583 -> 584.

### Step 0712 - all ten checks, and a baseline that was wrong

The harness covered eight of the ten checks the gate runs. The two it missed
were the one that scans headers for an unparenthesized macro operand and the one
that binds the theorem counts, and both are now probes: a synthetic header whose
parameter sits bare beside a plus, and a recorded constant moved by two.

The header probe exposed a design fault in the harness. Its baseline ran with
the probe file already present, so the check failed before the probe and the
harness reported the wrong reason; then the recovery run still passed the file
as an argument, so it reported a recovery that never happened. A probe that has
to create a file needs both runs to omit it.

With that fixed, all ten checks name their break. The harness was tested again
by disabling one of them, which is reported as that check staying green after
its probe, and the tree is unchanged after every run. Census 582 -> 583.

### Step 0711 - the audit becomes a script, and the script is
tested too
The perturbation audit was eight manual experiments, and a manual experiment
decays: it proves the check fired once, in one session, and says nothing about
the next. The experiments are now a script that walks the checks the gate runs,
introduces the defect each exists to catch, and requires a non-zero exit naming
the break.
It restores every file it touches and compares the tree with git afterwards, so
a probe that leaks a change is itself a failure. The script is not a gate
target: it edits the tree, runs each check twice, and the mutation harness alone
takes fifteen seconds.
The script was tested for the same property it tests. Making one check always
exit zero is reported as that check staying green after its probe, so a harness
that quietly stops working is caught as well as a check that does. Census 581 -> 582.

### Step 0710 - the last two scripts, and all nine now fail when
broken

The last two scripts were broken too. A helper id moved by one was reported as
the name, the spec id and the kernel id it should have had; and a generator
whose validation was disabled let its mutation survive, which was reported by
generator, by the literal that changed, and by the guarded count dropping from
twenty-nine to twenty-eight.

The second took three attempts because the mutation harness edits the first
meaningful numeric literal in a quoted string, and the generator chosen first
has none, so weakening its validation could not matter. Choosing one that the
harness does mutate settled it.

That is the same lesson as the macro check: a perturbation has to enter the
defect's population, and a wrong perturbation looks identical to a check that
does not work. All nine scripts the gate runs now fail when broken, each naming

### Step 0709 - three more checks, each naming the disagreement

Three more checks were broken in the way each exists to catch. A host that
includes the simulator header and calls a composed contract without driving the
composition was reported by host and macro, with the two remedies named. A
generator whose coverage note names a host that does not exist was reported by
generator and note. A recorded dispatch predicate the chain does not branch on
was reported by predicate and host.

All three name what disagreed rather than merely failing, and the first and
third also say what to do about it. That is the difference between a check a
reader can act on and one that sends them to the source.

Eight of the nine scripts the gate runs have now been broken on purpose and
reported the break. The ninth is the one whose sub-claims are many and whose
perturbations were already exercised while writing it, in steps 0652 and 0653.
Census 579 -> 580.

### Step 0708 - two more checks, broken the way they exist to catch
Two more checks were tested by perturbation. A conditional-jump opcode moved by
one was reported as the mnemonic it disagrees with and the condition code each
value implies, and a truncation length changed from fifteen to sixteen was
reported as the two lengths the sides now use.
Both name the disagreement rather than merely failing, which is what makes a
perturbation test worth running: a check that exits non-zero without saying what
is wrong is only half checked, and neither of these does that.
The five checked so far cover the three kinds of assertion in the gate: an
absence, a shape, and an agreement between two independently written sides. Each
was broken in the way it exists to catch, and each reported the break. Census
578 -> 579. Census 578 -> 579.

### Step 0707 - three checks tested by perturbation, and the
population problem

The third question about the checkers is whether a check fails when it should.
Three were tested by perturbation: a sorry appended to a module, a macro whose
parameter is used as a bare operand of a sum, and a header citing a module that
does not exist. Each was reported by file and symbol, and each left the tree
unchanged after restoration.

The macro check took four attempts because the defect it looks for is narrow. A
parameter written as a parenthesized operand is clean even inside a larger
expression, and so is one nested two levels deep; only a parameter with no
parentheses of its own, adjoining a binary operator, is the defect. A synthetic
header settled it in one line.

That is worth recording as a property of the checks rather than of the paper:
their population is precise, and a perturbation that misses it looks exactly
like a check that does not work. The same subtlety applied to four of my own
censuses this session, where the check under-read its pattern while the sentence
was right. Census 577 -> 578.

### Step 0706 - every check script is invoked, which is not the same
as existing

The call-graph audit asked whether every function is reachable from main. The
question underneath it is whether every check is invoked at all: a script that
exists and is never run passes by not running, and from outside that looks the
same as passing.

Nine check scripts are in the gate, and the two that are not are the ones that
need a log the gate is still producing, so neither can run alongside it. The
readme checker now compares the gate's invocations with the scripts on disk, so
a check dropped from the recipe is reported by name and by count.

It also confirmed that the two scripts which declare a check flag and are
invoked without it do not depend on it: one never reads the argument, and the
other behaves identically either way. That is a wart rather than a defect, and
it is written down here so the next reader does not re-derive it. Census 576 ->
577.

### Step 0705 - a call graph, not a search for names

The audit that found the uncalled citation check was by name reference, which
catches an orphan but not a function reachable only from another orphan. A
call-graph pass from main closes that: no function in either checker is
unreachable from the entry point.

It found one in the paper checker, a nested helper left over from the shake
rewrite. It was never called, and it iterated an empty list, so it would have
returned false for every input if it had been. Both faults are invisible to a
reader who sees the docstring rather than the call sites.

The other eleven check scripts and the axiom census are fully reachable too.
Dead code in a checker is worse than dead code elsewhere: an uncalled check and
a passing check look the same from the outside, and the gate reports both as
green. Census 575 -> 576.

### Step 0704 - a check that was written and never called

While auditing the checkers for dead code, one function in the Lean checker
turned out never to be called: the one that reads each simulator guard's claim
that its macro is the generated, proved bound of a named module. The check was
written, worked, and had simply never been wired into the run.

It is now called. Three guards make that claim, and all three name a module that
carries a refinement for the macro. Pointing one at a module that does not exist
is reported by macro name and module, which is the failure the function was
written for and never had a chance to catch.

That is the dead-code rule earning its place in the other direction from usual:
not a function nobody needs, but a check nobody ran. Its absence was invisible
because a check that is never called and a check that passes look the same from
outside. Census 574 -> 575.

### Step 0703 - one memory row in the BT table, and its index

A seventh absolute claim says the bracket-without-PTR fixture is the only shape
reaching the BT memory-immediate width default. That rests on the opcode table:
exactly one row reads memory, and the row that does takes an immediate index,
which is the shape a fixture with no PTR suffix produces.

The table confirms it. Three rows, one of which reads memory, and that row's
index is the immediate form, so it is the only one whose encoding omits the
pointer suffix and falls through to the width default. A second memory-base row
is reported with both the count and whether the index is still immediate.

Seven absolute claims have now been checked and all seven were true. That is the
pattern of this tier: the claims were written while looking at the structure, so
confirming them is cheap and correcting them has not been needed. Census 573 ->
574.

### Step 0702 - the equal case, computed rather than asserted

A sixth absolute claim is arithmetic again: the equal case is the only one
separating a subtract carry stated as greater-or-equal from one stated as
strictly greater. The sentence uses it to explain why a table of distinct
operands never found a fault of that shape.

Computing over a grid of operands confirms it. The two predicates differ on
seventeen pairs and every one of them has equal operands, so a table restricted
to distinct registers exercises neither side of the difference. That is exactly
the gap the sentence says the first draft had.

The check recomputes the identity rather than trusting the prose, and it is
verified by substituting a comparison that differs off equality and watching the
count come back with pairs that are not equal. Census 572 -> 573.

### Step 0701 - the fifth absolute claim, and all five hold

A fifth absolute claim says two writes agree at the only width the outer gate
opens, which it names as sixty-four. That rests on the width specification: the
absent code must fall back to a 64-bit default, and exactly one width may carry
64 bits.

The specification confirms it. Four widths at codes one, two, four and eight,
with the absent code falling back to the wide one, and only that width carrying
64 bits. Adding a second 64-bit width is reported twice, once as the count and
once as the codes no longer being the four the simulator resolves.

Five absolute claims have now been checked and all five were true. The sequence
is worth recording as a result in itself: the claims were written by someone
reading the structures they describe, so the checks confirm rather than correct,
and their value is that the confirmation repeats whenever the structure moves.
Census 571 -> 572.

### Step 0700 - the half of a two-effect claim a contract decides

A fourth absolute claim says the store-exclusive body is the only one of its
remainder with two observable effects, because it writes the source to memory
and then a status word to the destination. The second half of that is a property
of the contract rather than of prose: the status must derive from the width mask
and must be proved zero at every width.

The contract confirms it. The spec is the width mask subtracted from itself,
which is the exclusive-monitor success encoding, and a theorem states it is zero
by case analysis over the opcode and the four widths. Removing the subtraction
is reported as the status no longer being derived from the mask.

So the sentence's two-effect structure has one half that a contract decides and
one half, the memory write, that only the simulator body shows. The check covers
the half it can and the step says which half that is, rather than implying the
whole claim is bound. Census 570 -> 571.

### Step 0699 - a join to a set, and the attribution it cannot see

Seventeen sentences say a harness retargets the generator's re-check messages
and give the count: two, four, five, six, seven, eight, ten, twelve. Each is a
count of the messages a generator can raise, which is a figure in the
generator's own source.

The sentence names no generator, so the join is to the set of counts any
generator can raise rather than to one file. That catches a figure with no
source at all, and it cannot catch a figure attached to the wrong generator, so
the weakness is written where the check is.

The counts hold: all eight stated values are counts some generator has. This is
the same join shape as the harness sizes, and it carries the same caveat, which
is why it is stated in the docstring rather than left for a reader to discover.
Census 569 -> 570.

### Step 0698 - an absolute claim that is arithmetic, not structure

A third absolute claim is arithmetic rather than structural: the most negative
value paired with minus one is the single pair whose product is exactly the
negative bound, and therefore the only place the two candidate overflow bounds
disagree. Nothing in the tree decides it; the numbers do.

Computing over the operand pairs that can reach the bound gives one unordered
pair, the two orders of the same operands. And over a grid of the extremes, no
pair makes the two tests disagree, which is what the sentence's therefore
depends on: the disagreement is about magnitude, and only this pair sits exactly
on it.

So the claim stands on its own arithmetic, and the check recomputes it rather
than trusting the prose. The guard was verified by asserting a different count
and watching it fire. Census 568 -> 569.

### Step 0697 - one gate in the arm table, and four widths
A second sentence of the same shape says the default arm is the only gated one
and that the ladder is total over the resolved width codes. Both halves are

The table confirms it. Four arms, at width codes one, two, four and eight, and
exactly one of them carries the overflow gate, on the full-width arm which is
the default. Adding a gate to a second arm is now reported with the count and
the sentence it contradicts.
Two sentences of this shape have now been checked and both were true, which is
the expected result: an absolute claim written by someone who knew the table is
usually right, and the check is what keeps it right when the table moves. Census
567 -> 568. Census 567 -> 568.

### Step 0696 - the cell table's contiguity is the claim

A sentence says that unlike the AArch64 mirror there is no zero register to
omit, so the only register number that is not a cell is the all-ones sentinel.
That is a claim about the cell table rather than about prose: the numbers must
run contiguously from zero, and the sentinel must sit outside them.

Both hold. The x86 table holds sixteen cells numbered zero to fifteen, and the
arm64 table thirty-one numbered zero to thirty, which is what the sentence's
contrast with AArch64 refers to. A cell number moved out of range is now

The claim needed no number of its own to check; it needed the structure the
numbers imply. That is the sixth mechanism this campaign has used, after the
log, the tree, derived populations, partitions and historical series: an
invariant over a table whose contiguity is what makes the sentence true.

Census 566 -> 567.

### Step 0695 - five unread numerals, and all five explained

A final sweep asked, for every hyphenated numeral in the section, whether

So the section's numerals are now read by one of six mechanisms -- the log, the

### Step 0694 - a partition that names no harness size

Five sentences describe a harness by what it plants and what it keeps: a hundred
and forty-nine rows that plant a hundred and seven catches and keep forty-two

All five do. The form went unread because it names neither a harness size nor a

The sweep found it by counting every claim of the form rows, rather than by

### Step 0693 - eighteen caught counts, and the shares that reach

Eighteen sentences say how many mutations a battery caught and then name, in the

All eighteen reach it exactly. The sweep that found them listed every numeral

That is the third time in this stretch that a check under-read its own pattern,

### Step 0692 - the second-largest figure, and its seven terms

One sentence accounts for what a sweep added to the recipe: twelve million two

Each of the seven resolves to a banner, so this decomposition can be checked

It is the only sentence of its shape, and it went unread because its phrasing is
unlike the counts, the products and the partitions the other patterns look for.

### Step 0691 - the same figure in two spellings, one of them read

The same host is sized twice in the section, once as four thousand four hundred
and seventy with the thousands brace-grouped and once as the bare digits, and
the check read only the first. The two sentences differ in one punctuation mark:
one puts the figure in parentheses after the host path, the other after a comma.

Both are claims about the same host, so both have to resolve to the same banner.
The check now reads either punctuation and either numeral spelling, and either
one drifting is reported against the run.

That is the smallest form of the pattern this stretch has been finding: a claim
written twice, in slightly different clothes, with a check that recognised one
of the clothes. The brace-grouped numeral and the bare numeral are the same
number, and a reader sees no difference at all. Census 561 -> 562.

### Step 0690 - a tense, not an arithmetic, distinction

One paragraph records a step that added an oracle to the recipe and ends by
saying the gate prints two hundred and twenty cross-check banners, was two
hundred and twelve. The summary elsewhere in the same section says a full run
passes two hundred and forty-eight. Both numbers were true of their own moment,
but the paragraph's verb was present tense, so a reader would take two hundred
and twenty for the current count.

The verb now says what happened: the gate then printed those banners, up from
two hundred and twelve. The current figure has a single present-tense statement,
and the aggregate that binds it is what catches a change to it.

The lesson is about tense rather than arithmetic. Twenty-one sentences record a
gate's banner count at the step that changed it, and every one was accurate when
written; only the one phrased in the present could be misread as a claim about

### Step 0689 - a partition in a third word order

A sweep of numerals by the noun they count turned up eighteen mentions of rows
that no check read, because the bound patterns looked for specific phrasings:
rows that catch, rows that split by stage, and a fraction of rows caught. The
eighteenths state the same partition in a third word order.

One says the harness has fifty-nine rows, of which fifty-seven catch and two
survive. That is the partition the other forms state, written as a total and two
of its parts instead of a fraction, and it was the one shape the census did not
read. Fifty-seven and two are fifty-nine, and the check now requires it.

The sweep is what found it: counting numerals by their noun, rather than by the
phrase around them, is what surfaces a figure whose sentence happens to be
worded differently from its neighbours. Census 559 -> 560.

### Step 0688 - every number in the checkers now has a rule

The checker held seventeen numbers that guard completeness: how many files the
section cites, how many sweep claims it makes, how many shake claims, how many
stage splits. Those are not figures the run computes, so they cannot be derived;
they are the count of claims in a family, and their job is to notice a claim
added or removed. All seventeen are exact.

The one of them that is a figure rather than a family size is the file count, so
it was verified against the section directly: forty-seven distinct file names,
each resolving in the tree. Looking for names outside the texttt spans, which
the file census would not see, found one fragment of a build path and no real
citation.

So the derived-versus-written rule now covers every number in both checkers.
What the run computes is derived; what the paper states is read from the paper;
what only the agreement of two independent measurements establishes stays
written and guarded by its identity; and what counts the size of a claim family
stays written because it is the guard. Census 558 -> 559.

### Step 0687 - the scene check reads the prose, not a third copy
The scene check compared the counts it measured against two numbers written in
the checker. That is the same shape the percentage guard had: a measured value
held against a memory of itself, so a sentence and a file were both being
compared with a third hand-written copy rather than with each other.
The counts are now read from the prose, the way the checker reads every other
figure, and compared with the file. That also makes the check see a drift in
either direction: a host that loses a scene, or a sentence that miscounts one,
is reported with both numbers.
The prose writes these counts as numerals rather than words, which the first
version of the change did not handle and so skipped silently -- a check that
reads nothing and reports nothing looks exactly like a check that passes. Census
557 -> 558. Census 557 -> 558.

### Step 0686 - the guard derives the values it guards

The percentage guard kept its set of expected values as written-down strings,
including the four bucket shares, the two tree shares, and the total the four
sum to. Every one of those is computed elsewhere in the same run, so the guard
was comparing measured percentages against a memory of them.

The set is now derived: the four bucket shares come from the buckets the split
already built, their floored sum is computed rather than written, and the two
tree shares come from the checker that owns those populations. The guard's
purpose is unchanged -- a percentage the section states that nothing accounts
for is reported -- and a fabricated seventy-seven is still caught.

This is the same asymmetry the host decomposition showed: a value that the run
computes cannot be wrong, so restating it by hand only adds a place for it to
drift. The guard now has no hand-written figure in it. Census 556 -> 557.

### Step 0685 - five axis decompositions, bounded rather than
reconstructed

Five hosts state their size as axes: four widths by seven seed rows by five
immediates, four widths by eight seed rows by four shift amounts, and three
larger grids of scenes by checks. The axes are hand-written while the totals are
generated, which is the asymmetry that hid the fifteen-hundred and thirty-six
scene host's wrong check count.

The invariant that covers all five without knowing the remaining axes is that
the stated axes multiply to at most the total. An axis product over the banner
is arithmetic that cannot be true whatever follows it; a product under the
banner has room for the axes the sentence continues with.

Two of the five also state their remainder, seven selector cases and sixteen,
and there the product and the remainder must reach the total exactly, which is
what caught the check count. The other three leave the remainder to further
axes, so the bound is all that can be said. Census 555 -> 556.

### Step 0684 - a decomposition that did not reach its banner

Two battery-local hosts state their size as a product: so many scenes times so
many checks, plus a handful of selector cases. Both hosts run in the gate, so
the total is a banner and cannot be wrong; the product is prose and can. One of
the two was wrong: fifteen hundred and thirty-six scenes at sixty-four checks
reaches ninety-eight thousand three hundred and twenty, and the host prints
ninety-nine thousand eight hundred and fifty-six.

The total settles which factor moved. The host drives four directions as one
axis, and its per-scene grid is a hundred and twenty-eight cells, so the scene
count must divide by a hundred and twenty-eight; fifteen hundred and thirty-six
does and fifteen hundred and sixty does not. The check count is therefore
sixty-five, and fifteen hundred and thirty-six times sixty-five plus sixteen is
the banner exactly.

This is the first defect found in a decomposition rather than in a total, and it
survived because the total is generated while the decomposition is written by
hand. The check now multiplies the stated parts and compares them with the
stated total, and requires that total to be a banner. Census 554 -> 555.

### Step 0683 - two words that name a spec, and one that did not

Two more shared sizes are identified by the words their sentence uses: a harness
retargeting the lane specification is the byte-lane one, and one retargeting the
offset and prepost spec is the memory-offset one. Both are checked by size as
well, and both resolve.

The join is weaker than a name and is used sparingly. A single prose word can
match the wrong specification: the path specification's harness has the same
size as four others, and one of those has offset in its name, so a word match
sent the path sentence to the wrong file. Only words that are themselves a
segment of the spec's name are accepted, which keeps lane and offset and drops
path.

That rule resolves two of the forty-three rather than three, and the third was
excluded because it was wrong rather than because it was hard. The count of
exactly-identified harnesses is now fourteen. Census 553 -> 554.

### Step 0682 - a count that reads like an enumeration is a field
length

Eleven sentences state a count and then list the items in a parenthetical: four
fields, two arms, two masks, two kinds, and so on. Ten of them list exactly as
many items as they claim. The eleventh lists its items with nested commas, so a
comma splitter counted two where the prose says eleven.

The eleven is right, and it is not a count of prose at all: the modifier
specification holds eleven operations, one empty and four shifts and six
extends. So a claim that reads like a careful enumeration is in fact a field
length, and it can be checked against the file rather than against the sentence.

That is the distinction these censuses keep finding. A count of items in a list
is arithmetic on prose; a count of operations in a specification is a figure
with a source. The second is checkable, and it is what the sentence turns out to
be. Census 552 -> 553.

### Step 0681 - a step number is a pointer into the record

Four sentences cite a numbered step for provenance: the batteries of 0454, 0456,
0457 and 0458 are named as the origin of figures the section reuses. A step
number means nothing on its own; it is a pointer into the record, and a pointer
into a record that does not hold it is worse than no pointer.

All four resolve against the README's history, and the check now requires it.
This is the first cross-document reference the paper check has made: the
section's citations were checked against the tree, and this one is checked
against the record the numbers index.

It also closes a class that no other check could see. A step number is not a
figure and not a file, so neither the count census nor the identifier census
would notice a miscited number, and the prose would read exactly the same.

### Step 0680 - a row count in the sentence is a join a name could
not give

Three sentences give a specification's row count beside the harness size: the

Two of the three resolve exactly. Six rows belongs to only one specification of
that size, and fifteen rows to one more; the two-row case is shared by four,
because a two-row specification is common. So the join is exact where the row

This is the strongest harness join available without editing the prose, because

joins two of the thirty-three shared sizes, bringing the exact set to twelve and

### Step 0679 - five figures in one sentence, all derived from

A sentence states five figures about the decision procedure in one breath: the

Forty-three distinct harness sizes are stated, and only ten of them belong to a

split, because the split is into two groups rather than four, but it needs no

The shake check joined by size alone. It now joins on the family word that opens

Joining a shake to its harness by the module the paragraph names is better than

### Step 0673 - a field is exercised by its value, not only by its
key

Fifteen sentences say a shake exercised every field of its specification. That

Three of the fifteen row counts identify a single harness, and all three name

The naming between specifications and harnesses is exactly regular: all a

### Step 0670 - counting parentheses is not counting mutations

Thirty-one sentences size a dedicated mutation harness: retargets the shared

Two sentences size a route host by how many scenes it holds: the x86 host at

### Step 0668 - five historical sizes for one harness, and the

Five sentences record one mutation harness at successive sizes as detectors were

Those sizes are historical rather than current, which is why they are not
banners: each sentence describes the harness as it stood when that detector was
added. Checking them against the run would fail on the first one. What can be
checked is that the series ascends, that the stride is consistent, and that the
harness has not shrunk below its last stated size.

That last condition is the one with teeth. A sentence saying the harness is at a
hundred and twelve is still true while the harness holds a hundred and sixteen
and false the moment it drops, and nothing in the paper would notice, because

### Step 0667 - twenty-four row splits, three parts read and one

Twenty-four sentences state a row count and then split it by the stage that made

### Step 0666 - thirty-eight enumerated lists, bounded rather than

Forty-two sentences state a number of binding mutations and then list them.

The section states two shares of the tree: twenty-three per cent of its theorems

Both are floored rather than rounded, which the section says it does for every

### Step 0658 - two harness splits that must reach their own total,

The section describes mutation harnesses in two forms, and both carry their own

The checker records twelve constants rather than deriving them, because each

Three sentences give an oracle's size and the dimensions it sweeps, in two

Three sentences make the widest comparison claim in the section: the whole

difference is one constant in one memcmp rather than any change in the model.
Thirty-two cases would still be checked; four thousand and ninety-six bytes
would no longer be.

Thirteen oracles compare the whole window and the slot tags, and the three
claims are a subset. Narrowing one of those comparisons to eight bytes drops the
count and fails the check, which is the only way this sentence can go wrong
while every figure in it stays right. Census 519 -> 520.

### Step 0648 - a macro name is a spelling, the comparison is the
behaviour

Eight sentences say an oracle compares the whole register file with its tags and
all four flags, and the first attempt to count the oracles that could support
them found six, which would have made the section claim more than the tree does.
The count was wrong because the search looked for the macro that unrolls the
comparison, and several oracles spell the same comparison out under their own
loop variables.

Matching the comparison rather than the macro gives thirty oracles that compare
both halves and every flag, so the eight claims are a subset. That is the right
shape and it is now held: the claims may not outgrow the oracles, and either
number changing alone is reported.

The general lesson is that a mechanism claim is only as good as the search for
its mechanism. A macro name is a spelling; a comparison against the model arrays
is the behaviour, and only the behaviour can support a sentence about what an
oracle checked. Census 518 -> 519.

### Step 0647 - the strongest oracle claim, and the half a value
comparison would skip

One sentence makes the strongest claim of this kind in the section: 9,585,135
modeled cases, every one checked against an independent condition, writeback and
tag model. The figure is a banner of the run; what makes the sentence strong is
the model, and the tag part is what a value-only comparison would skip.

The oracle compares each register's value and tag in an unrolled loop and all
four flags beside it, which is the model the sentence names. Fifteen oracles
live in the build directory and only this one compares both halves, so the
pairing is specific rather than incidental, and both halves are now bound: the
banner must still print the count, and the oracle must still compare tags.

Removing the tag comparison leaves the sentence describing a stronger check than
the oracle performs, which is the failure this class produces: the figure stays
right while the model silently narrows. Census 517 -> 518.

### Step 0646 - the check is a proxy, and four oracles are
exceptions it accepts

The section says every family the chain routes is driven by an oracle that
includes the simulator header, and that a check measures the gap. The check is
real and its scope is narrower than the sentence: it flags an oracle that
includes a simulator header and calls a contract macro without ever driving the
composition, which is a proxy for driving the simulator and not a proof that it
did.

Four oracles are accepted as exceptions, each with a stated reason and each
naming the oracle that covers the path it leaves out: a cross-ISA differential
that compares contracts to each other by design, a wide-arithmetic oracle the
simulator cannot use, one that reads only the decode table, and one that calls
three lane decoders directly.

The section did not say so, which read as though the check were airtight. It now
discloses that the check reviews four exceptions, and the number is bound to the
check's own accepted set, so a fifth entry fails the paper check until the
sentence that describes it catches up. Census 516 -> 517.

### Step 0645 - thirteen claims about whole-state comparison, and
twenty-seven oracles that iterate

Thirteen sentences claim an oracle compares the whole register file rather than
the fields it drove, which is the strongest thing an oracle can be said to do:
it rules out a comparison that would pass while other state was wrong. Whether a
particular oracle does it is a reading of its source, but the claim population
and the mechanism can both be counted.

Thirteen claims against twenty-seven oracles that iterate every register,
sixteen on AArch64 and eleven on x86 through the macro each architecture names.
The claims are fewer than the oracles, which is what a set of specific sentences
about specific contracts should look like; the check reports the pair and fails
if the claims outgrow the oracles that could support them.

It also fails if either number changes without the other, so a sentence added to
this family and a macro removed from an oracle are both visible. That is the
limit of automating this class: the pairing is countable, the reading is not.
Census 515 -> 516.

### Step 0644 - the sentences that pair a size with a sweep

Twenty-two sentences tie an oracle's size to an exhaustive opcode sweep: a case
count, then a clause saying the oracle sweeps all 256 values. Both halves have a
source, the count in a banner and the sweep in the C file, and the pairing is
what says the number describes an exhaustive sweep rather than some other oracle
of the same size.

All twenty-two counts are banners of the run. The census holds that population
and would report a sweep claim whose count no banner prints; a count that
drifted to another oracle's value still passes, which is the same limitation the
case-count census has, and why the per-claim extraction remains the check that
matters.

The sweep phrase was chosen the way the fork phrase was: a repeated structural
form with a source on each side. Two hundred and three oracles sweep 256 values,
so the sentences are not an enumeration of them; they are specific claims about
specific oracles, and the census keeps the count of those claims from silently
changing. Census 514 -> 515.

### Step 0643 - a structural claim about how the oracles run, not

The section makes a structural claim about how its oracles work, not just what

The mechanism is in the C files and the claim is checkable. Twenty-two oracles
fork, and nine of those also sweep 256 values, which is the specific combination

Checking the pair means losing the mechanism is reported: renaming the fork
calls in that oracle leaves twenty-one and eight, and the sentence still says

### Step 0642 - two more references that would resolve to the
wrong thing

Two more ways a reference can resolve to the wrong thing are silent in a clean
LaTeX run with the directory on the path. A label defined twice resolves to
whichever the class file saw last, and a reference into a section the paper does
not include resolves to nothing, because the label exists on disk even though
the paper never inputs the file.

Neither occurs: the paper defines nine labels, none twice, and its twenty-five
references all point into the live set. The dead section files hold twenty-three
further labels, which is what makes the second failure plausible rather than
theoretical: fourteen live references would have had somewhere to go wrong if
any of them had strayed.

Both are now reported by name. The check is a small addition to the one from the
previous two steps, and it is the last of the reference-integrity invariants:
defined, unique, cited, and inside the document. Census 512 -> 513.

### Step 0641 - the check read ten sections where the paper has

The check added last step reads main.tex for the sections the paper includes,

The defect did not change any figure, because the appendix carries no label and

This is the second time in two steps that the population was the defect rather
than the check: the directory has twelve broken references and the paper none,

### Step 0640 - the directory has twelve broken references and the

The paper directory holds more sections than the paper includes. Older section

Over the included set the document is clean: nine labels, all referenced labels

That distinction is the same one the paper's own prose makes about its dead
sections, and it is why the numbers differ by so much between the two readings:

### Step 0639 - the checks have inputs whose absence they did not

Censusing the naming surfaces in the other direction finds little left: the

### Step 0638 - the paper cites forty-seven Lean modules and

The paper itself cites Lean modules by file name in fifty-three places, across

The check is existence only, because the section names modules rather than

### Step 0637 - sixteen modules are cited, and ten of them say

The headers cite more than the three guards. Ten more say that a named module

All sixteen resolve and all sixteen state refinements. The check now reads every

Two censuses in a row have grown the population this way: one citation, then

### Step 0636 - one citation was checked and the class has three

The previous step followed one citation from a simulator header into the proof

All three resolve. The check reads each citation, finds the module it names, and

### Step 0635 - a header comment cites a theorem, and nothing read

The AArch64 simulator header explains its tag-array guard in a comment that

Both halves hold. The slot macro is the round-up of the capacity by eight, which
is what one byte per word means, and the refinement theorem the comment names is

Renaming the theorem makes the citation dangle, and the check reports it.

This is the first citation from prose or comment into the proof tree that the

### Step 0634 - why the divergence is safe, and a macro name that

The tag sentence does not only say the vocabularies differ, it says why that is

they are what make the divergence harmless rather than a latent bug.

Both hold, and each fails visibly if it stops holding. Neither header names the
other's tag macro, in either direction, and no array is indexed by a tag
constant; the two tag arrays the headers do declare are sized by a slot count
and indexed by a word index, which is a different thing and had to be told apart

That distinction is the increment: a loose scan counted two violations, and

505.

### Step 0633 - the fallback oracle checks eight invalid codes,

The width sentence describes the one place the typed model does not reach: the

They are eight: the absent code plus seven codes that reuse the field. The

and a bit count. The sentence overstated the oracle's coverage by three, which

The count is now read from the oracle's own call list and compared to the

family the sentence got wrong since the harness paragraphs were closed, and it
was found by following the sentence to the file it describes rather than by any

### Step 0632 - the sentence is a contrast, and only one half
existed

The tag sentence is a contrast: the provenance vocabularies are not identical

The tag half was checked last step. What was not was the contrast itself: if the
two tag vocabularies ever came to agree everywhere, the sentence would be false

So the check now fails when the divergence is empty, which is the statement's

### Step 0631 - the tag sentence was prose about two files, and

The tag vocabulary sentence is why the section's other hand-kept figures exist:

Checked against both headers it holds precisely: seven names agree, codes zero

This is the first qualitative claim the checkers read, and it was chosen because

### Step 0630 - percentages were the one class two checkers

Percentages are the one figure class split across both checkers. The ISA split

The section states seven: four in the ISA split, the floored total, and the two

It is a small census with a narrow purpose, and it is the last class that
spanned two owners. Everything else a checker owns it also counts; this was the

### Step 0629 - the stages are numbered, and the numbering is a

Each stage of the growth chain also says which detector it adds, and the

Both constraints are now checked, and each catches what the other cannot. The

This is as far as these values can be constrained without the harness's history,

### Step 0628 - the chain has an end the tree can confirm

The growth chain has an end the tree can confirm. The section states a hundred

That converts three unverifiable figures into a sequence whose every value is

### Step 0627 - the three exempt totals are one chain, and 104 was

The three mutation totals that match no harness size are stages of one harness

The presence of a size is too weak a test, since one of the four is another

That is the only arithmetic the tree cannot supply for these figures and the

### Step 0626 - forty-seven mutation totals stood beside nothing

Seventy-one places in the section state how many mutations a harness runs.
Twenty-four of them sit beside a catch claim and were compared to their harness

Thirty of the distinct totals are a harness's present size, so a total that

### Step 0625 - the case-count checker never counted how many

The case-count checker knows four prose forms and verifies each figure it

A harness claim states three figures: the mutation total, how many rows catch,
