reported as such rather than folded into a bucket.

The two claims that test this are the auxiliary harness, which names a routed
oracle and a host oracle separately, and the sieve that keeps the one movk-regex
row. Both now match exactly. The measurement is the same ten claims as before,
but it now covers three quarters again as many rows and no longer guesses at the
label of a third of them. Census 486 -> 487.

### Step 0615 - the census guessed at labels it did not recognise,
and guessed wrong

The census folded every detector whose name it did not recognise into the host
bucket, which made a routed oracle indistinguishable from the host oracle in
both directions. A claim naming both then could never match its harness, because
the claim kept them apart and the tool did not.

The auxiliary harness is where that showed: 9 host rows and 30 route rows catch,
and the sentence names both counts. With route folded into host the tool saw 39,
so the paper's 9 and 30 read as two wrong figures rather than the two right ones
they are. Route is now its own bucket on both the harness and the claim side.

Two normalisation gaps in a row, after the tuple arity, and both produced
plausible output rather than an error: a tool that guesses at unrecognised
labels will always report a figure, and the figure will look like a measurement.
The counts now reconcile exactly for all ten claims that resolve to a harness.
Census 485 -> 486.

### Step 0614 - one claim had been made worse by trusting the
broken reader

With the equivalent flag read correctly, every harness claim touched by the last
five steps was re-checked against its source. Two had come out right after
earlier corrections, two had not, and one had been made worse by a correction
that trusted the broken reader.

The auxiliary harness is the one made worse. Its rows divide, among the caught
ones, into 21 generator stage, 27 Lean chain, 9 host, 30 route and one
movk-regex: 88 catch out of 92 rows, 4 surviving. Earlier steps moved the
generator and Lean counts to 22 and 25 and the total to 87, which matched
neither partition the broken reader could see.

The store-exclusive and bitfield claims were already right after their
corrections, and now all ten claims that resolve to a harness agree with source
and none disagree. That is the first time the matched set has been both complete
and consistent since the census was written. Census 484 -> 485.

### Step 0613 - the census read one field from the wrong index, and
three corrections followed it

The census read a harness's equivalent flag from a fixed index, four. Half the
harnesses pad their rows to five elements with the flag last, so in those the
reader found no equivalences at all and counted every row as catching. The
effect was invisible in the output: a harness reported 78 rows, 78 catching, 0
equivalents when the truth was 78, 70, 8.

That silently corrupted three of the corrections made over the previous four
steps. The reduction harness really does have 57 catching, the extract/reverse
harness 124, and the move-wide harness 67; the paper said exactly that, and the
steps that changed them to 59, 128 and 70 changed correct figures to match a
broken reader. All three are restored from source, and the move-wide count is
the one genuine error among them, 68 against the harness's 67.

The lesson is the one this section keeps re-teaching: a measurement tool that
under-reports a field reports a plausible figure, and nothing distinguishes it
from a correct one. The arity is now read from the tuple's last element, 152
harnesses show their equivalences, and the nine claims that resolve to a harness
all agree with source. Census 483 -> 484.

### Step 0612 - the totals were right and four rows were on the
wrong side of the line

The extract/reverse harness states 132 mutations, and the harness marks 4 of
them equivalent, so 128 catch. The sentence said 124 catch and 8 surviving,
splitting the 8 into 4 genuine equivalences and 4 detector-invisible rows. That
last clause was the error: the four rows it listed as survivors are marked
equivalent=False in the harness, so the harness expects them to catch, and the
paper was reporting them as surviving while counting the same total.

This is a different kind of defect from the earlier wrong counts. Those had
figures that no reading of the harness produced; here both totals were right,
132 rows, and the disagreement was about which side of the line four specific
rows fell on. Only reading the harness's own equivalent flags settles it, which
is what the census does.

The sentence now gives the harness's split and names the four equivalences, and
the claim matches its harness under the caught partition. That makes nine claims
resolving uniquely to a harness, all nine agreeing with source. Two remain
unmatched, both naming mutation totals the tree does not have. Census 482 ->
483.

### Step 0611 - two of the three stage counts agreed, which is why
the claim read as checked

The bitfield harness states a 104-mutation run whose caught rows divide 33
generator stage, 30 Lean chain and 29 host, with 12 rows marked equivalent. The
sentence said 94 catch, 31 host and 10 surviving, so three figures were wrong
and only two of the three stage counts were right: enough of the breakdown
agreed that the claim looked checked.

That pattern has now appeared in every wrong harness claim: the totals and most
of the split agree, one or two entries drift, and the drift is small enough to
read as rounding rather than error. The three that agreed gave the claim the
appearance of a figure copied from the harness, while the two that did not were
never compared to anything.

With the correction the claim matches its harness under the caught partition,
which brings the matched set to eight claims, all agreeing with source. Four
claims remain unmatched for want of an identity in prose, and each of them names
a mutation total no harness in the tree has, so they are more likely stale
totals than unmatched-by-ambiguity. Census 481 -> 482.

### Step 0610 - the matcher compared two names for one detector and
found nothing

The census could count rows and index by Step, but not yet answer the question
the audit began with: does a given claim agree with its harness? Matching by row
total alone was ambiguous, because several harnesses share one, and matching by
the detector split alone failed because the section sometimes quotes the
all-rows partition and sometimes the caught one.

Matching against both partitions, with the detector names normalised, resolves
six claims to exactly one harness each and leaves none ambiguous. All six agree
with their source, including the three corrected in the two previous steps, so
the corrections were right and the remaining claims in this family are
consistent.

The matcher needed one fix to work at all: the harnesses write lean_chain where
the section writes the Lean chain, so the two sides never compared equal and the
match count was zero while every piece worked in isolation. The five claims that
still match nothing need an identity the prose does not give, and stay out of
scope until it does. Census 480 -> 481.

### Step 0609 - one claim mixed figures from both partitions, and
each number looked plausible

Two more claims were wrong against their harnesses. The 61-mutation reduction
harness has 59 catching rows and 2 equivalents, split 30, 18 and 11; the
sentence said 57 catch, 4 surviving, and listed four equivalences that the
harness marks as catching rows. The 87-row auxiliary harness has 87 catching
rows, split 22, 25, 9 host, 30 route and one movk-regex: the sentence said 88
and read the generator and Lean counts from the all-rows split while taking the
host and route counts from the caught split.

The second kind is the interesting one, because every individual figure was
defensible in isolation: 27 and 11 each appear in the harness, just in different
partitions. A reader adding them gets the right total for the wrong reason, and
only the harness itself says which rows were which.

The checker's relation was also wrong. It required the stage sum to equal the
caught count, when the breakdown counts every row and the catch figure excludes
the equivalent ones; so a correct claim looked like a mismatch whenever a
harness had survivors. The relation is now a bound, stage sum at least the
caught count, which is the property that actually holds and the one a stale
figure would break. Census 479 -> 480.

### Step 0608 - two of the recorded mismatches were simply wrong
numbers

With the census indexed by Step, the recorded mismatches could be resolved
against source instead of guessed at. Two turned out to be genuinely wrong
numbers.

The 53-row store-exclusive harness has 49 catching rows and 4 equivalents, and
by the detector each row names they split 26 generator stage, 15 Lean chain and
12 host oracle. The sentence said 8 host. The 74-row move-wide harness has 70
catching rows and 4 equivalents, split 32, 21 and 17; the sentence said 68
catching and 18 host. Neither figure was reachable by any reading of the
harness, so both were stale counts rather than a convention applied
inconsistently.

Both sentences now carry the harness's own numbers, and the 53-row one states
the convention inline so the split cannot be read as a partition of the caught
figure. Three claims remain in the recorded list, all of which agree with source
under the all-rows reading and are kept only because resolving them needs their
Step to be identified in the prose. Census 478 -> 479.

### Step 0607 - the census could count rows but not say whose
rows they were

The census could count a harness's rows but had no way to say which harness a
claim means. The paper never names a script: its harness paragraphs describe
contracts, so a claim and its harness share only the Step number. Most harnesses
cite one in their module docstring, and the census now reads it, which turns a
guess from a row total into a lookup.

That mattered immediately. Matching by row total had been unreliable, because
several harnesses share one: the 61-row claim matched three different scripts
and none of them had its numbers. With the Step index the claim can name its
harness, and the numbers can be compared exactly instead of by coincidence.

The reader also needed an audit: it printed one harness's split as 29/17/11
while the source said 30/17/12, and the difference was a stale bytecode cache
rather than a bug, which the tool now reproduces correctly after clearing it. A
census whose output depends on a cache is worse than no census, so the run
clears it first. Census 477 -> 478.

### Step 0606 - the mismatches were a counting convention nobody
had written down

Step 0605 recorded five harness claims whose detector breakdowns did not add up
to their caught totals, and said the difference was unexplained. It is
explained, and the explanation is a convention the section never states: the
breakdown counts every row by the detector that must catch it, while the catch
figure counts the rows not marked equivalent. On the verified harness, 30 + 17 +
12 = 59 rows and 29 + 17 + 11 = 57 catch, so both figures are right and they
describe different partitions of the same table.

harness_census.py now derives all of it from the harness source, reading each
row's declared detector and its equivalent flag through the AST so a multi-line
row call counts once. On the 59-row harness it prints rows=59 catch=57 equiv=2
by row gen=30 lean_chain=17 host=12, which is exactly what the sentence says.

The convention is now stated where it matters. That one sentence spells out 59
rows, 57 catching, 2 surviving, and the detector split as a count of rows; the
other four remain in the recorded list until each is matched to its harness,
which needs an identity the paper does not give. Census 476 -> 477.

### Step 0605 - a second wording of the same claim was outside
every check

The harness paragraphs write their detector split two ways. The 44 claims that
say "N rows catch (...)" are now checked, and the 13 that say "N catch (...)"
without the word rows were not: a different phrasing of the same quantity,
invisible to a pattern keyed on one word.

Reading those 13 against their own breakdowns, seven agree exactly and five do
not, by between one and four. There is no note explaining any of the five, and
the differences run both ways, so a mutant counted twice in one claim and not at
all in another would explain the signs but nothing in the text says so. That is
a real inconsistency in how the section attributes catches to detectors.

Correcting the five needs the harnesses re-run, which is a larger job than a
prose fix, so they are recorded instead: the checker holds the list of five
known mismatches and fails if it changes in either direction. A sixth would
appear, and a silent edit to one of the five would be reported as well, so the
discrepancy stays visible and is not mistaken for a clean section. Census 475 ->
476.

### Step 0604 - the parser now reports how much of the section it
read

Step 0603 widened the row-count parser after finding it silently covered half
the claims. The lesson generalizes: a checker that parses a subset reports the
same clean run as one that parses everything, so the count of parsed instances
belongs beside the verdict. Without it, partial coverage is indistinguishable
from correctness.

The section now states both numbers. harness_claims counts the claims by their
wording alone, harness_sums counts the ones the parser understood, and the
split-first form is counted separately because it legitimately carries the
stages without the catch clause. The gate fails if the parser accounts for fewer
claims than the section contains.

Verified by restoring the narrow parser from step 0602: it reports parsed 23 of
44, so the rest went unread, which is the exact failure the previous step had to
be told about by inspection. The guard costs one regex over text the checker has
already read. Census 474 -> 475.

### Step 0603 - the invariant from the previous step saw half the
claims and called the rest clean

Step 0602 bound the row-count invariant and reported that all 23 claims it could
parse were consistent. That was wrong twice over: the pattern required the third
stage to be followed immediately by a closing paren, and a third of the claims
put a parenthetical expansion there, so the check saw 23 of 45 and reported a
clean run.

Matching the inner group to its closing paren and then reading the three counts
by their labels finds 44 claims. On the correct reading they all hold: the
stated catch count equals the generator, Lean-chain and host-oracle counts added
together. The one claim the old pattern had accepted and this one rejects was
the 57-row harness, where the stages sum to 71 because they describe the whole
run, not the caught subset.

That claim is now written the way the other 44 are: 71 rows split 29, 26 and 16,
of which 57 catch and 14 survive. So the section uses one convention instead of
two, and the invariant is stated over the convention it finds rather than over
the subset that happened to match. A one-row drift is reported. Census 473 ->
474.

### Step 0602 - one harness stated 93 caught rows and its own stages
added to 101

The harness paragraphs were the largest unverified arithmetic surface left: 23
claims of the form "N rows catch (a at the generator stage, b through the Lean
chain, c by the host oracle)". Nothing compared the stated N with the stages
beside it, and one of the 23 said 93 while its own stages added to 101.

The paragraph now says 101 rows split 46, 27 and 28, with 8 surviving as
equivalences, which is the reading consistent with all three numbers: 101 total,
8 documented as equivalent, 93 caught. The old form left the reader to notice
that 93 and 101 could not both be the row count.

The invariant is now checked across all 23. It parses the stated total and the
three stage counts, ignores the survivors because they are a separate class, and
reports any claim whose total differs from its breakdown. The other 22 all hold,
which is evidence the format is the right thing to bind and the one mismatch was
a real slip rather than a convention I misread. Census 472 -> 473.

### Step 0601 - an axiom was named by the tactic that usually
reaches it

The sentence introduced Lean.ofReduceBool as "the axiom native_decide also
reaches". That is a universal over a tactic, and it holds for 483 of the 488
native_decide proofs: five reach only propext and Quot.sound. In a paragraph
whose subject is exactly which proofs carry which footprint, naming an axiom by
the tactic that usually reaches it is the loose phrasing the paragraph exists to
replace.

Both populations now appear side by side with their counts, which is also
clearer than the parenthetical was: 69 of 165 from bv_decide, 483 of 488 from
native_decide, and the 96 kernel-only discharge spelled out separately. The
reader can see the asymmetry the paragraph argues about without having to hold a
tactic name as a proxy for a footprint.

Rewrapping the sentence also removed a 113-character line left by an earlier
edit, so the paragraph fits the measure. Census 471 -> 472.

### Step 0600 - the recorded axiom figures could be stale and
still consistent

Step 0599 gave the axiom figures a reproducible source, but the gate still only
checks that the recorded counts partition the tree and agree with each other.
Six numbers can be jointly consistent and jointly stale, and they were wrong
three times before the census existed.

The census costs three minutes, so it stays out of the build. Four modules
spanning every class are cheap enough to re-probe inside it: one entirely
axiom-free, one with a single propext theorem among axiom-free ones, one whose
theorems all assume the compiler, and one that holds three classes at once.
Together they exercise each branch of the classifier, including the namespace
fallback the third error came from.

The check is on the class set per module rather than on counts, because a set
mismatch names the module whose classification moved and cannot be satisfied by
two errors cancelling. It costs 3.9 seconds, and a wrong expectation fails with
the full comparison for both sides. Census 470 -> 471.

### Step 0599 - the axiom figures had no reproducible source, and
the first one found another error

The axiom figures had been recorded from throwaway probes and were wrong twice:
once because the probe scored the axiom-free class through a string test that
matched its error path, once because a choice sweep qualified every theorem as
`KProgFormal.<name>` and silently dropped the two modules whose namespace
differs. A published figure should not depend on someone retyping a probe
correctly.

So the census is now a script in the tree. It reads each module's declared
namespace from the source, batches one `#print axioms` invocation per module,
and prints the four-way split plus the choice breakdown. It reproduces
617/623/785/40 and it immediately found a third error: choice is 179, not 177,
because `CrossIsaRev`'s two choice-bearing theorems resolve only under the
module's own namespace.

It is deliberately not a Makefile target. The gate already takes seven minutes
and 306 Lean invocations would add three, so the division is: the census
regenerates, and the gate holds the recorded counts with the partition and
identity checks added over the last three steps. A stale figure therefore fails
in the gate, and a fresh one is one command away rather than a re-typed probe.
Census 469 -> 470.

### Step 0598 - the case-count script was described as part of the
build and is not one

The case-count sentence said the section's counts are kept honest "the same way"
as the rest, which reads as build coverage. They are checked by a second script,
and that script is not a Makefile target: eleven checkers run in the build and
two do not, this one and the README count check. Both pass, but neither runs
when the gate runs.

The sentence now says so, outside the build, which is the honest framing and
also the more useful one: a reader can tell which figures the build re-derives
and which depend on someone running a second command. That distinction matters
more than usual here, because the case counts are exactly the figures that
drifted ten times in the past.

Keeping the distinction true costs one scan of the Makefile. Moving either
checker into the build without changing the sentence now fails, and the test is
the same shape as the reachability and partition checks: a property of the tree
the prose depends on, verified where the prose is verified. Census 468 -> 469.

### Step 0597 - the module count and the theorem count came from
different traversals

The paragraph pairs two figures in one clause: "306 Lean modules that prove
2,065 theorems". The module count is the gate's reachable closure and the
theorem count iterates every file on disk, so the pairing holds only while every
file is reachable. Nothing checked that, and the two figures come from different
traversals.

An unreachable module is not a cosmetic problem here. Its theorems would be
counted and published while the gate never compiles it, so the paper would claim
more proved theorems than the gate proves, and every individual figure would
still match. The check now reports any module outside the closure by name.

Verified by planting one: a file with a single trivial theorem and no importer
is reported as unreachable, and removing it clears the report. That is a
stronger property than the file count matching, because it names which file and
why, and it is free since the closure is already computed for the module figure.
Census 467 -> 468.

### Step 0596 - the three choice figures were one population and
nothing said so

The three choice figures are views of one population: 177 theorems draw on
Classical.choice, 137 of those also reach Lean.ofReduceBool, and 40 sit in the
kernel-only class. Nothing enforced 177 minus 137 equals 40, and a partial
re-measurement is exactly the failure mode that breaks it while all three
figures keep matching their own claim patterns.

That is the same defect the axiom partition had before step 0593, one level
down: recorded numbers that were individually plausible and jointly unchecked.
Both identities are now enforced, and both are cheap, since neither needs a
probe.

Two bounds went with it, because a choice count can be inconsistent without
breaking the identity. The 40 kernel-only choice theorems cannot exceed the 825
kernel-only theorems, and the 137 cannot exceed the 623 that assume the
compiler. Each is a one-line comparison and each would have caught a figure
entered against the wrong class, which is the error that produced the
40-instead-of-177 reading two steps ago. Census 466 -> 467.

### Step 0595 - the sentence counted six forms and its checker
scans five

The sentence said the tree proves its theorems "with no sorry, no axiom, and no
opaque/unsafe/partial definitions---each of the six checked by the gate". It
names five forms, not six, and the checker it describes scans five: sorry and
admit as one placeholder class, then the four declaration keywords. So the
sentence both miscounted and omitted admit, which the scanner does catch.

The count is now derived from the scanner rather than restated, so the two
cannot drift: adding a keyword to check_no_sorry.py moves the published figure,
verified by adding extern to the declaration pattern and watching the count go
from 5 to 6. Changing the sentence alone fails, and changing the scanner alone
fails, which is the pair the claim actually asserts.

This is the arithmetic kind of defect rather than a measurement one, and it is
the reason to bind it rather than correct it: a form added to the scan without
the sentence would have left the paper claiming a smaller guarantee than the
gate provides, and a sentence naming a form the scan omits would have claimed a
larger one. Census 465 -> 466.

### Step 0594 - the choice figure held for one class and read as
the whole tree

The three-way split says 40 theorems draw on Classical.choice. Measuring every
theorem that does, regardless of class, gives 177, of which 137 also reach
Lean.ofReduceBool. Both numbers are correct and they measure different things:
40 is the choice population inside the kernel-only 825, 177 is the population
across the whole tree.

The sentence only supported the first reading, because it sat inside the
enumeration of the 825. A reader who counted choice theorems would find 177 and
could not reconcile it, so the sentence now states both and says what each
counts. That also makes the stronger assumption visible where it actually is:
choice appears mostly in the compiler-assuming arithmetic, not in the
kernel-only definitional residue.

One wording fix went with it. The split's first clause read "617 theorems depend
on no axiom at all", and the next paragraph asserts "no axiom" of the whole tree
while meaning no axiom declaration, so the two sentences used the same phrase
for different measurements two paragraphs apart. The clause now reads "depend on
none at all", which cannot be read as the declaration-level claim.
Census 464 -> 465.

### Step 0593 - the axiom split was four constants that nothing
tied to the tree

The four axiom figures were recorded constants with nothing tying them to the
tree. They happen to sum to 2065, but that was arithmetic luck rather than an
enforced property: add one theorem and every figure would still have matched its
own pattern while the split described a tree that no longer existed. This is the
same failure the rest of the paragraph was written to rule out, one level up.

The sum is now checked against the theorem count. A one-theorem shift in the
recorded compiler count fails by name and tells the reader to re-run the #print
axioms sweep, which is the only thing that produces those numbers; a gate cannot
recompute them in the time it has.

The sentence's 'a third of the tree' was 30%, and like the other shares in this
section it is now derived and floored rather than rounded: 100 times 623 over
2065. A drift to 33% is reported. That makes every figure in the TCB paragraph
either derived from the tree or guarded against the tree drifting away from it.
Census 463 -> 464.

### Step 0592 - the three-way split shipped with the axiom-free
class miscounted

Step 0591 shipped a three-way axiom split of 670 / 619 / 776. Re-measuring the
whole tree with a probe that distinguishes "does not depend on any axioms" from
a parse failure gives 617 / 623 / 825. The 0591 probe had recorded the
axiom-free class by a string test on output that also matched its error path, so
52 theorems were misfiled, and the paper published the wrong three figures.

The corrected measurement is verified rather than assumed: sixteen theorems
sampled across both disputed classes were re-probed individually and all sixteen
agreed with the new sweep, including four that the old one had filed as
axiom-free and the new one also calls axiom-free, so the correction is not
merely a different parse of the same bug. Every theorem in the tree is
classified: 618 + 623 + 824 = 2065.

The re-measurement also split the 824 properly. 784 depend on propext and
Quot.sound alone, and 40 also draw on Classical.choice, which is a stronger
assumption: propext and Quot.sound are definitional, while choice lets a proof
select a witness without exhibiting one, so a reader auditing the artifact
should see the 40. Census 462 -> 463.

### Step 0591 - the tree's axiom footprint has three classes, and
670 theorems need none

The paragraph framed the whole TCB as "kernel-checked given a correct compiler".
Measuring #print axioms over all 2065 theorems shows the assumption covers a
third of the tree, and the tree divides three ways rather than two.

670 theorems depend on no axiom at all: proofs that close by rfl or by case
splits into rfl reach nothing, so even propext is unnecessary
(`x86_mem_dispatch_src_refines` is a case split into rfl over three Bools). 619
reach Lean.ofReduceBool and so do assume the compiler. The remaining 776 use
only propext, Quot.sound and sometimes Classical.choice — classical logic, but
no compiled verdict.

Two consequences. The framing was too pessimistic about 1,446 of the 2,065
theorems, which need no compiler assumption and in 670 cases no axioms at all.
And it was too coarse: "given a correct compiler" applied uniformly is a much
weaker statement than the per-theorem footprint, which is what a reader deciding
whether to trust the artifact actually needs. Census 461 -> 462.

### Step 0590 - the deployment claim never named the population
that has to be re-discharged

The deployment sentence was the one place the paper's trust argument became
operational: a deployment that will not trust the compiler "can re-discharge
nearly every finite enumeration and example". It named no population, and the
population it needs is not the tactics' totals — it is the theorems that
actually assume the compiler.

That set is the one step 0589 started measuring, now completed on both sides:
483 of the 488 native_decide proofs and 69 of the 165 bv_decide ones reach
Lean.ofReduceBool, 552 in all. The other 261 proofs are already kernel-only, so
a deployment that avoids the assumption does not need to touch them — 96 of the
bv_decide population never had it in their trust chain at all.

Stating 552 as the population also fixes what the sentence promises about. Its
last clause said the bit-vector identities "apart from a handful of small
exceptions, have no kernel-only discharge", which is true of the 69 that assume
the compiler and false of the 96 that do not; the sentence now says "that do
assume it". So the re-discharge story and the enforcement story finally describe
the same set. Census 460 -> 461.

### Step 0589 - only 69 of the 165 bv_decide proofs reach the
axiom the paragraph named for all of them

The paragraph said bv_decide "lowers the goal to a bit-vector problem, evaluates
it, and admits the verdict through Lean.ofReduceBool, the axiom native_decide
also reaches". The inference drawn from that — that a bv_decide evaluation is
trusted "in the same way" — holds only if every bv_decide proof reaches the
axiom, so the footprint was measured with #print axioms.

It does not. Of the 165 bv_decide proofs, 69 depend on Lean.ofReduceBool and 96
depend only on propext, Quot.sound, and sometimes Classical.choice. The 96 close
by kernel-checked reflection: the goal reduces to a literal equality the kernel
verifies itself, with no compiler-produced verdict in the chain.
`arm64_stack_arena_word_index_refines` is the smallest example — it depends on
propext and Quot.sound and nothing else.

That makes the trust story sharper rather than weaker: bv_decide can discharge
an open-ended identity either with the compiler in the loop or without it, and
which one happened is recorded per theorem. The blanket claim was the only part
that could not distinguish them, so the sentence now gives the split and says
the footprint decides. Census 459 -> 460.

### Step 0588 - the split predicted two failure modes and the tree
has one

The paragraph split the 165 bv_decide obligations by proof shape and predicted
two failure modes: 61 that split by cases cannot state the goal until the split
is reverted, and 104 that bind a bit-vector directly are stated and then give
up. Classifying every failure by its error text against the theorem holding it,
the tree has one mode.

58 of the 61 and 103 of the 104 are "expected type must not contain free
variables", which is the cannot-be-stated error, and not one of the 165 is
stated and then fails to reduce. So the split predicts a distinction the tree
does not make: the cases split is not what stops the plain tactic, and reverting
it changes 2 of 165.

That also corrects a claim inherited from the older record, that reverted goals
then exhaust the kernel's recursion budget. On this population they do not — the
two that revert compile, and the other 159 still cannot be stated — so the
recursion-budget outcome belongs to a different experiment than the one the
sentence described. The paragraph now reports the measured mode and drops the
budget claim for this population. Census 458 -> 459.

### Step 0587 - the gap survives the remedy Lean itself proposes,
so it belongs to the tactic

Step 0586 established that a bare `decide` fails on 1 of 488 native_decide
theorems and 161 of 165 bv_decide ones. The open question was whether that gap
is an artefact of the replacement tactic rather than of the tactic being
replaced, so the sweep was re-run with `decide +revert`, the remedy Lean's own
error message proposes.

It moves one side only. On the bv side two theorems now compile —
`arm64_ccmp_fallback_refines` and `arm64_bitfield_mask_refines`, both of which
the bare tactic could not state at all — so 159 of 165 still fail. On the native
side nothing changes: `x86_specialization_no_insertion` fails with the same
"decide failed for proposition", the only one of 488. The gap is therefore a
property of the tactic, not of which replacement was tried.

### Step 0584 - the product clause is the load-bearing one and

The paragraph ended with a prohibition: no bv_decide identity "reduces a product

separates an identity from a product on the kernel-budget boundary, and nothing
checked it.

all, and each multiplies by the byte width rather than by another operand —

multiplicand pair in a statement the tactic closes is reported by theorem name.

second, so the shape the clause forbids is reachable, and a probe with exactly

sentence puts it. Census 454 -> 455.

### Step 0569 - a split said to be measured from the log had nine

The section said the gate's cases were "split evenly across the two ISAs" and

`sim_split` now derives it. A banner is attributed through the `./build/<bin>`
line that ran it to the compile line that built it, and the translation unit's

as the preprocessor resolves them — says which simulator root it reaches.

their file name and reach no simulator, since an oracle can check a generated
macro without driving the architecture behind it.

The partition is what makes the measurement trustworthy. The first version kept
the source path from the compile line and dropped the rest of it, so the `-I`
list was empty and the split came out 47/59/140/2 — plausible, internally
consistent, and wrong. Requiring the buckets to cover every banner and sum to

sentence. The measured split is 58 AArch64 / 62 x86-64 / 3 driving both

sentence says it excludes.

`check_lean_claims.py` gained `family` and `artifact_families`: it lists

The tree passes: 138/138/138 with empty differences. Census 435 -> 436.

### Step 0564 - the dispatch-sweep clause was singular,
and three theorems satisfied it

The non-vacuity sentence's third clause was the last one nothing measured: "the
dispatch sweep pairs its range over the armed ids with explicit non-membership
checks". Two things were wrong with it. It was singular, and three theorems do
the pairing -- `arm64_reg_dispatch_full_range`, `x86_reg_dispatch_full_range`,
and `x86_helper_dispatch_full_range` -- and no rule said what made a theorem a
pair, so a sweep that swept its range and pinned nothing outside it would have
kept the sentence true.

Membership is the statement again, read per conjunct: a top-level conjunction
with exactly one `(List.range n).all ...` or `(List.finRange n).all ...` part
and at least one part of the form `(... = none)`. Splitting on `∧` needs depth
tracking, because the swept part carries its own parentheses and the pinned
parts carry type ascriptions (`cellOf (0x1f : BitVec 8) = none`). Two theorems
pin three outside values (the last GPR, the byte above it, the sentinel); the
helper sweep pins four (ids 0, 8, 21, 22). The published figures are the class
size and the smallest count, 3 and 3, so a sweep that dropped its outside checks
fails the check instead of reading as prose.

`check_lean_claims.py` gained `conjuncts` and `sweep_checks`, and the three
per-theorem rules now append into one `counters` dict, from which all seven
published figures for the sentence are read. The paper's clause now reads
"each of the 3 dispatch sweeps pairs the range it sweeps over the armed ids
with at least 3 explicit non-membership checks". Census 434 -> 435.

### Step 0563 - the exactness clause named five
theorems and matched none

The same sentence's second clause was looser than the first, and wrong. It read
"the exactness theorems assert two independently defined lists equal and both
sides measure non-empty", naming a class by nothing but a theorem-name suffix.
Four theorems end `_exact` and a fifth is called one; of those five, one is a
boundary conjunction and four compare a projection of a table (`table.map f`),
so no member is a pair of list literals. The clause described a class the tree
does not have.

The class that does exist is the refinement equality: a statement that is
exactly one bare name equal to another, one side a literal list in the module
and the other a literal list in a generated module it imports. That is
"independently defined" spelled out, and it holds of 25 theorems -- all named
`_refine`, none named `_exact`, and disjoint from the 45 table-length theorems.
Loose shapes were rejected on purpose: `sourceOf base = spec base` implies such
an equality after unfolding, and `arm64_cc_decode_conds_exact` equates two
projections, so neither is covered by what the sentence says.

Both sides are literals, so the checker counts their entries (skipping commas
inside strings, which the name tables are full of) and publishes the shorter
side: 2 at minimum, which is what "non-empty" now means -- a theorem equating a
table against `[]` would fail the check. Prose moved to "the 25 refinement
equalities ... both sides hold at least 2 entries". `check_lean_claims.py`
gained the rule and a `statement` helper that cuts binders off before either
shape is matched; the gate re-runs for the checker. Census 433 -> 434.

### Step 0562 - the table-length count was nineteen, and the
class has a rule now

Step 0488's non-vacuity audit survives as one sentence in the safety section,

Naming the class is the difficulty, and the obvious rule is wrong twice over:

(their right-hand side is a function of a width), while the shape picks up three

`def <name> : Nat := <digits>` through the module's own imports. Per-module
resolution is not pedantry: `armCount` is 2 in one generated specification and 4
in another, and resolving per module is what leaves out the three theorems that
compare a hand-written list against a literal digit.

The sentence's other half was weaker than it looked. "No generated count is
zero" stayed true even if the class were empty, so the paper now quotes the
range the constants span -- 2 to 31 -- and a generator that emits an empty table

### Step 0561 - why 150 shared modules and 138 shared
specifications are both right

Correcting the split's digits left a contradiction in the same subsection. One
sentence says the prototype has 138 shared specifications; the corrected
sentence twelve lines below says 150 shared modules. Both are true and neither
is wrong, but nothing said why they differ, and a reader holding the two numbers
has no way to tell a second bucket from a counting error.

The reason is the rule step 0560 pinned. A module counts toward an architecture
only when its own file name starts with that prefix, so everything else falls in
the shared bucket: the 138 generated specifications, plus twelve hand-written
modules that are shared by construction -- eleven cross-ISA compositions and the
tag-erasure model. That is the whole gap, and the sentence now says so in one
clause, spelling the twelve out rather than leaving them to be inferred.

Two details were checked before writing it. The twelve are named by the same
prefix test the checker uses, so the count is the rule's output and not a
hand-tally; and the added clause states no digit the checkers do not already
bind, so no gate figure moved -- the case counts and both gate totals still
match the log, and the paper compiles clean.  Census 431 -> 432.

### Step 0560 - the architecture split was stale, and

The trusted-base work left the section's last hand-kept figure unexamined.

`over 306 Lean modules` was current while the sentence twelve lines later
splitting those modules by architecture was not. It read 69 AArch64 modules
with 773 theorems, 85 x86-64 with 1,126, and 140 shared with 42. Those
sum to 294 modules and 1,941 theorems, so the sentence had been true of a tree
twelve modules and a hundred theorems smaller and no checker noticed, because
nothing read it.

Binding it meant pinning the split's rule, not just its digits. Two rules divide
the tree honestly: strip the `Generated` prefix first, which files an
arch-rendered specification with its architecture, or match the file name as it
stands, which puts every generated module in the shared bucket. The paper's own
history chooses: it called 138 generated specifications "shared" two sentences
earlier, and the old numbers decompose under the second rule -- 69 and 85 hand-
written arch modules plus 138 generated and 2 cross-ISA in the shared bucket.
That rule still holds today, and its three buckets sum to exactly the published
306 modules and 2,061 theorems, which is the property that makes the split
checkable rather than merely plausible.

So the checker now reads all six numbers, plus the bare `2,061` sitting in the
totals sentence -- a figure quoted in one sentence and bound in another still
drifts when only one is corrected. The extended checker reported exactly the six

150 shared. No new component joined the gate; an existing one got wider, which
is why the full `make check` re-runs for this step.

### Step 0559 - the kernel-only escape, measured

Step 0557 left a promise untested. The trusted-base paragraph says a deployment
that will not trust the compiler can re-discharge the finite enumerations and
examples by case analysis "at a proof-script cost, with no change to any
statement". Nobody had tried it. So every module naming an evaluation tactic --
117 of them, 653 counted theorems -- was copied, the tactic token replaced by a
plain `decide`, the copy compiled as a dot-file module with line numbers
preserved, and each error attributed to the theorem whose range held it. Nothing
else in any statement moved, so a success is exactly the paper's wording and a
failure names the reason.

The answer splits by tactic, not by statement shape, which is the opposite of
the boundary the paragraph drew. Of the 488 `native_decide` theorems, 480
re-discharge: enumerations, examples, and quantified identities alike. Of the
165 `bv_decide` theorems, 4 do. The mechanism is visible in the error text and
has two stages. On 161 of the 165 a bare `decide` cannot even be stated, because
the `cases` split leaves free variables in the goal; applying the remedy Lean
itself proposes (`decide +revert`) turns 152 of those into "maximum recursion
depth has been reached" -- the kernel does not merely run slowly, it gives up --
and 6 more fail to synthesize an instance. Six close under `+revert`, and
reading them shows why: masking, shifting, and flag-funnel identities, none
reducing a product of two wide operands.

Two artifacts were checked rather than counted. `x86_popcount_refines` carries
`bv_decide (config := { timeout := 120 })`; a token-only swap orphaned that
block and reported a `DecideConfig` parse error, and re-measured with the block
removed it fails like its neighbours, so it is not a semantic outcome. The same
script's `pathlib` glob matched its own dot-file probes at first, which counted
661 theorems instead of 653; the plan now excludes dot-files, and the count
agrees with the census. Cost was measured too: paired serial timings over the 66
modules where both versions compile give 29.7 s against 53.0 s, so the promise's
"cost" is roughly a doubling, dominated by one module.

The paragraph now reports the measured boundary and no gate-bound figure moved:
the section's 154 claimed case counts and both gate totals still match the log,
and the paper compiles clean. The sweep is a measurement, not a checker --
promoting it would be a new obligation for the operator to authorize.
Census 429 -> 430.

### Step 0558 - the one configuration knob no checker
reads

`check_no_sorry.py` reads declaration keywords, so it cannot see configuration:
a `set_option` line changes what the kernel is willing to reduce, and no checker
in the gate reads one (searching every checker script for the word returns
nothing). A census over the proof tree found its complete trust-adjacent
configuration to be two `set_option maxHeartbeats` lines and nothing else:
`@[implemented_by]`, `@[extern]`, `@[macro_inline]`, `unsafe`, `partial`,
`opaque`, `axiom`, `elab`, `syntax`, `macro_rules`, and `#eval` each appear zero
times. That zero is what makes step 0557's four-axiom universe complete rather
than lucky, because `native_decide` documents its trust as "the Lean compiler
and all definitions with an `@[implemented_by]` attribute" -- a keyword
`check_no_sorry.py` never looks for.

Whether each raised budget is needed was measured rather than assumed: rewrite
the budget in a copy, compile it as a dot-file module, unlink it, and bisect for
the smallest budget that builds. Lean's default is 200,000, and the two sites
disagreed. `arm64_mul_refines` carried 1,000,000, yet compiles at the default
and needs only 10,431 heartbeats, so the raise was worth nothing and is deleted.
`arm64_bitfield_refines` needs 239,834, which is above the default: at 200,000
it stops with a deterministic timeout after 21.6 s, so its 4,000,000 is
load-bearing and stays. One site out of two was dead weight, which is why the
budgets were measured and not merely listed.

The full gate re-runs green after the deletion, and the theorem, module, and
`native_decide` totals are unchanged -- the check that removing an option line
deleted no proof. Two caveats travel with the number: a minimum budget is
machine- and version-dependent, so it records why the raise exists rather than
fixing a new floor, and nothing in the gate watches these lines, so a future
edit can raise one silently. Promoting a heartbeat budget into a checker would
be a new proof obligation and is left for the operator to authorize.  Census 428
-> 429.

### Step 0557 - the trusted base no textual checker
can see

The axiom footprint of every counted declaration was read off the kernel
with `Lean.collectAxioms`, once per module in that module's own environment
(306 modules, 0 failures), then joined to the 2,061 counted names by
namespace-qualified name -- 0 unknown. The join has to be by qualified name:
the dump omits axiom-free rows, so a bare-name join reports every name it
fails to match as axiom-free, which is the wrong answer for the right reason.
Tree-wide the trusted base is exactly four axioms -- `propext`, `Quot.sound`,
`Classical.choice`, `Lean.ofReduceBool` -- and none is declared here. 617
counted declarations are axiom-free.

The finding is the third group. 723 declarations (35%) depend on
`Lean.ofReduceBool`, the axiom that admits a verdict computed by compiled
code. 488 of them run `native_decide` in their own script -- the published
figure, still exactly true -- but 119 run `bv_decide` and 116 run neither
(88 `simp`, 18 `exact`, 7 `rfl`). Those 116 decide nothing themselves: they
inherit the assumption from a lemma they cite, over 215 carrier edges to 70
declarations, five of which carry 115 of the 215.

`bv_decide` is the route no gate check looked at: 165 scripts over 52
modules, disjoint from `native_decide`. Its cost is not uniform -- 46 of the
165 land on `[propext]` alone -- and the outcome turns on goal shape, not
width: `(x &&& y) = (y &&& x)` over `BitVec 64` pulls in all four axioms
while `x + y = y + x` over the same type pulls in one. `Classical.choice`
reaches 274 declarations, 139 of them through `bv_decide` and exactly one
through `native_decide`; none of the 274 mentions `Classical`.

Escaping evaluation is not on the menu. `decide` -- kernel reduction, no
`ofReduceBool` -- exhausts the heartbeat budget on a `BitVec 8` identity at
widths 8, 12 and 16 alike and then reports `sorryAx`. Where it does finish,
and for `omega`, the footprint is `[propext, Quot.sound]`.

None of this becomes a published figure. Re-deriving it needs a `lake env
lean` run per theorem-bearing environment -- a greedy transitive-import
cover of the 183 theorem-declaring modules is 105 environments -- so it is a
gate obligation the measurement does not buy, and 488 stays the number.

What did change is the paper's trusted-base paragraph, which exempted
handler compositions, value and flag identities, and width-narrowing steps
from evaluation. Composition is exempt; the rest are not. It now names
`bv_decide` as a second evaluation route and cites the heartbeat result for
why no kernel-only discharge exists, and it states nothing countable, so
both claim checkers pass with no new figure wired to them.
Census 427 -> 428.

spot in the theorem counter

documents said 2060, and the checker reported `all claims current` because it

The fix belongs in the derivation, not the prose: the published figure is
computed, so a hand-edited number would drift again the next time a theorem
moves. `THEOREM` now tolerates a leading `@[...]`. Scope was measured first:

on its own line, none `private`/`noncomputable`/`protected`, so this is the
whole of the miss rather than its first symptom.

`signature()` carried the same assumption one layer down. It sliced binders from
the block's start using `len("theorem " + name)`, correct only when the block
starts at `theorem`; behind an attribute it returns text offset by the
attribute's length. Re-anchored to where the name actually occurs and compared
with the previous implementation over every block: identical for all 2060, and
empty for the newly visible one, which takes no binders.

Nothing else moved, measured rather than assumed: the theorem closes `by

decided, and quantified-by-cases stays 28. The floored share is still 23%, now

is not wrong by one -- it is wrong by however many the anchor hides, and only
the tree gets to say.

The tree was asked directly. Every module environment was dumped for its

`.injEq`, `ofNat_toCtorIdx`) removed: what remains is the checker's set, with no

### Step 0554 - a hypothesis that
closed the case it should have proved

A proof that takes `(h : op ∈ arm64DispatchOps)` and never mentions `h` is
not obviously safe to weaken: `simp_all` can consume a hypothesis silently.
Textual search proved nothing -- of the 86 hypotheses a proof body names,
none was droppable, while 29 of the 46 it never names were load-bearing.
The only sound test was to delete the binder and recompile the module. 132
rows across 44 modules look like numeric bounds; stripping identifiers shows
51 whose only digits sit inside a name (`op ∈ arm64DispatchOps`,
`width ≠ .w64`) and 2 type parameters (`high : BitVec 64`), leaving 79 real
side conditions -- 7 of them written as a type-ascribed literal, like
`(hb : (1 : BitVec 8) ≤ bits)`. Deleting all 132 binders one at a time:
115 load-bearing, 17 free.

Six were artifacts, and each had been hiding something. The four
`*_member_handled` theorems took `h : op ∈ *Ops`, but membership is *total*
-- `∀ op, op ∈ arm64DispatchOps` holds by `cases op <;> decide` -- so the
bound always held and was doing the opposite of its job: with a gate
missing from the table, the uncovered opcode's case closes on an `h` that
cannot hold. A three-constructor enum with two gates shows it; with the
hypothesis the theorem compiles, without it `decide` reports the
disjunction is `false`. The two `hnoWrap : capacity.toNat + 1 < 2 ^ 32`
bounds err the other way -- `windowEnd` is `Nat` addition and the generated
C widens to `__u64` before adding, so no wrap exists to exclude, and the
bound had been dropping `capacity = 0xFFFFFFFF`. Those theorems are now
strictly stronger. The `have hv` and `have hcapLt` each bound left dead went
with them; the four `simp_all` lists stay, as bare `simp_all` no longer closes
any of them. Of the eleven free hypotheses left, nine are kept on purpose: the
six Extrev narrowing fits record where the C pipeline narrows (the
unconditional form already exists as `*_refines_raw`), and `hb : 1 ≤ bits` with
the two `words_tight` bounds state the C contract's own domain. The last two,

unsatisfiable, so their docstrings say the arm is vacuous and name
`*_member_handled` as the operative half. `lake build` RC=0 at 2060 theorems;
gate 248 banners, 124,531,802 modeled cases; twelve checks green.

### Step 0549 - a set union could not tell
an agreeing side from an absent one

`check_lookup_ambiguity.py` compared
`{.bytes().take(N) in x86} | {.bytes().take(N) in main.rs}` against
`BPF_OBJ_NAME_LEN - 1`. A union has no per-side membership, so a side that
stops matching the pattern leaves the set and the other side's 15 satisfies the
check alone. Planting `name.as_bytes().iter().take(16)` in x86's helper -- a
legal Rust spelling of the same operation with a different length -- made the
old logic report `lens=[15] want=15` and print "both sides truncate at 15"
while x86 truncated at 16. Each file now states its own length, read from the
`*truncate_bpf_obj_name` helper and required to be exactly one `.take(N)`; a
file stating no helper, two, or no length inside it is named.
`BPF_OBJ_NAME_LEN` is read as the uapi header writes it, `16U` or bare `16`,
and must appear once -- the old pattern required the suffix, so a header
dropping it silently stopped pinning anything.

The convergence guard had the same shape of bug: AArch64's absence-of-error was
tested with x86's pattern, which demands the literal prefix `"x86 "`. A bail
reading `"arm64 ... truncation-matches multiple"` -- the wording AArch64 would
actually use -- ended the divergence with the banner unchanged. It is now
tested without the prefix. Both x86 paths are now checked by the same template
with no `kind not in x86` guard, so a path whose name leaves the file is
reported instead of skipped. Dead `--check` removed; the Makefile runs the
script bare. Battery: 17 mutations -- 12 caught with their own message, and 5
equivalent spellings accepted (one side's iterator re-spelled at the same
length, a spaced `take`, a bare-`16` header, a comment naming the phrase). The
decisive mutation -- a re-spelled iterator at a different length -- was run
through both logics side by side: the old one reports no finding, the new one
names the two lengths. Gate rc 0, 248 banners, 124,531,802 cases; no Lean or C
file changed.
Census 419 -> 420.

### Step 0548 - a checker that claimed every
site saw seven of them

`check_jcc_opcodes.py` asserts that every jump the x86 encoder emits agrees
with the `X86_CC_*` contract, and its opcode class was `0x[0-9a-f]{2}`. The
encoder spells conditional opcodes in lower case and its three unconditional
`0xEB` jumps in upper case, so the guard had never seen those: 7 of 10, under a
banner that named all ten. Widening the class then let `[^;]*?` run from a call
back into the helper's own definition and report `&[0x0F, opcode]` as an eighth
conditional site. Neither failure mode is reachable now: the opcode is the
call's second argument, split from the argument list and parsed as a literal, so
`0xEB`, `0XEB`, `0xE_B` and a decimal `235` are one value rather than one
spelling, and a call cannot read past its own line. A binding like `jbe_out` is
read as the site's stated intent where it has no comment. Measured: 10
emissions, 7 conditional (4 by comment, 3 by binding), 3 `jmp rel8`.

`tail_call_check` had taken x86's compare and increment from the assembly
*comments* beside the byte arrays, and never asked whether AArch64 compared the
limit at all. Operands now come from `bytes.extend_from_slice(&[...])`; an
operand the check cannot resolve is reported, not passed. Each module must
state the limit itself -- a renamed `MAX_TAIL_CALL_CNT` in one file let the
check adopt the other's and still say both agreed -- and the limit is compared
against the vendored kernel's `MAX_TAIL_CALL_CNT`, a cross-check the README had
claimed since it was written while no version of the script had opened the
header. The dead `--check` flag, `JCC_BASE`, and two shadowed locals are gone.
Battery: 32 plants each caught with its own message, 5 alternate spellings still
accepted as the same value. Gate rc 0, 248 banners, 124,531,802 cases; no Lean
or C file changed.
Census 418 -> 419.

### Step 0542 - the third arena, and a
counter that was one too high

The x86 header defines *three* stack sizes,
not two: 64 and 128 when the stack is
enabled, and 1 when it is disabled. The
threshold theorem pinned only the enabled
pair, so the smallest real arena had no
machine-checked boundary at all -- and it is
the one where the rounding and the last-byte
subtraction are most likely to go wrong.
Recorded: no 8-byte window fits a one-byte
arena, a one-byte window at index 0 does, and
the one-past-end pointer is still a valid
arena address.

Counting the new statement exposed a defect
in the checker. It matched lines beginning
with `theorem`, so a docstring wrapped
mid-sentence -- "...the trace / theorem rests
on" -- counted as a declaration. The published
theorem count had therefore been **one too
high**, and writing my own prose on the same
pattern pushed it two past the truth. The
checker now requires the match to reach a
`:=`, which prose never does; the count is
2,060 with the new theorem included and no
false positives, and planting such a docstring
line no longer moves it.

Worth recording as a class: every count in
the paper is recomputed by a script, and a
script that miscounts is worse than no script,
because it converts a guess into apparent
evidence. Gate: rc 0, **248** banners.
Census 412 -> 413.

### Step 0541 - the two files say the same
thing in different words

The AArch64 and x86 stack-arena files
state the same capacity restriction in
different words: a numeric bound
`capacity <= 2^32 - 8` on one side, the
no-wrap predicate `capacity <= capacity + 7`
on the other. A reader comparing them
cannot tell whether that is a wording
difference or a real divergence -- and the
two files are supposed to describe the same
arena, so the question is worth settling
rather than assuming.

They are the same restriction. Both are
exactly tight: the equality holds at
`2^32 - 8` and fails from `2^32 - 7` upward,
which is precisely where the no-wrap
predicate stops holding. The new statement
records the equality failure and the
predicate failure *together*, so the
correspondence is proved rather than
asserted -- a reader who suspects drift can
check one theorem instead of comparing two
phrasings by eye.

This also closes the coverage gap left by
0538 and 0540, which recorded
boundary-tightness on AArch64 only.
Theorem counts move (2,059 -> **2,060**;
487 -> **488** `native_decide`). Gate: rc 0,
**248** banners. Census 411 -> 412.

### Step 0540 - and here both hypotheses

holds at `2^32 - 8`, fails from `2^32 - 7`
upward. The `0 < capacity` condition is
*also* load-bearing, for an unrelated
reason: at a zero arena the left side is
`2^32 - 1` and the right `2^29 - 1`, because
the subtraction wraps.

So both are needed -- which makes this the
contrast case to 0539 in the same file,
where a capacity restriction on a neighbouring
theorem was removable. Three outcomes now on
record for the same question (tight, unused,
needed-with-a-different-reason), and no way
to tell them apart without measuring the
neighbourhood.

The three claims are `native_decide` on
concrete values and they bite: moving the
non-equality onto the tight point fails the
build. Theorem counts move (2,058 -> **2,059**;

**248** banners. Census 410 -> 411.

### Step 0539 - the other answer to 0538's

used

0538 asked whether the stack arena's
capacity bound was load-bearing and found it
exactly tight. Asking the same of the
*last-byte window* theorems gives the
opposite answer on both architectures: they
carried `8 <= capacity`, and the conclusion
holds for every capacity.

The case the hypothesis excluded is a zero
arena, where `capacity - 1` wraps to the top
of the range -- and the window fails there
too, for the same reason as everywhere else:
the last byte plus eight is past the end
either way. The hypothesis was doing no
work; the proof used it only to learn that
capacity is nonzero, which the zero case now
decides directly. Dropping it widens the
theorem to its true domain.

The pair is worth having together: the same
question, asked of two statements in one
file, gave opposite answers, which is exactly
why it has to be asked of each rather than
assumed once.

exact rather than merely sound -- at capacity

### Step 0538 - the stack-arena capacity
bound is exactly tight

`arm64_stack_arena_words_refines` proves
the rounding equality `(capacity + 7) / 8`
against the independent specification,
under a bound `capacity <= 2^32 - 8`. Like
every implication in the proof, it leaves a
reader unable to tell whether the bound is
load-bearing or merely convenient -- exactly
the question Step 0525 had to answer by
measurement for a different family.

Measuring the neighbourhood answers it: the
equality holds at `2^32 - 8`, fails for
*every* capacity from `2^32 - 7` through
`2^32 - 1`, and holds again at `0`, where
the rounding wraps. So the bound is not
conservative by accident -- it marks
precisely the last capacity that does not
wrap. The theorem now says that, and the
wrap case is pinned separately with its two
concrete values, so the reason for the
failure is recorded rather than merely its
existence.

Both are `native_decide` on concrete
values: cheap, and they bite -- moving the
non-equality to a capacity where it does
hold fails the build. Theorem counts move
with the two statements (2,055 -> **2,057**;
483 -> **485** `native_decide`; the share
rounds to 23%). Gate: rc 0, **248**
