### Step 0531 - the x86 call/return
pair, where stack discipline is the
property

Steps 0529/0530 executed the AArch64
emission surface (census 401 -> 402). The
x86 surface is larger -- it models a real
call/return pair through the stack where
AArch64 uses a link register -- and none of
its five emission macros was executed
either.

The pair is worth more than the AArch64 one
because it moves the stack pointer. CALL
decrements it by eight and writes the return
address at the new top; the subroutine
return reads that word and increments by
eight. A pair that disagreed would corrupt
the pointer and return through a stale word,
while any check inspecting only the address
still passed.

The host checks the decrement, the stored
word, the read back, the restore, control
transfer, and the round trip as a pair.

Two details cost real time and are recorded
in the host. The modelled arena indexes at
offset + capacity, so a frame pointer outside
it trips the window guard -- and that guard
is `__builtin_trap`, so a wrong address shows
as SIGILL with no output rather than a
failure line. And the aligned 64-bit slot is
`q[wordIndex(index(off))]`, not `q[index(off)]`;
using the latter read the wrong word and
produced plausible failures against a correct
simulator.

Verified by planting each direction:
decrementing by 16 fails, incrementing by 16
fails. Gate: rc 0, **245** banners,
124,531,696 cases. Census 401 -> 402.

### Step 0530 - call and return, where
two writes must agree

Steps 0528/0529 executed the five branch
emitters. CALL and RET are the rest of the
emission surface and had the same history
(census 400 -> 401).

They are worth more than symmetry. CALL
performs *two* writes that must agree: it
sets the modelled link register `__a64_lr`
and the architectural `x30` from the same
value, while RET dispatches on the former
and a callee would return through the
latter. A call that set one and not the
other passes any single-register check and
returns to the wrong place at run time.

The host checks that both registers receive
the address and agree, that control actually
transfers, and that RET dispatches on the
link register -- taking an installed arm for
an installed target and reaching the
unsupported hook otherwise, so the dispatch
is not vacuous.

One detail worth recording: the return macro
ends in a `return` from the *calling
function*, so the observation is read from a
file-scope global rather than a local.

Verified by planting both faults -- setting
`__a64_lr` without `x30` fails, and removing
the transfer of control fails. Gate: rc 0,
**244** banners, 124,531,687 cases. Census
400 -> 401.

### Step 0529 - the three other AArch64
branch emitters, with no x86 twin to
notice their absence

Step 0528 executed the condition-code
emitter. The same region defines three
more -- CBZ_IMPL, TBZ_IMPL and the
wrappers selecting their kind through the
generated branch-test contract -- and none
of them was executed by any host
(census 399 -> 400). The x86 simulator has
no counterpart at all, so unlike the JCC
case there was not even a sibling oracle to
reveal the absence.

They differ from the condition-code emitters
in where the predicate comes from: not NZCV
but the register itself, zero-ness for
CBZ/CBNZ and a single bit for TBZ/TBNZ. Two
independent things can therefore go wrong,
both silent: the test could select the
wrong predicate, or the emitter could invert
it.

The host drives all four through the real
macros over ten operands, four bit indices
and both edge directions, observing the
arrival address through `goto` labels.
Verified by planting both shapes -- masking
the tested bit index to 62 instead of 63
fails 36 cases, and dropping the inversion
on the CBZ backward arm fails 160. Gate:
rc 0, **243** banners, 124,531,678 cases.
Census 399 -> 400.

### Step 0528 - the AArch64 branch
emitter was never executed, though the
x86 one was

Step 0528 moves to a different surface
(census 398 -> 399). Dispatch selects an
arm; *emission* writes the control edge.
0499 proved the two shapes compose to the
same next PC and the arm64 shape host
compares the contract against an ordering
oracle -- but neither executes the emitter.
The x86 side has had a route host driving
its emitter since before this sequence;
`ARM64_SIM_A64_JCC` was driven by nothing.

The asymmetry matters because the arms are
not symmetric code: the backward shape is
an *inverted* conditional jump over a local
fall-through label. A body that failed to
invert, or that took the fall-through on the
wrong predicate, would compile and terminate
-- it would just take the wrong edge.

The new host drives the real macro over all
15 conditions, 16 flag states and
forward/equal/backward addresses, observing
which arm fired through `goto` labels.
Dropping the inversion fails 960 of 1,201
cases.

Its one deliberate limit is a *proved*
irrelevance: changing `target <= current`
to `<` passes, because at equality both
shapes select the same next PC -- exactly
`arm64_branch_emit_shape_irrelevant` from
Step 0499. Gate: rc 0, **242** banners,
124,531,197 cases. Census 398 -> 399.

### Step 0527 - the same question asked
of x86, where the answer is empty

Step 0526 closed the AArch64 dispatch gap
(12 live / 0 model-only). x86 had never
been measured -- the question simply had
not been asked of it (census 397 -> 398).

Asked now: the x86 chain branches on 53
`HANDLED` predicates and the generated
dispatch model names every one of them.
What looked like a mismatch was a `disp_`
prefix difference in ten family names;
normalising it makes the sets coincide, and
the two Lean-only entries are non-family
artifacts.

So x86 needed no work -- worth establishing
rather than assuming, since the AArch64 side
needed twelve route hosts. The checker now
reports both architectures and fails when
either gains a predicate the model does not
name, verified by planting one on each side.
Gate: rc 0, **241** banners. Census 397 ->
398.

### Step 0526 - complemented OR completes
the sweep: twelve families, zero
model-only

The last of the twelve (census 396 -> 397).
ORN is the family whose *second source is
modified before use*: the dispatcher applies
the AUX-encoded shift or rotate-extend
modifier and passes the modified value in.
A model oracle feeding the contract an
unmodified operand therefore exercises only
modifier kind 0 and cannot see a fault in the
other four.

The oracle drives all five kinds at both
widths and shift amounts either side of the
wrap point, recomputing the modifier from
its definition so a wrong second source is
caught before the OR is considered, and
asserts a non-identity kind was exercised so
the run is not vacuous.

Verified by planting each half: an off-by-one
in shift-left fails 78 cases, dropping the
complement fails 595.

With this the dispatch-model check reports
**12 live / 0 model-only** -- every family
the C chain routes is driven by an oracle
that includes the simulator header. What
began as a recorded gap in Step 0519 is now
empty, and the check that measures it fails
if any new family appears without one. Gate:
rc 0, **241** banners, 124,529,996 cases.
Census 396 -> 397.

### Step 0525 - extract/reverse/extend,
and a proof hypothesis the oracle showed
was unnecessary

Sixth of the model-only families (census
395 -> 396), and the largest: six opcodes
over 26 shifts and masks. Step 0496 related
its REV opcode to x86 at the contract layer,
but nothing drove the dispatcher to it, and
EXTR, REV16 and the three sign extensions
had no live oracle at all.

Writing one also found something in the
*proofs*. EXTR's refinement theorems carry
a hypothesis that the operands are already
narrowed to the destination width, which the
dispatcher does not discharge -- it passes
raw registers. The forms genuinely differ
before the final narrowing
(`0xffffffffffffffff` against `0x1ffffffff`
at `w32`), so the hypothesis was doing work
at the wrong point. It is also unnecessary:
both sides are narrowed to the destination
width at the end, which is what the C
register write does, so the refinement holds
without it. Three raw-operand theorems now
carry that; the 64-bit case already needed
none.

That is a stronger statement than the tree
had, and an oracle found it rather than a
reading of the proof.

Verified on the C side by planting one
fault per opcode family: EXTR's shift off by
one fails 175 cases, SXTB's mask narrowed
fails 80, SXTW's likewise 80, SXTH's sign
bit moved 280. The dispatch-model count
moves from 10 live / 2 model-only to
11 / 1. Gate: rc 0, **240** banners, 2,055
theorems, 124,529,295 cases. Census 395 ->
396.

### Step 0524 - address generation: the
tag is the whole contract, and only the
tag check finds it

Fifth of the remaining model-only
families (census 394 -> 395). ADRP copies
its immediate into the destination as a
pointer, and the only thing the opcode
decides is which *kind* of pointer it is.
A dispatcher with the two arms swapped
leaves the address byte-identical and
labels it as a different pointer class:
invisible to any address comparison, and a
change to later behaviour rather than to
this instruction's result.

`test_arm64_adrp_route_host.c` therefore
checks two independent facts -- the address
equals the immediate, and the tag is the one
the opcode names -- with the expected tags
written from the simulator's vocabulary
rather than read back from the contract. It
also asserts the two arms select *different*
tags, so the check cannot pass with both
arms identical.

Verified by planting each half separately:
swapping the tags fails 60 of 61 cases with
identical addresses, and adding 8 to the
address fails 60 with the tags correct. The
dispatch-model count moves from 9 live / 3
model-only to 10 / 2. Gate: rc 0, **239**
banners, 124,527,615 cases. Census 394 ->
395.

### Step 0523 - the vector reductions
defeat the obvious oracle twice over

Fourth of the remaining model-only
families (census 393 -> 394). REDUCTION
breaks two assumptions an oracle would
naturally make: the dispatcher writes the
SIMD register `v0`, not a GPR destination,
so comparing the destination observes
nothing at all; and the result is assembled
lane by lane, so a fault can move a single
byte while the rest of the value stays
correct.

`test_arm64_reduction_route_host.c` drives
CNT and UADDLV through the dispatcher and
compares `v0` against a lane-by-lane
recomputation written here, over operands
whose bytes are all distinct -- which is
what makes a single misplaced lane visible.

Verified by planting each lane fault
separately: moving one CNT lane from bit 32
to bit 40 fails 7 of 21 cases, and shifting
one UADDLV contribution by a single bit
fails 6. Both differ in one byte or one
word of an otherwise correct value, exactly
the class a model-side comparison would
miss. The dispatch-model count moves from
8 live / 4 model-only to 9 / 3. Gate: rc 0,
**238** banners, 124,527,554 cases. Census
393 -> 394.

### Step 0522 - the store-exclusive arm,
the only remaining family with two
observable effects

Third of the remaining model-only
families (census 392 -> 393). STLXR is
the only one with two effects: the
dispatcher stores the source to memory
*and* writes a status word to the
destination. A misroute can therefore
corrupt the atomic-success signal while
leaving memory correct, or the reverse --
and a model-side oracle comparing one
effect would miss half of it.

`test_arm64_stlxr_route_host.c` checks the
three things independently: the memory
word written, the status the destination
receives (in the low 32 bits, since the
dispatcher writes it at a fixed 32-bit
width regardless of the access width), and
that the source register is unchanged.

Verified by planting each effect alone:
making the status non-zero fails all 200
cases; dropping the store fails 155 as a
MEMORY mismatch, so neither effect is
riding on the other's check. The
dispatch-model count moves from 7 live /
5 model-only to 8 / 4. Gate: rc 0, **237**
banners, 124,527,533 cases. Census 392 ->
393.

### Step 0521 - the condition-gated
negation, where the flag chain meets the
arithmetic

Second of the six remaining model-only
families (census 391 -> 392). CNEG is
worth more than most: the dispatcher does
not take a boolean, it evaluates the
condition code in `AUX` against the live
NZCV flags and passes the result in. So
this arm is where the flag-to-condition
chain proved in Steps 0490 and 0493 meets
the arithmetic -- and a wrong route is
silent twice over, since negate and
not-negate cost the same and nothing writes
a flag.

`test_arm64_cneg_route_host.c` drives it
through `ARM64_SIM_L_EXEC` over all 15
condition codes, all 16 flag combinations,
both widths and 11 operands, with the
condition evaluated independently from the
architecture rather than from the generated
table: 26,400 cases.

Verified by planting both halves of the
composition -- inverting GE in the condition
contract fails 1,360 cases, dropping the
negation in the CNEG contract fails 10,880.
The dispatch-model count moves from 6 live
/ 6 model-only to 7 / 5. Gate: rc 0,
**236** banners, 124,527,333 cases.
Census 391 -> 392.

### Step 0520 - the unary arm gets a
live oracle, and one expectation was
wrong

Step 0519 listed seven families with only
model-side hosts. This closes one (census
390 -> 391). UNARY (MVN, NEG) is worth
driving through the dispatcher because the
two opcodes are each other's plausible
neighbour: both take one source, both write
at the access width, neither writes NZCV.
Sending NEG down the MVN arm therefore
yields a full-width complement instead of a
negation -- a wrong value with no flag to
give it away.

`test_arm64_unary_route_host.c` drives both
opcodes at both widths through
`ARM64_SIM_L_EXEC`, expected value computed
from the architectural definition. The
dispatch-model count moves from 5 live / 7
model-only to 6 / 6.

One expectation was wrong against the tree.
I first required a narrow write to preserve
the destination's high half, and got 156
failures. `arm64_write_arm.h` states the
value is masked to the access width before
the body is chosen, so the narrow and full
bodies are observationally equal and the
high half is *not* preserved. The oracle now
expects what the simulator does -- the
difference between a finding and a mistake
in the model, which by now is a familiar
distinction.

Verified: swapping the opcode in the
dispatcher fails 312 cases; corrupting the
source by one fails 312. Gate: rc 0, **235**
banners, 124,500,933 cases. Census 390 ->
391.

### Step 0519 - the dispatcher and the
model of it were never compared

Steps 0517/0518 prove coverage over the
*generated* dispatch tables (census 389 ->
390). The C chain branches on its own list
of `HANDLED` predicates, and nothing tied
the two lists together -- so the theorem
described a subset while reading as a claim
about the chain.

Measured: the AArch64 chain branches on
**35** families, the model names **25**.
Twelve are routed by the code and absent
from the model.

`check_dispatch_model.py` records that set
rather than concealing it, and fails on a
new predicate with no counterpart or a
recorded gap that has since been modelled.

Writing the entries honestly took a
correction worth keeping: the first version
claimed each of the twelve had a route
host, and only five do -- CSEL, MUL, MOV,
SHIFT and LDRSX are driven through the
dispatcher; ADRP, CNEG, EXTREV, ORN,
REDUCTION, STLXR and UNARY have model-side
hosts only. That is the gap 0503 closed for
MUL, now enumerated for the rest instead of
being assumed absent.

The totality module's docstring now states
its scope: the modelled subset is complete
and exclusive, which is not the same as the
chain being so. Gate: rc 0, **234**
banners. Census 389 -> 390.

### Step 0518 - x86 dispatch coverage,
where the unrouted set is a category
rather than residue

Step 0517 gave AArch64 a coverage statement
to sit beside its exclusivity; x86 had only
exclusivity (census 388 -> 389). The mirror
turned out to differ in kind.

AArch64's two reserved codes are unused
filler. The x86 five are JCC, JMP, CALL,
CALL_HELPER and RET -- the control-transfer
opcodes, which the emitted code carries
directly rather than through the modelling
chain, and which is exactly why the chain
has no final `else`. So "unrouted" is an
architectural category on x86, not leftovers,
and the module records it as such.

Proved: both routed lists duplicate-free
and mutually disjoint; the unrouted set
disjoint from routed in *both* directions;
non-empty; characterised exactly by
membership; and its five codes distinct.
Adding a control opcode without routing it
breaks a theorem rather than passing
quietly.

Verified in both directions: dropping RET
from the list breaks four theorems, and
adding an already-routed code breaks six.
Gate: rc 0, **234** banners, 2,052
theorems. Census 388 -> 389.

### Step 0517 - the dispatcher's
exclusivity was proved; its coverage was
not

Step 0517 proves the half that was missing
(census 387 -> 388). The existing theorem
says no opcode is gated by two arms -- "at
most one". Nothing said "at least one", and
the difference matters, because an opcode
with no arm falls through the chain to the
unsupported hook: a silent behavioural hole
rather than a compile error.

`Arm64DispatchTotality` partitions the
opcodes the two generated tables name into
family-routed, singleton-routed and
unrouted, and proves the routed lists are
duplicate-free and mutually disjoint; the
unrouted set is disjoint from both,
non-empty, and *enumerated* rather than
discovered, so adding an opcode without
routing it shows up as a diff; and
membership is characterised exactly.

Getting the unrouted set right took
measurement. A first scan of the `HANDLED`
macros suggested three opcodes; evaluating
the generated tables showed `RET` is a
routed singleton, and only `ADD_IMM` and
`SUB_IMM` are reserved. The scan was wrong,
not the tree.

Adding one element to the unrouted list
breaks four of the eight theorems. Gate:
rc 0, **234** banners, 2,042 theorems.
Census 387 -> 388.

### Step 0516 - the C surface is
mutation-tested, and mostly guarded at
generation time

Step 0515 showed the proofs stop at the
language boundary, so the compiled side
rests on oracles. Whether that is enough
is measurable (census 386 -> 387):
`mutate_contracts.py` finds the first
meaningful literal in each generator's
emitted-C string, bumps it, regenerates,
and records what fires. Over 31 generators:

| outcome | count |
|---|---|
| rejected by the generator | 24 |
| caught by a host | 3 |
| stopped by a static assertion | 2 |
| header exports no macro to call | 2 |
| **survived** | **0** |

Three quarters of the C surface never
reaches a build: the generator's own
validation refuses the change. That is a
stronger property than the earlier steps
established, and it is now measured on
every gate rather than argued.

Getting the number honest took four passes,
each discarding a false survivor -- a
docstring, a static-assert message, a
Python format-padding width, and a generator
diagnostic prefix. All four are inert; all
four initially looked like a mutation
nothing caught. Gate: rc 0, **234** banners.
Census 386 -> 387.

### Step 0515 - a refinement proof
covers the Lean formula, not the C one

Step 0515 measures the boundary of the
proofs (census 385 -> 386). A generator
renders one specification into a C header
and a Lean module; the Lean carries a
refinement theorem, so a mistake *there* is
caught at build time. But the C formula is
a separate string literal in the same
generator, and the proof is stated over the
Lean one.

Measured rather than assumed: changing
`mid1 >> 32` to `>> 16` in the multiply
generator's C string leaves
`lake env lean KProgFormal/Arm64Mul.lean`
green, because the Lean literal still says
`>>> 32`. The extract/reverse/extend
generator's C `<< 56` becomes `<< 55` with
its proof passing too.

So the C needs its own oracle, and
`check_dual_emit_coverage.py` records which
host covers each of the seven dual-emitted
generators -- confirming coverage by
mutating the C string alone, since nothing
else establishes it. One of the seven is
caught even earlier, by a static assertion
in `x86_sim.h`. A new dual-emitted
generator with no recorded coverage fails
the gate.

The script's own first draft mis-read
Lean's `<<<` as a C shift and produced a
false finding; the lookbehind now
distinguishes two- from three-character
shifts. Gate: rc 0, **234** banners.
Census 385 -> 386.

### Step 0514 - four oracles tested a
contract but not the simulator's path to
it, so the class is now checked

Step 0513 found one oracle recomputing
what the simulator computes. It was not
alone (census 384 -> 385): the shift-flags
oracle and the register-lane-aux oracle
had the same shape. Measured on the
shift-flags one, shifting the sign bit by
one *inside* the simulator survived all
90,112 cases.

That host now drives the simulator's own
composition as well and compares the two.
Doing so needed the flags seeded
identically on both paths, because some
arms deliberately leave ZF/SF untouched --
without it the comparison reported 24
spurious mismatches, which is the same
"my model was wrong" pattern as Steps
0504 and 0505.

`check_oracle_composition.py` generalises
the search rather than leaving three more
to be found by hand: it reads the simulator
sources, collects the contract macros
reached from inside each `SIM_L_*` body,
and reports every host calling one of them
without calling any `SIM_L_*` macro itself.
Four hosts match; each is recorded with the
reason it is acceptable and which host does
cover its composition. A new one fails the
gate with that instruction.

Gate: rc 0, **234** banners. Census 384 ->
385.

### Step 0513 - an oracle that tested
the contract but not the simulator's own
composition

Step 0513 extends the 128-bit oracle to the
x86 multiply-overflow flags (census 383 ->
384). They decide CF/OF from magnitudes
rather than by multiplying -- `A_ABS != 0 &&
B_ABS > LIMIT / A_ABS`, with LIMIT chosen by
the product's sign -- so there are two
independent chances to be wrong: the
division rounds down, and the sign
selection is a separate expression.

The oracle's first form included only
`x86_sim.h`, recomputed the limit itself,
and passed it to the generated macro. So it
tested the contract and never the
simulator's own sign selection: planting
`xor` to `or` in the simulator left it
green. Driving `X86_SIM_L_SET_IMUL_FLAGS`
-- the composition the simulator actually
performs -- makes that fault fail 40 cases.

The operand table needed widening too. The
most-negative value against `-1` is the one
pair whose product is exactly the negative
bound, so it is the only place the two
candidate limits disagree; without it a
sign-selection fault was invisible even to
the corrected oracle.

Verified: the boundary test fails 216
cases, the sign selection 40. Gate: rc 0,
**234** banners, 124,500,620 cases. Census
383 -> 384.

### Step 0512 - dual emission protects
against drift, not against a shared
error

Step 0512 tests a contract that no proof
relates to its definition (census 382 ->
383). The multiply header and its Lean
module are rendered from one specification
in one pass, so they cannot drift from each
other -- but they can both be wrong the
same way, and nothing in the tree relates
either to the architectural definition.

The family is shaped to hide exactly that.
`UMULH` computes the high half of a
128-bit product with a shift-and-add
decomposition; a term placed in the wrong
position still yields a plausible number,
and re-reading the same formula would
reproduce the same mistake.

The independent oracle is C's 128-bit
integer type -- available to an x86 host,
not to the BPF-target simulator.
`test_arm64_mul_wide_host.c` checks all
eight opcodes against it over boundary
operands: zero, one, the 32-bit split,
all-ones, and values whose halves differ.
27,648 cases.

Verified by planting two faults of the
shape a shared error takes: moving the
mid1 term from a 32-bit to a 16-bit shift
fails 1,008 cases; changing the carry's
shift from 32 to 24 fails 1,872. Gate:
rc 0, **233** banners, 124,498,572 cases.
Census 382 -> 383.

### Step 0511 - the two architectures
resolve ambiguous map names differently,
and nothing said so

Step 0511 records a cross-architecture
difference rather than removing it (census
381 -> 382). Both encoders answer "given
a native map name, which lookup site is
this?", and both truncate at
`BPF_OBJ_NAME_LEN - 1` because the kernel
stores at most that much.

They answer it with different structures.
x86 runs an exact pass, then a separate
truncated pass that *errors* when two
sites truncate-match the same name -- in
both the lookup and the update path.
AArch64 folds exact and truncated matching
into one predicate used with `find`, so
the first of several matching sites wins.

For a name matching more than one site,
one architecture reports an error and the
other picks silently. Neither is wrong,
but a program can lower on one and fail on
the other, and nothing said so.

`check_lookup_ambiguity.py` measures the
divergence instead of picking a winner,
and fails if the two converge without
someone deciding they should -- convergence
means one side changed, which is equally
worth a look. It also pins both truncation
lengths to the kernel's limit. Verified by
removing x86's lookup-path error, which is
reported by path name. Gate: rc 0, **232**
banners. Census 381 -> 382.

### Step 0510 - the two architectures
lower tail calls independently and
nothing compared them

Step 0510 is the first cross-*architecture*
check rather than a cross-language one
(census 380 -> 381). `bpf_tail_call` is
lowered separately for x86 and AArch64, in
separate modules, each with its own
spelling of the kernel's limit -- `u8` on
one side, `u32` on the other. The same
program lowered either way must behave the
same, so the limit, the comparison and the
increment have to agree. Nothing compared
them.

The check now requires one statement of
the limit across both modules, an
unsigned-greater-or-equal branch on each
side (x86 `jae`, AArch64 `CS`), and an
increment by exactly one on each side,
with the limit cross-checked against the
vendored kernel header where
`MAX_TAIL_CALL_CNT` is 33.

Measured: both sides state 33, both branch
on unsigned greater-or-equal, both
increment by one. Verified by planting
three divergences -- AArch64's limit moved
to 34, x86's branch changed from `jae` to
`ja`, AArch64's increment reduced to zero
-- each reported by name.

A related measurement that looked like a
discrepancy and is not: the encoder
reserves 512 bytes of stack for its own
frame, the kernel's `MAX_BPF_STACK` is
also 512, and the simulators model 64/128
and 160. The arena is a model size, not
the architectural one, and an access past
it is reported rather than silently wrong.
Gate: rc 0, **232** banners. Census 380 ->
381.

### Step 0509 - the same crate emits
AArch64 conditional branches, also
unchecked

Steps 0507/0508 covered the x86 encoder's
conditional jumps. The same crate also
emits AArch64 conditional branches from a
literal word whose low four bits are the
condition code, and nothing checked those
(census 379 -> 380).

Six sites, all in tail-call and map-update
lowering, where the branch decides whether
an index is out of bounds, whether a map
module is missing, or whether an argument
is invalid. The buffer-index name states
which check the branch belongs to, so here
the expected condition is a property of the
*site*: bounds/limit/null are "greater or
equal", module existence is equality, and
the invalid-argument test is "higher".

One name did not say enough.
`null_branch` follows the same
`cmp X9, max_entries` as the bounds
branches, so it is a bounds check too --
visible from the surrounding code, not from
its name, which is worth recording because
a checker keyed on names inherits their
imprecision.

Measured: 6 sites, all encode the
condition their check requires. Verified
by planting two faults -- bounds as
equality, reported against the check it
implements; and a plain unconditional `B`
in place of the `B.cond`, reported as not
being a conditional branch at all. Gate:
rc 0, **232** banners. Census 379 -> 380.

### Step 0508 - closing the jcc
checker's own stated blind spot

Step 0507 checked four commented
conditional-jump emissions and said
plainly that an uncommented opcode was
invisible to it. There are seven (census
378 -> 379), and the three uncommented
ones sit in the tail-call lowering path,
where jbe/jae/je decide the callee-saved
mask, the tail-call count and the null
program check. All three were correct --
but nothing knew that either.

The binding name supplies the missing
intent: `let jbe_out = ...rel32(..., 0x86)`
states the condition without a trailing
comment. The checker takes intent from the
comment when present and from a
`j<cond>_out` binding otherwise, and says
which route each site used.

The near form is now handled properly too:
rel32 adds `0x80` to the condition code
where rel8 adds `0x70`, so the base is
per-form rather than assumed.

Measured: 7 sites -- 4 by comment, 3 by
binding -- all correct. Verified by
planting a wrong opcode at each of the
three previously-unchecked sites. An
emission with neither a comment nor a
`j<cond>_out` binding is still only
range-checked, which the script states.
Gate: rc 0, **232** banners. Census 378 ->
379.

### Step 0507 - the encoder's jump
opcodes had no link to the condition
contract

Step 0507 joins two languages (census 377
-> 378). The x86 encoder is Rust and
emits conditional jumps as raw opcodes
beside a comment naming the mnemonic; the
C simulator decides conditions from the
`X86_CC_*` table. Nothing connects them,
and an opcode is only a number -- an
off-by-one compiles, runs, and branches on
the wrong condition.

x86's encoding rule supplies the link:
short conditional jump opcodes are
`0x70 + condition code`, and the
`X86_CC_*` values are those codes.
`check_jcc_opcodes.py` requires every
mnemonic-commented site to satisfy that,
and runs on every gate.

Measured: 4 sites (ja, jae, je, jne), all
correct. Pressed in both directions --
changing jne's opcode to `0x74` reports
the site; drifting `X86_CC_NE` to 6
reports it too. The script also states its
own limit: an uncommented `0x7x` constant
is invisible to it, so the check is as wide
as the encoder's commenting, not wider.
Gate: rc 0, **232** banners. Census 377 ->
378.

### Step 0506 - the helper-id table was
stated but never checked against the
kernel

Step 0506 covers a contract that is
*stated* rather than reached (census 376
-> 377). `arm64_helper_idents_spec.json`
gives each of 61 BPF helpers the kernel id
the encoder renumbers against. The ids are
hand-maintained, and the generated
header's assertions only pin them to the
spec -- so a wrong id yields a
self-consistent header, green oracles, and
a program renumbered onto the wrong helper
at runtime. The simulator dispatches by
*name* at compile time and never reads the
table, which is why nothing had checked it.

The independent source was already in the
tree: the vendored libbpf ships
`bpf_helper_defs.h` with one entry per
helper. `check_helper_idents.py` parses
it, compares, and runs on every gate.

Measured, not assumed: all 61 ids match
the kernel enum exactly, and the name set
matches what the simulator forwards to in
both directions. The checker separates
three fault classes -- an id that
disagrees with the kernel, a name the
kernel does not define, and a name-set
mismatch either way -- and each was
planted to confirm it reports. Gate: rc 0,
**232** banners. Census 376 -> 377.

### Step 0505 - the conditional-select
family had no live oracle, and writing
one corrected the model twice

Step 0505 continues the simulator-called
but never-driven sweep (census 375 ->
376). `arm64_csel` names eight opcodes --
CSEL, CINC, CSET, CINV, CSINV, CSINC,
CSETM, CSNEG -- and the dispatcher
reaches them at one arm that evaluates
the condition, picks the pointer-tag or
scalar path, then writes the destination.
No host including the simulator header
drove any of them: perturbing the CSINC
arm left every existing oracle green.

The new host drives all eight through
`ARM64_SIM_L_EXEC` at both widths, with
the condition both always-taken and
flag-dependent so each opcode's two arms
are each reached, and with the expected
value computed from the instruction
definitions rather than from the macro.

Writing it corrected the model twice, and
what it exposed is about the contract.
`CINC` and `CINV` take `src` on *both*
paths and ignore `src2` -- right for the
one-operand forms, but it means an operand
pair chosen for the two-operand shape
cannot distinguish them. The first model
assumed the two-operand form for all eight
and produced 24 spurious failures; the fix
was to read the generated arms instead of
the instruction-set pseudocode. A `+1` to
`+2` change in the CINC arm now fails on
12 of 192 cases, and a `-1` in CSNEG on
12. Gate: rc 0, **232** banners,
124,470,924 cases. Census 375 -> 376.

### Step 0504 - the flag contract was
reached only through a model, and the
first oracle missed the case that matters

Step 0504 takes the most consequential
of the 48 simulator-called but
model-only contracts (census 374 -> 375):
`arm64_flags`, reached through ADDS/SUBS
via `EXEC_ARITH_WRITEBACK`, which picks
the family, computes the result and sets
all four flags.

A wrong flag is worse than a wrong value:
invisible at the instruction that caused
it, wrong at the next branch.
`test_arm64_flag_route_host.c` therefore
compares the destination *and* all four
flags against an independent architectural
model of ADD/SUB and of N/Z/C/V, computed
here rather than by calling the macros.

The oracle's first draft was wrong twice,
and both are the lesson. The overflow
model omitted ADD's operand-agreement
complement, which the contract has --
fixed against the definition, not against
the macro. And the operand table used
distinct registers, so `lhs == rhs` was
never generated; that is the *only* case
separating a subtract carry of "lhs greater
or equal rhs" from "lhs strictly greater".
A planted fault of exactly that shape
survived. Adding equal-operand immediates
took the run from 432 to 1,152 cases and
made the planted fault fail on 24 of them.

Gate: rc 0, **231** banners, 124,470,732
cases. Census 374 -> 375.

### Step 0503 - the multiply arm was
proved and modelled but never driven

Step 0503 separates two claims that were
being conflated (census 373 -> 374).
Classifying all 214 hosts by whether they
include the simulator header gives 89 that
drive the real dispatcher and 125 that
compare a hand model against a generated
contract. The second does not imply the
first: a contract can be proved, modelled,
and still never exercised through the code
that runs it.

Fifty-five of the 138 contracts appeared
only on the model-only side. The AArch64
multiply arm was the one *arithmetic*
family in that position -- proved in Lean,
modelled in a host, and never driven
through `ARM64_SIM_L_EXEC`. So the
dispatcher could stop routing to it, read
the wrong source, or write the destination
at the wrong width, and every existing
check would stay green.

`test_arm64_mul_route_host.c` closes it:
MADD/MSUB/MUL over distinct, non-zero
operand triples at both widths, so a
swapped source, a wrong addend position
or a truncated write each produce a
different value; the expected value is
computed from the architectural
definition rather than by calling the
contract, so the check is not circular;
and a non-member opcode must reach the
unsupported arm, so the counter is not
vacuously zero. Flipping MSUB's operand
order fails it on 432 of 1,296 cases.
Gate: rc 0, **230** banners (one new),
124,469,580 cases. Census 373 -> 374.

### Step 0502 - two arm64 memory models
had the wrong stack-pointer value

Step 0502 fixes a defect found by the
same search (census 372 -> 373). Both
arm64 memory-model hosts defined
`ARM64_SP` as 31, but in this simulator
31 is `XZR` and 32 is `SP` -- the
simulator tests `REG == ARM64_SP` with
`SP == 32`, and reads 31 as zero. So the
models treated a register the simulator
reads as zero as though it were the stack
pointer.

There was a second consequence, and it is
the more interesting one. The base sweep
ran `bi < 32`, so with `SP == 32` the
actual stack base was **never driven at
all** -- the hosts believed they were
testing the stack path because 31 was
labelled SP. Correcting the value and
running the sweep one past the register
file takes them from 9,216 cases to 9,504.

What these hosts can show is bounded, and
the step records it rather than implying
more: `contract_step` and `model_step`
share `run_halves` and the read/write
helpers, so they compare two *labellings*
of one model, not an independent
reimplementation. A semantic error inside
that shared model is invisible to both.
What changed is that the stack-base path
and the XZR discard are now exercised
rather than assumed. Gate: rc 0, **229**
banners. Census 372 -> 373.

### Step 0501 - two condition-decode
oracles could not see the simulator drift

Step 0501 turns the coverage question
around (census 371 -> 372). Rather than
ask which contracts have a host, it asks
which contracts the *simulator* never
calls -- and the answer pointed at the
two condition-decode oracles, which
restated their ISA's `X86_CC_*` /
`ARM64_COND_*` codes as local literals.

That was the right instinct about the
generated tables and the wrong one about
the other side: it made the oracles blind
to whether the *simulator* still agreed
with the contract. Measured, not assumed:
drifting `X86_CC_A` in `x86_sim.h`, or
`ARM64_COND_EQ` in `arm64_sim.h`, left
both oracles green.

Both now include the simulator header, so
the drift fails at *compile time* through
the generated `_Static_assert`s -- a
stronger check than the runtime comparison
they had, and one that no longer depends
on the literals happening to match. Gate:
rc 0, **229** banners. Census 371 -> 372.

### Step 0500 - the theorem counts become a gate step

Step 0499 closed the control-flow chains, and the next thing the section states
is how many theorems the tree proves. That figure was maintained by hand, so
`check_lean_claims.py` went into the gate: it recomputes the theorem, module,
refinement and enumeration counts from the tree on every run and compares each
with the sentence that states it.

The paper submodule pointer moved in the same step, because the Lean-side counts
in the section had gone stale by the time the checker existed to notice.

Census 330 -> 331.

### Step 0499 - the two control-flow
chains compose to the same next PC

Twelve steps compared one contract at a
time; this one compares a *chain* (census
370 -> 371). Each ISA already proves its
own path in isolation -- a condition
evaluation refines to the architectural
predicate, the emitted shape selects the
architectural next PC -- so on either ISA
flags in means the correct next PC out.
Nothing showed the two chains agree with
each other.

The risk is specific: the chains are not
the same shape internally. AArch64
evaluates `(N Z C V)` and x86-64
`(CF ZF SF OF)` where C is the complement
of CF, so an intermediate step differs
while the endpoints should not. A chain
that composed differently on one side
would produce a divergent next PC while
every per-ISA theorem continued to hold --
exactly what per-ISA work cannot see.

`CrossIsaBranch.lean` closes the path:
same four architectural flag facts,
through each ISA's own condition
evaluation and shape selection, to one
next program counter. The correspondence
is what Steps 0490 and 0493 established;
what is new is that it composes through
emission rather than stopping at the
predicate. Dropping the carry polarity
breaks the theorem.

The compiled check runs the same
composition over 16 flag combinations, 14
conditions and 5 branch sites. Making the
shape selectors disagree at `target ==
current` fails it on 448 cases; inverting
one condition arm fails it on 96. Gate:
rc 0, **229** banners, 124,467,708 cases
(oracle 1,004,143). Census 370 -> 371.

### Step 0498 - the shared ALU vocabulary
must be recovered by a mapping, and one
pair needs its operands exchanged

Step 0498 relates the two ALU dispatch
tables (census 369 -> 370). Both
architectures execute arithmetic-logic
through one generated table, but the
tables are numbered differently and cover
different sets -- six arms against
sixteen -- so this is the first
correspondence that has to be *recovered*
rather than read off matching codes.

Five operations map one-to-one under a
renaming: add, sub, and, orr/or, eor/xor.
The add and sub cases also prove the
routing transparent, since x86-64 sends
them through the carry-aware adc/sbb with
a clear carry.

The sixth is the one worth the step.
AArch64's `BIC` complements the *right*
operand; x86-64's `ANDN` complements the
*left*. They agree only on exchanged
arguments -- dropping the exchange breaks
the theorem. Both names mean "and with a
complement", which makes this precisely
the pair a translator pairs wrongly, so
`CrossIsaAlu.lean` states both forms
separately, proves the exchange gives
agreement, and pins a concrete case where
the unexchanged pairing differs.

The compiled tables are checked over the
same mapping; breaking BIC's complement
fails the oracle on 264 cases. Gate: rc
0, **229** banners, 124,465,468 cases
(oracle 1,001,903). Census 369 -> 370.

### Step 0497 - the address offsets share
a core, and the rest is what the other
ISA lacks

Step 0497 relates the load/store address
offsets (census 368 -> 369), and the
interesting part is that "the same
function" is the wrong frame. Both
compute a base contribution plus an
optional scaled index with 64-bit
wrapping -- but AArch64 has *no scale*
and does have pre/post-indexing, while
x86-64 has a scale (a base-2 logarithm
in the addressing-mode byte) and *no*
pre/post-indexing.

So the shared core is one statement,
base + (index <<< scale), reached by
zeroing AArch64's scale and taking its
non-writeback form. The rest of each
contract is what the other ISA lacks.
`CrossIsaMemOffset.lean` proves the
reduction, states both case tables, and
records the concrete case where writeback
makes the two compute *different* things
rather than the same thing differently --
so the `prepost = false` restriction is
not mistaken for a technicality. Giving
x86-64 a unit scale breaks the theorem.

The wrap is checked too: both accumulate
with 64-bit two's complement, and a
signed/unsigned slip there would agree on
small inputs, so the oracle uses values
near the boundary. Gate: rc 0, **229**
banners, 124,464,460 cases (oracle
1,000,895). Census 368 -> 369.

### Step 0496 - agreement is not enough:
the reversal theorems pin the
involution too

Step 0496 relates the byte reversals
(census 367 -> 368). `REV` and `BSWAP`
do the same thing by different means --
a shift-and-mask disjunction over the
destination width against a width-first
reversal that clears above -- and agree at
the two widths AArch64 encodes.

Agreement alone would not have been
enough, and this is the step's point. A
byte-reversal fault is quiet: swap two of
the eight terms and it is still a
permutation, still agrees with itself, and
still changes plausibly on most inputs. So
`CrossIsaRev.lean` also pins the property
that gives the operation meaning --
reversal is an order-two permutation on
the width-truncated value. A transposition
breaks the involution while leaving many
inputs coincidentally correct.

The compiled check therefore runs a
pseudo-random stream rather than round
numbers and tests both properties:
1,000,652 cases in 0.1s. Displacing one
byte position fails it on 398,436 of them
-- round numbers would have agreed on
nearly all. Gate: rc 0, **229** banners,
124,464,217 cases (oracle 1,000,652).
Census 367 -> 368.

### Step 0495 - the two sign-extension
contracts agree, and the check is
exhaustive rather than sampled

Step 0495 relates the sign extensions
(census 366 -> 367). Both architectures
extend a narrow value into a 64-bit
register with entirely different code:
AArch64 states it generically ("extend
the low nb bits") and its C inlines the
mask-flip-subtract idiom, while x86-64
states each width as its own arm with the
constants written out. Two spellings of
one function, and nothing related them.

That is exactly the shape a signedness
fault takes. An extension that masks
before flipping the sign bit, or flips the
wrong one, still produces a plausible
register value and still round-trips for
positive inputs -- sampling would see
nothing wrong. `CrossIsaSignExtend.lean`
proves the two agree at all three widths
AArch64 parameterises and x86-64 names,
pins the `0x7f`/`0x80` boundary on both
sides, and records that the 64-bit case
has no AArch64 counterpart because `SXTX`
is not in the extend family.

The C check is exhaustive because the
paths are small enough that it costs
nothing: every 16-bit pattern through both
the byte and halfword extensions, plus a
stride across the 32-bit space -- 200,652
cases in 0.1s. Breaking the byte mask
fails it on 32,768 cases. Gate: rc 0,
**229** banners, 123,664,217 cases (oracle
200,652). Census 366 -> 367.

### Step 0494 - the shift-amount rules
agree exactly where AArch64 encodes
them, and provably differ where it does
not

Step 0494 is the third kind of cross-ISA
result, after "the same" and "deliberately
different" (census 365 -> 366). AArch64
takes a shift amount modulo 32 at 32-bit
width and modulo 64 at 64-bit width;
x86-64 takes it modulo 64 at 64 bits and
modulo 32 otherwise, because it has no
8- or 16-bit shift -- it shifts at 32
bits and truncates. At the two widths
AArch64 encodes (W and X) the rules
coincide exactly.

At 8 and 16 they do not, and the
divergence is real rather than
representational: with `v = 1` and an
amount of 32, AArch64 masks to `0` and
shifts by nothing, x86-64 masks to `32`
and shifts out of the window, giving `0`
against `1`. Measured over 11 values, 13
amounts and four operations, the reachable
widths agree on all 1,144 pairs.

That pair is unreachable from AArch64,
which never encodes a narrow shift, so the
disagreement is a property of the two
contracts rather than of any program
either simulator runs. Proving it is what
keeps the distinction explicit: a change
that starts emitting narrow shifts would
turn a proved agreement into a live
difference, and these theorems break.
Flipping the AArch64 mask breaks three of
them; the differential oracle catches it
on 131 cases, and now excludes the
narrow widths deliberately -- including
them would report a difference no program
can reach. Gate: rc 0, **229** banners,
123,467,609 cases (oracle 4,044). Census
365 -> 366.

### Step 0493 - the two condition
vocabularies decide alike, and the
mapping is not the obvious one

Step 0490 proved the one flag that
differs in meaning (census 364 -> 365).
The branches built on those flags were
still unrelated. Under the
correspondence `(N Z C V) = (SF ZF (!CF)
OF)` the two evaluators agree on all 14
comparable conditions -- and the mapping
is not what the names suggest. `CS` maps
to `AE`, not `B`: AArch64's carry-set
condition follows a compare that
*borrowed*, so its x86 counterpart is
`AE` (no borrow), while `CC` takes `B`.
`MI` maps to `S`, `HI` to `A`, `LS` to
`BE`.

Inverting any one is the classic
condition-inversion bug, and it
typechecks. So the mapping is a
function, the agreement is a theorem
over it, and injectivity is proved so
two distinct AArch64 conditions never
collapse onto one x86 condition. `AL` is
separated out: it is unconditional, so
it is a lowering question rather than a
flag one.

The differential oracle pins the same
table in the generated C, over all 16
flag combinations. Its default arm calls
a function rather than being a no-op
statement, so a fallthrough is a counted
failure. Inverting `CS` breaks three
theorems and fails the oracle on 16
cases. 1,998 theorems. Gate: rc 0, 229
banners, 123,466,465 cases (oracle
2,900). Census 364 -> 365.

### Step 0492 - the same defect was in
the condition evaluators, and is now
checked mechanically

Step 0491 fixed five flag generators;
this finds the class (census 363 -> 364).
The two condition evaluators had it
too: a parameter used as an operand of
`==` or `&&` takes whatever binds
tighter from the caller.
`KPROG_ARM64_EVAL_COND(ARM64_COND_GT,
p || q, 0, 0, 0, 0)` evaluated
`(p || q == V)` as `p || (q == V)`,
returning `GT = 1` where the answer is
`0`; the mirror case returned `0` where
the answer is `1`. Both now emit `(N)`;
Lean output unchanged.

`check_macro_hygiene.py` scans all 138
generated headers for a parameter used
as the bare operand of a binary
operator and runs on every gate. It is
verified against the pre-fix text:
fed the old `(A < B)` form it reports
both operands and exits 1, so the check
is known to fire rather than assumed to.

The general lesson, recorded because it
is the recurring shape here: a generator
that renders one specification into two
languages can be right in the language
with the proofs and wrong in the one
without. Lean's `Nat`/`Bool` API has no
precedence surprises, C's does. Gate:
rc 0, **229** banners, 138 headers
clean. Census 363 -> 364.

### Step 0491 - the generated flag
macros were a hygiene trap

Step 0491 extends the differential
oracle to the flags (census 362 -> 363)
and fixes a latent bug the extension
exposed. The five x86 flag generators
emitted their C operands
unparenthesized, so
`KPROG_X86_SET_SUB_FLAGS(..., a & mask,
b, ...)` expanded `(A < B)` to
`(a & mask < b)`, which C parses as
`a & (mask < b)` -- the carry computed
from the wrong comparison, `0` where
the answer is `1`. The simulator passes
only plain variables at every call site,
so nothing was wrong today, but the
generated contract was a trap for the
next caller. All five now emit `(A)`;
the Lean output is byte-identical
because the fix touches only the C path.

The oracle now also cross-checks the
flags both ways: the carry is
*complementary* and zero, sign and
overflow *agree*, over 144 operand
pairs at four widths. Planting `>=` ->
`>` in AArch64's subtract carry -- a
one-character change that still looks
right -- fails it on 88 cases. Gate:
rc 0, **229** banners, 123,466,241
cases; the extended oracle runs 2,676.
Census 362 -> 363.

### Step 0490 - the carry flags are
proved complementary, not just different

Step 0490 relates a cross-ISA
difference that was previously only
visible as a difference (census 361 ->
362). AArch64 sets `C` after a
subtraction to *not-borrow* (unsigned
`lhs >= rhs`, so `CMP` then `B.HS`
means "no borrow"); x86-64 sets `CF` to
*borrow* (`lhs < rhs`, so `JB` means
"borrow"). Both are architecturally
correct and each is proved against its
own independent statement -- but nothing
related them, so a reader comparing the
specs saw `>=` against `<` and could not
tell an architectural difference from a
mistake in one of them.

`CrossIsaFlags.lean` proves they are
exact complements on the same narrowed
operands, at all four widths. Two
witnesses confirm the difference is real
rather than technical: `1 - 2` borrows
so AArch64's C is false and x86-64's CF
is true, and `2 - 1` is the other way
round, so the complement holds in both
directions.

This is the third kind of cross-ISA
result, alongside "agree" (widths, tags,
stack arithmetic) and "pinned at the C
layer" (the differential oracle): here
the two genuinely differ, and what is
proved is the exact relation between
them. Gate: rc 0, 229 banners, 1,994
theorems. Census 361 -> 362.

### Step 0489 - the cross-ISA theorems
are checked at the C layer too

Step 0489 closes the gap between what
the cross-ISA theorems prove and what
the simulators actually compile (census
360 -> 361). `CrossIsaWidth.lean` and
`CrossIsaStackArena.lean` prove the
generated *Lean* contracts agree. Each
ISA ships its own generated C header
though, so the proofs say nothing about
the C: a generator could emit C that
disagrees where the Lean does not, and
the hand-written C could drift from its
own Lean.

`cross_isa_differential_host.c`
compiles both simulators into one
translation unit -- they coexist, since
every decode is ISA-prefixed -- and
compares the compiled macros on shared
inputs: the four width masks, bit counts
and sign masks over boundary values, and
the stack window, pointer, slot and
alignment bounds over a capacity grid
including both arenas' real sizes (64,
128, 160) and the one-past-end indices.
372 cases, all agreeing.

The coverage is the point. Adding one
to the x86 window capacity *in its
generated header* -- a drift the Lean
cross-ISA theorem still proves correct,
because it compares Lean against Lean --
makes this oracle fail with 9
differences. Gate: rc 0, **229** banners,
123,463,937 modeled cases. Census 360
-> 361.

### Step 0488 - the table-shape
theorems are not vacuous

Step 0488 extends the non-vacuity check
from dispatch to the whole table-shape
family (census 359 -> 360). 426
theorems are closed by a bare `decide`,
and 42 are parameter-free assertions
about a list or table; a vacuous one
would be indistinguishable from a real
one, since both close by the same
tactic.

Three families were checked and all
have content. Nineteen
`*_codes_length` theorems assert
`codes.length = count` against a
generated count constant, and no
generated count is zero -- the 31 run
from 2 to 72. The exactness theorems
assert two independently defined lists
equal, so both must be non-empty:
measured at 36 mnemonics against 12
suffixes and 17 against 15 on arm64.
`x86_helper_dispatch_full_range` pairs
its `List.range` sweep with four
explicit `none` checks, so it has
content even at count 0. No code
change; the deliverable is the audit.
Gate: rc 0, 228 banners. Census 359 ->
360.

### Step 0487 - dispatch exclusivity is
proved, and the proof is non-vacuous

Step 0487 verifies a property a
reviewer would ask about and that was
only implicitly covered (census 358 ->
359). The opcode dispatch is an
`else if` ladder, so two overlapping
family predicates would make dispatch
order-dependent -- whichever arm came
first would silently win. Nothing in
the chain structure prevents that.

It is already proved, in both
directions that matter. Each family
predicate has a refinement theorem
against an independent restatement, and
`x86_dispatch_chain_codes_nodup` (plus
the arm64 pair) proves the combined
generated opcode list has no
duplicates, so the chain selects
exactly one arm per opcode. The
statement is non-vacuous: 43 singleton
plus 24 family codes give 67, and the
deduplicated list is also 67, so it
ranges over 67 real opcodes rather than
an empty or degenerate list. A hand
parse of the 53 predicates independently
finds zero overlapping pairs over those
67 opcodes.

No code change; the deliverable is the
verification and its record. Gate:
rc 0, 228 banners. Census 358 -> 359.

### Step 0486 - the two stack contracts
are proved to agree

Step 0486 completes the cross-ISA
series (census 357 -> 358). Twelve
theorems in the two stack-arena
modules share a concept name once the
ISA prefix is stripped, but the sharing
was structural rather than proved:
nothing showed the two generated
contracts compute the same arithmetic.

They are *not* textually identical,
which is what made this worth doing.
x86 carries `byteAt`/`assembleByte` for
its little-endian byte ladder; arm64
carries `tagSlotFits` for the tag array
x86 does not have. So
`CrossIsaStackArena.lean` proves
exactly the six definitions both sides
share -- `wordIndex`, `wordAligned`,
`words`, `windowEnd`, `windowFits`,
`pointerFits` -- and nothing more.
Changing the x86 `wordIndex` shift from
3 to 2 fails `wordIndex_agrees`, so it
gates spec drift.

With this, every vocabulary the two
simulators share has a cross-ISA
agreement theorem: widths (Step 0481),
tags (Step 0482), and the stack arena's
arithmetic (here). Gate: rc 0, 228
banners, 1,990 theorems. Census 357 ->
358.

### Step 0485 - the width fallback is
pinned rather than left implicit

Step 0485 turns a documented gap into a
tested one (census 356 -> 357). The
README said "behavior for other invalid
numeric widths remain outside the typed
Lean model", which understates what the
C actually does. `KPROG_X86_WIDTH_MASK`
is a chained ternary whose final arm is
the 64-bit mask, so *every* code that is
not one of the four widths resolves to
64 bits: the absent code 0, the opcodes
that reuse the field (`X86_OP_XCHG` is
25, `X86_OP_BZHI` is 30), and any future
drift. The Lean `mask` is total over
the four constructors and has no notion
of an invalid code, so the fallback is
outside the model rather than proved.

`width_fallback_host.c` pins the C
behaviour -- the four valid codes to
their own masks, and a representative
set of eleven invalid codes to 64 bits,
24 assertions. Changing the chain's
final arm to the 16-bit mask makes it
fail with 9 mismatches. The README
paragraph now states the wider form
rather than only the absent-code case.
Gate: rc 0, **228** banners,
123,463,565 modeled cases. Census 356
-> 357.

### Step 0484 - a needed hypothesis was
mis-describing which arenas it covers

Step 0484 corrects a docstring that
overstated a hypothesis's scope (census
355 -> 356).
`arm64_stack_arena_tag_guard_is_window
_guard` claimed its whole-word condition
held for "both the enabled 160-byte and
the disabled 1-byte arena". The 1-byte
arena is not a whole number of words,
and the equivalence genuinely fails
there: at capacity 1 slot 0 is
addressable (`tagSlotFits 1 (words 1)`
is true) while a one-byte window at
index 1 does not fit (`windowFits 1 1 1`
is false), because a slot covers eight
addressable indices and the arena covers
one byte.

So unlike the implication widened in
Step 0483, this hypothesis is
load-bearing -- dropping it makes the
statement false, verified by `bv_decide`
finding a counterexample at capacity
`2^32 - 1` in the neighbouring lemma too.
The counterexample is now a theorem so
the claim cannot drift back, and the
docstring says why the condition is
necessary here but not there. Gate:
rc 0, 227 banners, 1,983 theorems.
Census 355 -> 356.

### Step 0483 - a theorem covered only one
of the two arenas it describes

Step 0483 widens a hypothesis that was
stronger than needed (census 354 ->
355). `arm64_stack_arena_window_implies
_tag_slot` -- the theorem that lets a
checked write cover both the arena and
the tag array with one test -- required
`capacity % 8 = 0`. The enabled
160-byte arena satisfies that; the
1-byte arena the arm64 header declares
in its `#else` branch does not. So the
theorem did not cover an arena the
simulator actually defines.

The precondition turns out to be
unnecessary. `index + width <=
capacity` gives `index < capacity`,
and `capacity <= words capacity * 8`
always, so `index / 8` is below the
slot count. The general form needs
only that the slot count's `+7` does
not wrap, which every arena in the
tree satisfies. Both forms are present,
the general one plus a witness at
capacity 1 -- the case the strict form
missed. Gate: rc 0, 227 banners,
1,982 theorems. Census 354 -> 355.

### Step 0482 - the tag vocabularies are
pinned across the ISAs

Step 0482 applies Step 0481's shape to
the provenance tags (census 353 -> 354).
Both simulators define a tag per
register, as independent hand-written
`#define`s: neither header includes the
other, and no generated contract binds
them. Seven names are shared and carry
the same code on both sides; a drift in
either header would silently change what
a tag means on one ISA while every
per-ISA theorem kept holding.

The vocabularies are deliberately not
identical, and the oracle states the
difference rather than assuming
uniformity: codes 0--6 are the shared
seven (`SCALAR`, `ABI`, `PACKET`,
`PACKET_END`, `STACK`, `MAP_PTR`,
`MAP_VALUE`), code 7 is `RELOC_ADDR` on
arm64 and `HELPER_ID` on x86, and code
8 is `RODATA_ADDR` on arm64 only. The
collision is safe because no table is
indexed by tag across the two simulators
and no comparison mixes their constants;
all three ISA-specific tags are live
(78, 27 and 17 uses).

`cross_isa_tag_host.c` includes both
headers and pins the seven shared codes
plus the code-7 divergence, 10 cases.
Renumbering `ARM64_SIM_TAG_PACKET` to 9
makes it fail. This is the first oracle
to include both simulator headers at
once. Gate: rc 0, **227** banners,
123,463,541 modeled cases. Census 353
-> 354.

Step 0481 closes a cross-ISA gap

header and Lean module. A drift in one
-- a mask one bit wide, a bit count
off by one -- would make the simulators
disagree about what an 8-bit write
means while every per-ISA theorem kept
holding, because nothing compared them.

`CrossIsaWidth.lean` states the
agreement over all ten generated
definitions (`code`, `mask`, `signMask`,
`bits`, `narrow`, `zero`, `sign`,
`absentCode`, `defaultCode`,
`effective`) through a constructor map
between the two `Width` types. It is
purely a comparison; it does not
duplicate either contract. Verified by
planting a 16-bit bit-count of 17 on
the x86 side, which fails `bits_agrees`
and `sign_agrees` -- so it gates spec
drift rather than restating.

Wired into the recipe after both

### Step 0480 - the dispatch ladder's
depth costs nothing

Step 0480 measures what the dispatch
chain costs rather than assuming
(census 351 -> 352).
`X86_SIM_L_EXEC` is a 56-arm `else if`
chain and `ARM64_SIM_L_EXEC` a 34-arm
one, so `X86_OP_XCHG` at arm 49 walks
49 predicates per emulated instruction,
and the obvious follow-up question is
what that costs.

Nothing measurable. At `-O2` the chain
compiles to one indirect `jmp *` and
two `cmp`s -- a flat jump table, not a
linear scan -- and in a loop-carried
benchmark `XCHG` at arm 49 runs at
0.31 ns/op against `NOP` at arm 1 at
the same 0.31. So reordering the arms,
which the generated tables make easy,
would buy nothing, and the ladder's
length is a readability question rather
than a performance one. Recorded because
the answer was assumed. Gate: rc 0, 226
banners. Census 351 -> 352.

### Step 0479 - the x86 dispatch chain's
missing else is documented

Step 0479 records a design decision
that was only discoverable from two
test files (census 350 -> 351).
`X86_SIM_L_EXEC` has no final `else`,
so an opcode that matches no dispatch
predicate is a silent no-op. Driving
`X86_OP_JCC`, `X86_OP_RET`, and
`X86_OP_CALL` through the chain
confirms it: the state comes back
untouched.

That looks like a fail-fast
violation -- the repo requires an
unsupported capability to exit 1, and
the AArch64 chain does have an
unsupported hook -- but it is
deliberate and pinned: both dispatch
route hosts drive `X86_OP_RET`, which
has no arm, and require the whole
state to be byte-identical to its seed,
and their comments say so. Adding an
`else` arm, which is the obvious
"fix", invalidates both hosts; that
was verified by adding one and
reverting.

It is also not a fail-fast violation
in substance: the encoder raises
`unsupported mnemonic` before emitting
an opcode it cannot lower, so only a
decoded-but-unarmed opcode reaches the
chain, and by the hosts' definition
that is a no-op. The rationale now
sits at the chain rather than only in
the tests. Gate: rc 0, 226 banners.
Census 350 -> 351.

### Step 0468 - the two helper-argument
pointer contracts differ on purpose

Step 0468 documents an
ISA asymmetry that had no written
rationale (census 339 -> 340). No
contract, proof, or simulator change;
the deliverable is the measurement
that shows the asymmetry is required
rather than an oversight.

`X86_SIM_L_HELPER_ARG_PTR` and
`ARM64_SIM_L_HELPER_ARG_PTR` look
like they should be one contract. The
AArch64 helper rebases a stack-tagged
register into the arena before the
call; the x86-64 helper is the
identity on the register's pointer.
That is correct for both, because the
two register files hold different
things under the stack tag, and the
difference is measurable: with a
register holding frame offset `-8`,
the AArch64 helper hands the callee
arena byte `88` (bias 96 plus the
offset), while on x86-64
`mov %rsp, %rax` already stored a
real arena address, so the tagged
register holds a pointer with an arena
delta of `56` (capacity 64 plus the
offset) and passing it through is the
right action. Rebasing the x86 value
again would double-apply the capacity
bias; dropping the AArch64 rebase
would hand the callee a bare offset.
A change that "unified" the two would
move one ISA's helper arguments by the
capacity.

Both numbers are measured from the
committed headers, not derived on
paper. The paper's AArch64
helper-argument paragraph cited a
14-case and a 786-case oracle and a
36-mutation binding battery; all
three re-measured against the tree
and all three match, and the
paragraph now says the x86-64 helper
is deliberately different rather than
leaving the asymmetry implicit.

That check also found a rendering
defect outside the harness: three
spans in `4-safety.tex` used Markdown
emphasis (`*window*`, `*strictly*`,
`*not*`), which LaTeX typesets as
literal asterisks -- two of them
introduced by this session's Steps
0463 and 0466. All three now use
`\emph`, and a sweep of every
section finds no remaining Markdown
emphasis. Gate: rc 0, 226 `cross-check:
OK` banners. Census 339 -> 340.

### Step 0466 - stack bound relationships

Step 0466 proves how the three
stack bounds relate, instead of
leaving the relationship to
inspection (census 337 -> 338). No
simulator code changes; this is a
proof-only step over the existing
contracts.

Three results. First, a stack
*write* that fits its window always
lands in a tag slot the tag array
holds: `index + width <= capacity`
gives `index < capacity`, and the
last slot of an arena whose capacity
is a whole number of words is the
last tag slot. That is why
`ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_WRITE_TAG` carries
only the window guard, while the tag
*read* needs the slot guard -- a read
carries no width, so it can name the
one-past-end index, which is the slot
past the array.

Second, `pointer_weaker_than_window`
was stated with a nonempty-width
hypothesis that the proof never used,
and its docstring described the
converse of what it proved. A fitting
window names a valid arena pointer at
*any* width, since `index + width <=
capacity` already gives `index <=
capacity`; the hypothesis is gone and
the statement says what it means.

Third, the weakness is *strict*:
the one-past-end index is a valid
pointer but starts no nonempty
window (`pointerFits capacity capacity
= true ∧ windowFits capacity 1 capacity
= false`, for a capacity whose
successor does not wrap), with
concrete witnesses at the 160-byte and
64-byte framings. That strictness is
the reason the pointer helper keeps a
check separate from the window guard
rather than relying on it. Eight new
theorems, no `sorry`, no warnings.
Gate: rc 0, 226 `cross-check: OK`
banners, 123,463,285 modeled cases
(unchanged -- the theorems live in
already-compiled modules), 1970
theorems. Census 337 -> 338.

### Step 0465 - stack pointer bound (both ISAs)

Step 0465 closes the fourth and last
unguarded stack path (census 336 ->
337). Steps 0463 and 0464 bounded
every *access* -- the byte window,
the word view, the tag slot -- but
`ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_PTR` and
`X86_SIM_L_STACK_PTR` also hand out
`&b[index]` for a stack-pointer
register, and an 8-byte write through
a pointer at index 168 of the
160-byte arena escapes the array.
ASan reports it as a
`WRITE of size 8` against
`__a64_stack` on the previous
baseline.

The bound is deliberately weaker
than an access's. `&b[index]` is
well defined up to and including the
one-past-end index, so the contract
fixes `INDEX <= CAPACITY`; a window
needs `INDEX + WIDTH <= CAPACITY`.
Both arena specs gained
`pointer_guard: index_le_capacity`
and the generators emit a single
comparison widened to 64 bits, so a
negative index fails the same test
rather than letting the compiler fold
a branch away for one call site's
type (which `-Wtype-limits` caught on
the first attempt). The hand modules
prove the guard refines an
independent statement, the
one-past-end rule on a capacity whose
successor does not wrap, and that the
pointer bound is strictly weaker than
the window bound for any nonempty
window -- which is why the two
helpers carry separate checks rather
than sharing one.

Both helpers test it on the *biased*
index: the arena index is the offset
plus the capacity, so testing the raw
offset let every negative offset
through (ASan found that too, at index
`2285946441` -- a 32-bit truncation of
a negative 64-bit sum).

Five hosts had been driving pointers
outside the arena, which the bound
rejects. The arm64 helper-argument
sweep ran to index 248 of a 160-byte
arena and its arena sweep to 192 --
both now stop at the one-past-end
index. The x86 lea and mov sweeps had
*no* in-range row at all on the stack
arm (their displacements and sources
all resolve outside a 64-byte frame),
so that arm is driven by its own
in-range displacements and sources;
without that the arm would have been
silently untested, and
`mut_x86_stack_region`'s
`sim_site3_pin_rbp` and
`sim_site3_tag_repaint` rows caught
exactly that by surviving. Two hosts
also left the decoder's index lane
(RCX) holding a pattern pointer, which
the lea `AUX=X86_LEA_AUX_RODATA` byte
1 selects as index register 1; both
now plant it, as the specialization
host already did. Fourteen batteries
re-ran clean, two with anchors this
change moved. Gate: rc 0, 226
`cross-check: OK` banners,
123,463,285 modeled cases (the total
*fell*, because the corrected sweeps
drive fewer out-of-range rows),
1965 theorems. Census 336 -> 337.

### Step 0464 - stack tag-array bound (arm64)

Step 0464 closes the third unguarded
stack path in the arm64 simulator
(census 335 -> 336). Step 0463
bounded the byte window and the
word view, but `__a64_stack_tag[]`
is a *slot* array: one byte per word
slot, `TAG_SLOTS(CAPACITY)` entries.
A tag access at a byte index at or
past the capacity resolves to slot
`TAG_SLOTS`, one past the array, and
ASan reports the read against
`__a64_stack_tag` on the previous
baseline -- the same defect class as
0463, on a different array.

The fix goes through the same
generated-contract path rather than a
hand check. `arm64_stack_arena_spec.
json` gained `tag_slot_guard:
word_index_lt_tag_slots`, so the
generator emits `KPROG_ARM64_STACK_
TAG_SLOT_FITS`. `Arm64StackArena.lean`
restates it independently as "the
slot is below the array length" and
proves the generated form equal to
it, proves the largest tag slot is
the word holding the arena's final
byte (`words - 1 = (capacity - 1)
>>> 3`, via the round-up floor
identity), and proves the tag guard
equals the window guard at a one-byte
width -- so the tag array is tied to
the already-proved window bound
rather than carrying a second
inequality of its own. Five new
theorems, no `sorry`.

`ARM64_SIM_L_STACK_READ_TAG` now
tests the bound before indexing,
reports an out-of-range slot through
the unsupported-access hook, and
falls back to `ARM64_SIM_TAG_SCALAR`
without touching the array. The
fallback matters for the same reason
it did in 0463: the hook returns.
Under ASan, the last slot (index 159,
slot 19) is clean and index 160
reports and returns SCALAR with no
out-of-bounds read. `test_arm64_
stack_arena_host` gained slot
coverage (71352 -> 71558 cases); its
independent restatement is the slot
bound, not `index < capacity`, which
would be wrong because indices alias
into one slot (index 1 is slot 0 of
the 1-byte arena). Sabotaging the
generated guard (`slots` to `slots +
1`) turns the banner red at 32
mismatches. Seven stack batteries
re-ran clean, two with anchors this
change moved. Gate: rc 0, 226
`cross-check: OK` banners, 123,468,293
modeled cases (+206 is this coverage),
1958 theorems. Census 335 -> 336.

### Step 0463 - stack access-window bound (both ISAs)

Step 0463 closes the stack-window
memory-safety gap the harness README
had recorded as open, and does it
through the generated-contract path
rather than a hand check (census
334 -> 335). Both arena specs gain
`window_guard:
index_plus_bytes_le_capacity`, so
`generate_{arm64,x86}_stack_arena_
spec.py` emit `KPROG_*_STACK_
WINDOW_END` and `KPROG_*_STACK_
WINDOW_FITS`; the comparison is
widened to 64 bits so an access near
the top of the 32-bit index space is
measured rather than wrapping (a
32-bit sum there falsely accepts the
window, which `bv_decide` found).
The hand modules restate the bound
as `index <= capacity && capacity -
index >= width` and prove the
generated form equal to it, that a
fitting window's last byte is inside
the arena, that an access at the
arena's final byte does not fit, and
the concrete thresholds: 152/8/160
fits and 153/8/160 does not on
AArch64, 56/8/64 and 57/8/64 on the
default x86-64 frame, 120/8/128 and
121/8/128 on the deep frame.

Both simulators now route their
stack paths through it. `ARM64_SIM_L_
STACK_READ` and `ARM64_SIM_L_
STACK_WRITE_TAG` test `ARM64_SIM_L_
STACK_WINDOW_OK` first, report an
unfitting window through the existing
`arm64_sim_unsupported_opcode` hook,
and take a zero value without
touching the arena; that last part
is load-bearing, because the hook
returns, so reporting alone still ran
the access (ASan caught exactly
that on the first attempt).
`X86_SIM_L_STACK_READ` and
`X86_SIM_L_STACK_WRITE` test the
same bound and trap. Under ASan the
previously over-running reads now
report through the guard with no
out-of-bounds access and the last
fitting access is unchanged.

The arena hosts gained the coverage
the gap needed: `test_arm64_stack_
arena_host` (70558 -> 71352 cases)
and `test_x86_stack_arena_host`
(70571 -> 71533) drive the window
test at every grid capacity, index,
and width, plus the boundary rows;
sabotaging the generated comparison
(adding 1 to the capacity argument)
turns both banners red (15 and 17
mismatches), so the new rows are
gated rather than decorative. One
host had been driving windows outside
the arena while asserting the
opposite: `test_x86_mem_dispatch_
route_host.c` swept displacements
{0, -8, -32, 32, 56} against the
64-byte arena, so three of five put
the read at or past the end; the
sweep is now {-8, -16, -32, -64} and
the indexed case uses -16 so the
scaled index still fits at every
width. Eleven stack batteries re-ran
clean, including `mut_arm64_stack_
arena` (62 rows) and `mut_x86_stack_
arena` (28 rows); the two whose
anchors the change moved are updated
to the new text, and the arena
battery's exact-case-count banner is
read as a shape, since pinning the
number made its baseline fail
whenever the host grew coverage it
already gates. Gate: rc 0, 226
`cross-check: OK` banners,
123,468,087 modeled cases (the
+1,752 is this coverage), 1952
theorems. Census 334 -> 335.

The stranded-header hazard that blocked the gate is
reproducible rather than mysterious: a battery
repaints a simulator header, then runs a detector,
then restores. A `finally` block covers an
exception but not SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP, so a
battery killed mid-mutation leaves the repainted
body in the header and the next run measures that
mutant as its baseline. Measured directly on
`mut_arm64_helper_body.py`: killing it with SIGTERM
left `b7ce6a66d` (`ARM64_X0, 1` in
`bpf_trace_printk`) in the otherwise clean header,
and re-running would have reported a false
baseline. `mut_arm64_helper_body.py` now converts
those three signals into `KeyboardInterrupt` so its
guard restores, and the same SIGTERM test now
leaves the header byte-identical (`1de5665a5`) with
an empty `git status`. The other 329 batteries have
the `finally` guard but no signal handler (316
carry `finally:` at all, none uses `atexit`), so
the same interruption can strand any of them; this
is the most likely origin of the currently dirty
`x86_sim_local_bpf.h` line: that edit is verbatim a
row of `build/mut_x86_route.py`, i.e. an unrestored
mutation, not a hand edit.

That diagnosis is now confirmed rather than likely.
The dirty line is byte-identical to the `rep` half
of the row `equiv stack-write byte0 lane repaint
(no narrow-write scene)` (`build/mut_x86_route.py`
lines 415-419), including the padding before the
continuation backslash, and that battery has no
signal handler and no `try/finally` around
`mutate`/`detect_route` - only a `restore()` before
each row and one after the loop - so a signal
between `mutate` and `restore` leaves exactly this
line. Running `make check` over the dirty tree
reproduces the consequence: the x86 stack arm route
host fails with 45 arena-byte mismatches at
`index 61-63` (`got 0 want <value>`), precisely the
narrow-write scene the row's own name says is absent.
Against the committed header the same gate is rc 0
with 226 `cross-check: OK` banners and zero new core
files, so the failure belongs to the stranded
mutation and nothing in this step.

Core-dump fix: 22 arm64 host tests verify an
unsupported arm by forking a child that calls
`abort()`. With `ulimit -c unlimited` every child
wrote a core, about 240 per test per run - 21313
files and 7.0 GB had accumulated under
`kprog/formal/` before this was noticed. Each of
the 22 tests now includes the tracked header
`test_core_dumps.h`, whose constructor sets
`RLIMIT_CORE` to zero; the limit is inherited by
every forked child, so the fix covers `make check`,
a battery's own host build, and an interactive run,
where a per-recipe `ulimit -c 0` prefix would only
cover the first. The backlog was deleted; a full
gate and a 0455 battery run now each add zero cores.
